World.title: Cuban artist and dissident exiled from country after 5 years in prison arrives in US
World.content:
Cuban artist and dissident exiled from country after 5 years in prison arrives in US

toggle caption David Santiago/AP

MIAMI — A famous Cuban dissident artist and musician, Luis Manuel Otero Alcántara, arrived in Miami on Saturday after being released from a five-year prison sentence on the condition that he leave his country.

Alcántara, 38, was greeted at the airport by a crowd that was cheering, singing and holding their phones high in the air to get a photo of him. They draped him in a Cuban flag, printed with the words "Patria y Vida" — "Homeland and Life" — the title of a song he shared a Grammy for that became an anthem for Cuba's political opposition against repression.

Sponsor Message

The United States granted him parole into the country earlier this week, according to a social media page maintained by his friends and supporters. They wrote that he accepted exile as the only way to escape persecution and continue his art and activism.

Alcántara co-founded a group of Havana artists, writers and musicians called the San Isidro Movement — named for the neighborhood where Alcántara lived.

He was arrested on July 11, 2021, during a public protest. In 2022, a court sentenced him to five years in prison for public disorder, contempt and disrespect toward national symbols.

His arrest and incarceration had long been denounced by human rights organizations and the U.S. government. Groups including Amnesty International called him a political prisoner, an allegation the Cuban government rejected.

Alcántara was held in a maximum-security prison, he said, and was expected to be released last week. But for days, advocates said they still could not contact him and did not know where he was.

The organization Cubalex, which legally advises dissidents and reports human rights violations from outside of the country, filed a habeas corpus petition on his behalf Monday.

Until he boarded a plane Saturday, his advocates were not sure of his location, or if he was truly free.

Sponsor Message

His said his first stop on American soil would be at the Shrine of Our Lady of Charity to make an offering.

Other political prisoners remained imprisoned, including his fellow artist Maykel "Osorbo" Castillo Pérez, his advocates said, and they hoped Alcántara's release would prompt insistence that Pérez also be set free.

Alcántara brought from Cuba a broken statue of the Virgin Mary, which he described as a symbol of hope and healing, a chance to put back together something from fragments.

World.title: MLS works to bring in a new generation of fans as the World Cup comes to an end
World.content:
MLS works to bring in a new generation of fans as the World Cup comes to an end

toggle caption Ethan Swope/AP

CHICAGO — For the past five weeks, a bar in Chicago's West Loop neighborhood has become one of the country's biggest World Cup watch parties, with lines stretching around the block for the biggest games.

This is all the doing of Chicago's Major League Soccer club, the Fire. By the time the final whistle is blown on the World Cup between Argentina and Spain on Sunday, an estimated 60,000 people or more will have come through at some point in the summer for a taste of World Cup fever.

This watch party and others like it around the country are one piece of Major League Soccer's efforts to capitalize on this World Cup summer here in the U.S.

Sponsor Message

Hosting the 1994 World Cup was transformative for the sport of soccer in the United States. World Cup fever led millions of children to 

Since then, the league has done decades of work to grow its fanbase and stature in the world of soccer. MLS kicked off in 1996 with 10 teams; last season it reached 30 teams, the same number as Major League Baseball and the NBA. In the early years, only a few dozen games were on TV each season; today, every game is televised on Apple TV.

Now, MLS hopes that 2026 can be just as transformative as 1994. The question is: how?

toggle caption Caleb Bowlin/Getty Images

The Costco free sample experience

The Chicago Fire had a puzzle to solve. The FIFA World Cup was coming back to the United States — and with it would come a once-in-a-generation opportunity to use the world's largest sporting event as a potent accelerant to grow its fanbase, like harnessing a cart to a rocket ship.

Sponsor Message

But Chicago would not host any games, having sat out the bidding process at the behest of Mayor Rahm Emanuel, who found FIFA's demands for expensive renovations to the city's premier stadium, Soldier Field, too much to ask of city taxpayers.

"At the end of the day, this is the biggest sporting event in the world that takes place once every four years. And it's not happening in Chicago," said Dave Baldwin, the Fire's president of business operations.

"And we had a decision to make," he said. "One was to just bury our head in the sand and just watch on TV like everyone else, or the other one was to really rally behind it, put some dollars behind it."

In the end, the Chicago Fire put just under $3 million to build up the space at the bar, called Recess. It is massive, with ample space indoors and out. In the center of the patio stands what looks like a jumbotron plucked from an arena nearby and set it down on a platform, with all four sides showing that day's game. Around the space are Chicago Fire decorations, sign-up sheets, contests and team merch for sale.

"I compare converting non-soccer fans to soccer fans to my experience when I go shopping at Costco, which is I never knew that I needed 800 teriyaki meatballs, but I was walking through the line, I had a chance to sample, and I said, 'Oh my gosh, this is amazing,' and I go buy one of those giant boxes," Baldwin said. "I have met very few people that come out to a match and don't want to come back."

As the MLS season kicks back into gear, 22 clubs are running a promotion called "First Match on Us" or "Next Match On Us," with free tickets for first-time attendees.

Sponsor Message

Casual sports fans view soccer differently today than they did in the 1990s, said Brian Bilello, the president of the New England Revolution, one of the teams participating in the promotion.

Bilello played a key role in bringing World Cup matches to Gillette Stadium, the home of both the Revolution and the New England Patriots. The stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts, also hosted France and Brazil in a pre-World Cup tune-up friendly in March. The Revolution saw the World Cup as an opportunity to attract fans who aren't diehard soccer followers, but rather the Boston sports fan who simply had yet to try a Revs game.

"One of the most important fans that we need to grow collectively in our league is that core sports fan that also likes soccer. In 1994, I don't think those fans were open to that. They were just like, 'Ah, soccer sucks. I don't like soccer,'" said Bilello. "That doesn't really exist as much anymore."

toggle caption Carmen Mandato/Getty Images

The Messi effect

This week, Major League Soccer rolled out an ambitious, eight-figure marketing campaign called "Thanks World, We'll Take It From Here." It includes a star-studded commercial that aired during both semifinal games and will run again during Sunday's final, which is expected to be watched by tens of millions of American viewers.

The centerpiece of the ad is Lionel Messi, the 39-year-old global superstar and captain of the Argentina national team. In 2023, Messi left a wildly successful career in Europe to join the MLS club Inter Miami, a blockbuster move that has already paid dividends for the league as a whole, with attendance and viewership up since his arrival.

"There were a lot of people that thought he was coming here to retire, and it's been the opposite," said Camilo Durana, the league's chief business officer. "Rarely do you see him getting subbed off. He wants to play the 90 minutes. He's intense. He wants to win."

Sponsor Message

Messi's performance in the World Cup has been another  for MLS, Durana said. Argentina will play in Sunday's final against Spain; a win would be its second consecutive title with Messi at the helm and he's in the running to win the Golden Boot race for most goals scored in the tournament. Messi has scored eight times and is in second place behind France's Kylian Mbappé, who has ten goals.

"What Messi's arrival did — and what this World Cup we believe will do — is it'll encourage more players to come," Durana said.

Players are the other big audience MLS is targeting with this World Cup. Even as its quality of play has improved dramatically over the years, MLS is still dogged by a reputation for being a tier or two below Europe's domestic leagues.

MLS was directly involved in the U.S. bid for this World Cup to ensure that its teams' facilities would be front and center in the hosting plan.

Each host stadium was paired with nearby soccer facilities for visiting teams to train in the days immediately preceding each game; MLS worked to ensure those venues were, as often as possible, MLS team stadiums or training centers. (Other venue training sites included Division I college soccer facilities, municipal sporting complexes and one NWSL stadium, the Kansas City Current.)

Additionally, each World Cup team chose a base camp in North America to stay and train between games. Many chose MLS facilities. That included high-profile teams like Argentina, which stayed in Kansas City to train at a Sporting Kansas City center, and Brazil, which trained at Red Bull New York's state-of-the-art Columbia Park Training Facility in New Jersey.

toggle caption Juan Mabromata/AFP via Getty Images

The goal was to show top-flight players from around the world what life could be like in MLS.

"Players talk," said Durana. "Often before a player is transferred, they ask around and ask people what they think. So it's really important for us that players have great experiences as they experience the World Cup."

Sponsor Message

Many American soccer fans still prefer watching higher-tier European leagues like the English Premier League or Germany's Bundesliga. But improving the quality of players in MLS could lead to higher-quality competition — which then would draw more fans, MLS hopes.

"Major League Soccer players scored 10 goals in the group stage, and so I think that validates everything that we're doing, and it shows the quality that we have on the MLS pitch," Durana said.

World.title: Saskatchewan Roughriders linebacker and captain Jayden Dalke killed in crash
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Saskatchewan Roughriders are mourning linebacker and team captain Jayden Dalke, who died in a car crash Saturday evening.

The team announced his death in a statement Sunday.

"A relentless warrior on the field, Jayden's determination, toughness and work ethic inspired his teammates, who cared deeply for him and are heartbroken by his passing," the statement said.

"Jayden had a unique gift of making the people around him feel special and valued," the team said. "No one ever left a conversation with him without a smile."

The team said Dalke, 30, was "the true definition of what it means to be a Saskatchewan Roughrider," and offered condolences to a family that "traveled the country to watch Jayden live his dream."

Dalke grew up in Leduc, Alta., and played junior football with the Edmonton Wildcats before three seasons with the University of Alberta Golden Bears, where he was named a U Sports all-Canadian.

Roughriders linebacker and captain Jayden Dalke, who was killed in a crash Saturday night. (Submitted by Saskatchewan Roughriders)

Greg McCullough co-hosts the Piffles Podcast, a Roughriders fan show he's been working on for 11 years, and said his phone started going off Sunday.

McCullough said he was “gutted” to hear the news. "A guy that's 30, literally cut down in his prime."

He said he knew Dalke's family. They started following the podcast after Dalke was drafted in 2022, commenting online and turning up in person. At this year's home opener, he said, they were tailgating three stalls away.

"His dad came and brought us some watermelon," McCullough said. "There's a family hurting."

The Roughriders are scheduled to return to the field on Thursday, which will be an emotional game, McCullough says.

"You have to think it is going to be a struggle all week. Losing a brother in arms, a guy that was just there before and now you got an empty locker," he said.

"You've got a spot that someone else is going to definitely fill in, but it's not the guy [who] used to be a team captain, like a Grey Cup champion."

League, team tributes

The Canadian Football League (CFL) also released a statement Sunday afternoon. "It is with tremendous sadness that we share the tragic news of Jayden’s passing. He was a passionate competitor who played with incredible heart," the league said.

"Off the field, he will be remembered for his leadership in the locker room and his dedication to the community. "

The CFL said that it has lost a teammate, a Canadian brother and a friend. The league extended condolences to Dalke's family, friends and all those knew him.

The Winnipeg Blue Bombers paid their respects in a social media statement. The organization said it's heartbroken to learn of the passing of Dalke.

"Our thoughts are with the Saskatchewan Roughriders, Jayden’s teammates and coaches, and most of all with his family during this incredibly difficult time."

The B.C. Lions also posted on social media, saying "there are moments bigger than the game, and today we lost a brother."

World.title: Spain fires past Argentina in extra time to win World Cup final, denying Messi a 2nd straight title
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Ferran Torres' first goal of this year's World Cup was the goal of his life, and it put Spain back atop the soccer world. Denying Lionel Messi a second straight title in what he has indicated would be his final World Cup match, Torres came off the bench and scored in the 106th minute and Spain — in a match it simply dominated — ended Argentina's reign with a 1-0 win on Sunday. Torres pounced on a bouncing ball in the box and used his left foot to bury a shot just under the crossbar and into the back of the net. "It was a goal scored by 47 million people," Torres said, referring to Spain's population. Maybe not by them — but certainly for them. It was Spain's second title, this trophy getting added to the one claimed in 2010. And there's no question about the centre of the soccer universe now, not after this display. Spain allowed only one goal in eight matches at the tournament, setting a World Cup record for fewest goals allowed by a champion. And this title, combined with the World Cup won by Spain's women in 2023, makes the European nation the first to hold both the men's and women's titles simultaneously. "I feel sad," said Messi, who was moved to tears after receiving his runner-up medal and staring into the crowd at Argentina supporters. "They were better, to be honest." The score indicates this match was close, but only one team was in command. Spain took the game's first 20 shots on goal before Argentina — desperate for an equalizer — got its first attempt off in the second half of extra time. Spain took nine of the game's first 10 corner kicks, and only a World Cup final-record 12 saves by Argentina goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez gave the 2022 champions a shot at going back-to-back. Ferran Torres celebrates his match-deciding goal for Spain against Argentina in the 2026 World Cup final at New York/New Jersey Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., on Sunday. (Franck Fife/AFP via Getty Images) Spain is now unbeaten in its last 38 matches — 29 wins, nine draws — and now is the outright holder of the longest such streak by any European team ever. Italy went 37 matches (28 wins, nine draws) from October 2018 through September 2021, before Spain ended that streak. And for the last two-plus years, nobody has beaten Spain. Not even Messi. An Argentina team that was the kings of the late-game rally in this tournament had no answer this time. Messi took a corner kick with about four minutes left before the final whistle and the ball took a fortunate skip toward reserve Giuliano Simeone — who sent it high and over the crossbar, holding his head in disbelief afterward. "When you have Messi on the other side, well, you are nervous," Torres said. "At the end of the day, we always depended on us. We always come up with our football, and we showed it again." The win made Spain coach Luis de la Fuente, at 65, the oldest coach ever to lead a team to the World Cup title. "We are world champions," de la Fuente said. "It was together we reached this stage." WATCH | Donnovan Bennett's essay on 2026 World Cup: The 2026 World Cup: Terrific and toxic | Duration 2:01 CBC Sports' Donnovan Bennett writes this essay on the chaos that was the 2026 World Cup, and how despite all its shortcomings, brought people together. There was some pushing and shoving after the final whistle, which was quickly cleaned up and Spain commenced its celebration as most Argentina players sat on the turf in disbelief. Cooler heads prevailed, and Spain's players lined up minutes later to form an honor guard of sorts for Argentina's squad to walk through on its way to the stage for the runner-up medals. Enzo Fernandez was sent off in second-half stoppage time after getting his second yellow card, meaning Argentina was forced to finish the match with only 10 players. Fernandez was carded for a reckless play that sent Spain defender Pau Cubarsi cartwheeling into the air, and the card came out immediately. It was the 104th and last match of the biggest World Cup ever, a 48-team event that played out over the U.S., Canada and Mexico. Because there were more matches than any previous World Cup, it was no surprise that there were more goals than all other editions — more than 300, nearly three per match. Except, of course, when Spain was involved. Spain's plan was simple and flawless: Hold the ball as much as possible, denying opponents any hint of chances. It worked, all the way to the end. "There is sadness, but also the knowledge that we gave it our all," Argentina coach Lionel Scaloni said. "I could say a lot about how we got here, but it's not worth it. I am eternally grateful to these guys; they competed right to the end. The other team was better." Spain came into this tournament considered as one of the favourites, and with the full belief it could end Argentina's reign. It had to go through the game's greatest player — maybe ever — to make good on that promise. End of the Messi era? Messi is 39 and the math certainly suggests that the Inter Miami star is at the end of his international career. There have been hints — such as Messi himself declaring that a home World Cup qualifying match against Venezuela last year would be his final competitive contest for Argentina on his nation's soil. "I experienced a lot of things on this pitch, good and not so good," Messi said that night. "I'll take the good with me." In the Messi era, there was a lot of good. A lot of great, actually. There was the World Cup title in 2022, obviously topping the list. There was the Olympic gold medal at the 2008 Beijing Games. The two Copa America titles, the first in 2021 and the second in 2024. He won Argentina's player of the year award 16 times in a span of 19 years, first winning it as a teenager and continuing to win it all the way into his late 30s. He's a legend within the game and on all corners of the globe. But Spain was better Sunday. "I spoke to my players, and they said: `Look, we've won everything, coach. We've won everything,"' de la Fuente said. "And that is beautiful." The spectacle was not limited to simply soccer. There was a halftime show, a first for FIFA. There were a ton of celebrities there from stage, screen and sports: Brad Pitt, Tom Cruise, Matt Damon, Cillian Murphy, Daniel Craig, Stephen Curry, Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander, Jalen Brunson, Kevin Durant, Serena Williams, Carlos Alcaraz, David Beckham, Zinedine Zidane and dozens more. Prime Minister Mark Carney and his wife Diana Fox Carney watched the game from a glassed-in suite. Today, the FIFA World Cup comes to a close.

Hundreds of thousands of fans packed the streets of Vancouver, Toronto, and communities across the country to watch the beautiful game and cheer on Team Canada — who played with extraordinary character, resilience, and grit.

Our… pic.twitter.com/QXEjK3Ytnk —MarkJCarney As the match kicked off, Carney posted a message on social media noting how hundreds of thousands of fans packed streets across the country to cheer on Canada. The national squad played with "extraordinary character, resilience, and grit," the prime minister's post read. "Our team and our fans showed the world that Canada belongs on any pitch, against any team," it continued. "Canada's soccer journey is just beginning. The best is yet to come." They came to see a show. So did 80,000 other people, not to mention perhaps as many as 2 billion watching around the globe. Spain didn't disappoint. No team has won back-to-back men's World Cups since Brazil in 1958 and 1962, and Spain kept Argentina from pulling off that repeat. "We are gracious in victory," Scaloni said, "and we must be gracious in defeat."

World.title: U.S. military death toll rises amid renewed conflict with Iran
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Get the latest on CBCNews.ca, the CBC News App, and CBC News Network for breaking news and analysis.1 An American service member was killed Saturday in Iraq during "controlled detonation" of a downed Iranian drone, the U.S. military said Sunday, just a day after announcing the deaths of two other U.S. service members following an Iranian attack on a base in Jordan. Sunday's announcement brings the death toll of U.S. service members to 17 during the conflict with Iran. More than 430 American troops have been wounded. Step by step, the U.S. and Iran have returned closer to all-out war as last month's interim deal meant to permanently end the fighting has crumbled and shipping traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has largely stalled. Both sides have targeted civilian infrastructure relied on by millions of people. Earlier, the military said its strikes targeted Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) to retaliate for Friday's killing of troops in Jordan. One service member was missing after that attack, and the military's new statement said "unidentified remains" were found Sunday and were being examined. A U.S. warship fires a round from an unknown location in this screen grab taken from a handout video released Saturday. (U.S. Central Command/Reuters) The renewed exchanges of fire, now in their second week, have seen the U.S. target bridges, water desalination plants and electrical facilities in Iran. Tehran has hit U.S.-allied countries throughout the Middle East. Kuwait, Jordan and Bahrain again activated air defences for incoming Iranian drones and missiles. Israel warned that missiles launched toward neighbouring Jordan could cause fire to spill over into Israeli territory for the first time in weeks. Iran says nuclear site under construction struck The U.S. military's Central Command said it hit "Iranian military coastal surveillance and air defence facilities, maritime capabilities and missile and drone storage sites." It said the attack was designed to degrade Iran's ability to control the strait and "swiftly punish Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces," a power base in Iran's theocracy that controls its ballistic missile arsenal. Footage released by the U.S. military appeared to show strikes carried out by fighter jets and by Tomahawk cruise missiles launched from the sea. One target site appeared to be in a valley of a mountainous region. The IRGC often has missile bases and other military equipment tucked into mountain ranges. The Atomic Energy Organization of Iran condemned a U.S. attack on the site of a nuclear power plant under construction in Darkhovin, Iran's Mehr News Agency reported. The IAEA is looking into reports of an overnight attack on the construction site of a planned nuclear power plant in Darkhovin, Iran. The facility is in the very early stages of construction and contained no nuclear material when last visited by the IAEA.

While the reported… pic.twitter.com/Tdi5QxWcCE —iaeaorg Satellite images from Planet Labs PBC of the Darkhovin nuclear plant site showed earth clearing but little construction as of July 9. Iran did not previously announce it as being targeted. The International Atomic Energy Agency said it was investigating reports of an overnight attack, noting that the plant was in the early stages of construction. Iran targets Gulf neighbours Jordan's military said it shot down several Iranian missiles. The country hosts major U.S. bases and relies on U.S. air defence systems. The missiles did not cause casualties or damage, according to Jordan's military. Jordan later summoned Iran's chargé d'affaires to protest, state-run television reported. Israel's military said Iranian missiles launched toward the Jordanian port city of Aqaba just across the border could spill over, warning Israelis to expect the first air-raid sirens in weeks. Eilat, the Israeli city that neighbours Aqaba, cited security officials as saying two interceptors were launched from its outskirts to prevent the fall of debris. WATCH | CBC News in Iran: Reporting from inside Iran | Duration 6:46 In June, CBC senior international correspondent Margaret Evans and videographer Lyza Sale were granted rare access to report from inside Iran. Where they could travel and what they could report on was tightly controlled, but Iranian authorities had no editorial influence on the content and were not given access to CBC News material before it was published. During the latest fighting, Iran has focused attacks on U.S.-allied Arab states rather than Israel, which launched the war with the U.S. on Feb. 28. "We are prepared to immediately resume combat," the Israeli military chief of staff, Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, said. Kuwait said one of its power and water desalination plants was attacked for the second time in two days, causing fires. The Ministry of Electricity, Water and Renewable Energy said the power grid remains stable. In Kuwait, about 90 per cent of drinking water comes from desalination. In this handout photo, Kuwaiti Prime Minister Sheikh Ahmad Abdullah Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, second left, visits a person reportedly injured by an Iranian attack, in Kuwait City on Sunday. (Kuwait News Agency/Reuters) The secretary general of the six-nation Gulf Cooperation Council, Jasem Mohamed al-Budaiwi, has accused Iran of war crimes for strikes on infrastructure and civilian facilities. International humanitarian law generally protects civilian infrastructure such as bridges and power plants from attack, but such sites can lose protections if used for military purposes. In such cases, attacks must be proportionate and minimize civilian harm. Battle of Strait of Hormuz U.S. President Donald Trump has threatened to target Iran's power stations and bridges to try to compel Tehran to loosen its hold on the Strait of Hormuz, which saw one-fifth of global oil supplies transit before the war. Recent attacks suggest the U.S. military is carrying out that plan. In the past week, the U.S. reimposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports to halt its shipments of crude oil. The military on Saturday said it had redirected five ships and disabled one since then. A maritime organization overseen by the U.S. navy said on Sunday that the threat to mariners is severe after previous Iranian attacks, "with deliberate hostile action considered highly likely." It said traffic remained low, with eight transits on Saturday and three on Friday. The daily average before the war was almost 140. Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, in a statement on Saturday, warned of "unforgettable lessons" if the U.S. keeps attacking the Islamic Republic. An Iranian negotiator said Tehran was suspending its commitments to the interim deal and accused the U.S. of violating it. The halfway point has passed in the 60 days the deal set out to negotiate the permanent end of the war and other issues, including Iran's nuclear program. Iranian authorities on Sunday said at least 50 people have been killed and 517 wounded in the latest U.S. strikes. Iran has provided no overall information on its materiel losses. Far from the region, the war's effects on the prices of fuel and other goods have hit some of the world's most vulnerable areas hard.

World.title: 'Just dumbfounding': Tornado damages buildings, homes in central Alberta county
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A tornado touched down near Rocky Mountain House, Alta., Saturday evening, damaging multiple homes, businesses and trees in the area. CBC’s Nicole Healey has more from those impacted in the community.

Bryn Hansen was eating steak and potatoes for dinner with his grandmother Saturday evening, when they heard whipping winds, prompting them to hide in the basement.

When they returned upstairs, they saw tin swirling in the air as the tornado headed one way — and in the other direction, the destruction it wrought.

"All the buildings were gone. Just ruined," Hansen said.

He was grateful Sunday, as family and friends attended his grandparents' property to help clean up. The tornado damaged structures on their land, including his grandparents' shop, which was destroyed.

"Its been there my whole life," Hansen said. "Looking out the window and it just not being there anymore was just crazy."

Bryn Hansen says he's grateful family and friends are rallying to clean-up his grandparent's property after a tornado damaged structures on the land. (Nadeer Hashmi/CBC)

A tornado passed through parts of central Alberta Saturday evening, but particularly Clearwater County, a district about 210 kilometres southwest of Edmonton.

Environment Canada was tracking the thunderstorm from which the tornado stemmed. Around 5:20 p.m. MT, the agency issued a red tornado warning, describing the situation as "very dangerous and potentially life-threatening" as multiple communities were in the tornado's path, including the town of Rocky Mountain House.

The warning was briefly expanded to other counties, but lifted completely almost three hours later. After 9 p.m., Environment Canada left the area under a yellow advisory.

Buildings, homes, trees, roads and other local infrastructure in the area suffered "significant damage", according to county officials. But according to Clearwater County reeve Jordon Northcott, no injuries nor livestock deaths related to the tornado have been reported.

Rocky Mountain House Mayor Shane Boniface told CBC News other parts of the county seem to have been harder hit than his town. Most of the clean-up in town Sunday, he said, revolves around downed trees, blown garbage and knocked-off shingles.

Clearwater County officials say crews are working to clear debris and address immediate safety concerns left by Saturday's tornado. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

In Clearwater County, reeve Northcott said, the tornado destroyed buildings, damaged homes and tore down trees. He witnessed the "devastation" while driving near Leslieville, Alta.

"That's when it really sank in that this is quite a disaster," he said.

The damage caused by the tornado dumbfounded Amanda Olson, who was helping her family assess the damage to her mother-in-law's property and and clear out debris from the backyard, including decades-old trees that were broken or uprooted.

"There's kind of a loss for words when you actually look at everything," Olson told CBC News.

"We've been here for about 15 years, and the fires that we've had and the memories and camping here … it's been a second home, so to lose a piece of that is devastating," she said.

Amanda Olson says she's grateful for the tornado warning that was issued as a storm approached Clearwater County, Alta., Saturday. (Kevin Sabiston/CBC)

Olson expressed gratitude for Saturday's emergency alerts. She and her family were staying in that yard in an RV camper, but relocated after the tornado warning, she said.

"We got out lucky on this, though it looks as bad as it is," Olson said.

Crews are working to clear debris and address immediate safety concerns, Clearwater County said on social media, noting that residents are asked to avoid affected areas, exercise caution while on roads and stay away from downed trees and power lines.

A full damage assessment of the region will be completed in the coming days, the county said.

In a social media post on Saturday night, Jason Nixon, Alberta's finance minister who represents some of the affected areas as an MLA, said the province would be in close contact with both the county and town through the clean up.

Northcott confirmed Sunday the provincial government has reached out to Clearwater County, saying they are "very willing" to help, particularly with woody debris.

Multiple provincial ministers released a statement Sunday afternoon thanking first responders and offering sympathies to affected residents.

The Northern Tornadoes Project, based out of Western University in London, Ont., said in a social media post that it confirmed "at least one" tornado near Rocky Mountain House.

While tracking the storm which caused the tornado near Clearwater County, Alta., Environment Canada warned it could bring damaging winds, large hail and intense rain. (Lina Elsaadi/CBC)

The group's crews are currently investigating the twister, surveying affected areas Sunday on foot and by drone, said Matthew Woodward, the Alberta damage survey lead for the project's parent organization, the Canadian Severe Storms Lab.

"Today, specifically, we have seen roof damage. We saw a barn just down this road that was swept clean from its foundation," Woodward said.

After spending many years surveying tornadoes, Woodward said seeing communities come together, lending each other a helping hand, resonates with him every time.

"I admire that, throughout Alberta, people are coming together to recover from these tragedies, and I hope that continues throughout the province," he said.

Alberta members of the Northern Tornadoes Project, based in Ontario, flies a drone Sunday to investigate signs that a tornado touched down near Clearwater County, Alta. (Nadeer Hashmi/CBC)

Eric Van Lochem, an Environment Canada meteorologist, said it's too early to tell if more than one twister hit the Clearwater County region.

"It looks like it missed most of the populated areas, but it it did hit some structures," he said Sunday morning.

Nearly 75 per cent more tornadoes have hit Alberta so far in 2026 than during all of 2025, according to data from the Northern Tornadoes Project.

LISTEN | Tornado damages buildings, local infrastructure: Daybreak Alberta 9:19 Tornado touches down near Rocky Mountain House We hear from Environment Canada meteorologist Eric Van Lochem about this storm, its damage and where it came from.

It's difficult to attribute this change to one factor, Van Lochem said, but increased moisture, resulting in more thunderstorms, plays a large role in developing tornadoes. An active jet-stream pattern this summer is also a factor.

"It's just a recipe for repeated thunderstorms," he said.

"It's unlike some of the other years we've seen in recent memory."

World.title: Calgary police ask public to search their properties for missing 11-year-old boy
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Calgary police continue to search for an 11-year-old boy missing since Thursday, with hundreds of officers and volunteers dedicated to the massive search. On Thursday, Calgary police asked northwest Calgary residents, particularly in and around the Cambrian Heights neighbourhood, for help searching for the missing boy, named Parker. They expanded that search to the entire city Friday. Calgary police acting Staff Sgt. Scott Guterson asked the public on Friday to check their yards, garages, open vehicles, RVs, sheds, pools or anywhere else a child could go. “It is unusual that he has not been found yet, which is again why we are asking for that community help,” he said. At a Sunday press conference, Guterson said the search for Parker is not being scaled back as it enters its fourth day. About 120 trained search volunteers are assisting with police efforts Sunday, along with members of the RCMP. At a Saturday press conference, acting Insp. Rod MacNeil said the ongoing search for Parker has involved hundreds of Calgary Police Service (CPS) members, including investigators, patrol officers, specialized units and civilian staff. "There is nothing more important to us than finding Parker," MacNeil said. Police ask that any Calgarians choosing to search on their own do not interfere with police operations. They also ask any volunteer searchers to be mindful of the heat, so they do not end up requiring attention that could divert first responders from the search for Parker. An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) Guterson advised the public that if they come across Parker, they should not engage him, but instead call police. He said they believe the boy is non-verbal, and gets agitated when strangers approach him. He was last seen shirtless, wearing grey shorts, black Skechers shoes and black noise-cancelling headphones. He’s four feet 11 inches tall and weighs approximately 90 pounds, with brown hair and brown eyes. Guterson said Parker is autistic and functions at a two- or three-year-old level. Police say Parker's family has expressed that he loves Disney music, so officers have been playing some of his favourite songs from patrol vehicles driving in search areas. We know Parker loves Disney music, so officers are playing some of his favourite songs from patrol vehicles in the search area in the hope that it may help draw his attention and encourage him to come out if he is nearby.

This search remains our highest priority. We'll continue… pic.twitter.com/kGAw6R7uMI —CalgaryPolice An emergency alert was broadcast on Saturday afternoon for Parker. Although police previously said the case did not meet the threshold for an Amber Alert, as foul play is not suspected, Calgary police said the provincial government made an exception in this case. "We are hopeful that expanding the awareness through the Alberta emergency system will generate new information that may help us locate him," MacNeil said. Family issues statement In a statement Parker's family said they have been living "every parent's worst nightmare" since he went missing. "Every hour that passes without knowing where he is or whether he is safe has been incredibly difficult for us," the family said in its statement, sent out by CPS on behalf of the family shortly after Saturday afternoon's emergency alert. An undated photo of Parker shared by the Calgary Police Service. (Calgary Police Service) The family implored people to continue searching their properties for Parker. "Parker experiences the world in his own way. He may not respond when his name is called, and he can become frightened when approached by people he does not know," the family said. "Parker is deeply loved, and he is missed immensely. We just want our son home." After Parker was seen Thursday at his day home in the 0 to 100 block of Connaught Drive N.W. between 11:08 and 11:41 a.m., the boy was last seen in the Thorncliffe neighbourhood between 12:30 and 1 p.m. on Thursday, Guterson said. On Saturday, police released a CCTV photo of the boy captured during that time period Thursday on the 5000-6000 block of Travis Crescent N.E., in hopes it might aid in the search. On Sunday, police released CCTV footage of the boy at 12:52 p.m. in the 5500 block of Travis Crescent N.E. They had released a similar photo the day prior, in hopes it might help the search. WATCH | CCTV footage of Parker, missing in Calgary: CCTV footage of Parker, missing in Calgary | Duration 0:27 Footage released by the Calgary Police Service on July 19, shows missing 11-year-old, Parker, walking past a home on Travis Crescent N.E. on Thursday, July 16, 2026. Police said Sunday investigators have received and assessed about 90 tips from the public and are reviewing some 50 hours of CCTV, security camera and dashcam footage. Anyone with additional footage is asked to contact police. Clothing that’s believed to belong to Parker was found at noon Thursday in the 0 to 100 block of Northmount Drive N.W., police said. Police also said Sunday that search efforts are being increasingly focused on areas connected to Parker's last known movements. Guterson said police know the boy likes water and part of their search has been to check whether he's near bodies of water. He said Parker tends to lock doors behind him, meaning people searching their properties should take the time to check behind doors even if they're locked. Police are asking anyone with information about Parker's location, or who may have CCTV or dashcam footage, to call 403-266-1234 or reach the police's evidence submission portal. Situations like this warrant emergency alert, advocate says For Calgary mom Stephanie Karas, Saturday afternoon's emergency alert came far too late. "We've gotten alerts for tornadoes that have not touched down. We've gotten alerts for less, so I don't know why there wasn't," she said. Karas, a mother of two children with autism, says she's lobbying the municipal and provincial governments to create an emergency alert protocol specifically for situations like this. "Why isn't there something for vulnerable youth and adults that aren't equipped?" Karas said. "It's long overdue, so somebody's got to start it," she said. "And if the people of Calgary have to start it and are motivated behind Parker, then that's what we'll do." MacNeil said Calgary police indicated to the province that "it may not be a true Amber Alert, but we need to reach as many Calgarians as we can in such a short amount of time." "The government stepped up right away, made that exception and we were able to get that alert out," he said. In a statement to CBC News, the provincial government said it "worked closely with CPS to assess the situation and determined that this measure to increase the public’s awareness of this missing child in these extremely particular circumstances was important."

World.title: Poilievre names Conservatives' point person on the Alberta referendum
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre has tapped Alberta MP Dane Lloyd to serve as the party's referendum lead for Alberta, as the province prepares to vote on a question related to separation this fall.

Poilievre made the announcement Sunday morning, releasing a letter penned to Lloyd detailing the position.

Lloyd has held his Parkland riding since 2017, and is a lifelong Albertan, according to his website. Prior to politics, he served as a reservist in the Canadian Armed Forces, experience Poilievre said will give Lloyd the "fortitude" for his new role.

In his letter, Poilievre, who is campaigning for Alberta to remain a province of Canada, details the "legitimate concerns and grievances" that Albertans have with the status quo.

"So our task is not to scold Albertans. It is to hear them," Poilievre said.

"This is not a zero-sum fight. What is good for Alberta is good for Canada. More pipelines, more homes, lower taxes, safer streets, stronger borders and more freedom will help workers and families in every province."

CBC News has requested an interview with Lloyd. In a post on social media, Lloyd wrote he is "honoured to play a role in this important discussion," and said he believes deeply in a united Canada.

Last month, Prime Minister Mark Carney appointed Morgan Breitkreutz to serve as the government's senior adviser on Alberta, co-ordinating the federal response to the Alberta referendum, as well as stickhandling major projects like the proposed pipeline to the West Coast.

Separatist calls appointment 'par for the course'

Mitch Sylvestre, who led the petition drive for a separation referendum, says he is not surprised to see the Conservatives pushing for the remain side.

"It's par for the course. Everybody's lining up against this, and why wouldn't they? Why wouldn't they line up [to keep] the economic engine of Canada in Canada?" said Sylvestre.

Mitch Sylvestre holds a box of signatures before submitting his petition for a separation referendum to Elections Alberta in Edmonton, on May 4. (Jason Franson/The Canadian Press)

Sylvestre said the Conservatives are also motivated to keep Alberta in Canada due to the large number of seats they hold in Alberta — 33 out of 37.

"They just don't represent Alberta's views, they don't represent Alberta at all, in any way shape or form. And I understand they're terrified to lose their jobs because without Alberta, could you imagine the kind of trouble that the Conservative Party of Canada is going to be in?" he said.

Lloyd's appointment earned praise from Evan Menzies, a former United Conservative Party staffer now with Crestview Strategies, a consultancy, who has known Lloyd since the two attended Trinity Western University together.

Menzies calls him a "fantastic person, deeply principled, who has long had a heart for service for his community."

"H e understands Albertans and the reasons why they're frustrated and he'll be able to speak to a lot of what I would call frustrated federalists in the province who see that the path to expressing their form of patriotism the most is to make sure that they get Ottawa's attention," said Menzies.

But Poilievre leaning into those well-known grumblings about Ottawa could be the wrong approach, one political analyst said.

"It e choes the Canada-is-broken message that Pierre Poilievre has spoken of, " said Lori Williams, associate professor of policy studies at Mount Royal University.

"And that's a risky strategy that very much could be used by those who are already supporting separatism as fuel for voting for the second option, that is for a referendum to leave Canada."

One of the 10 questions set for the Oct. referendum will ask Albertans if they believe the province should remain in Confederation, or if they support the provincial government beginning the legal process of holding another, binding referendum on separation.

The other nine questions relate to issues around immigration and the Constitution.

Albertans will have their say on Oct. 19.

World.title: First Nation leaders, community members decry response to northern Ontario wildfires
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

With about 600 Eabametoong First Nation members at the centre of another evacuation due to northern Ontario wildfires, community leaders are speaking out about the conditions that make First Nations more vulnerable to such crises.

“The conditions in which they [First Nations] are dealing with, just in terms of air quality, are already poor — and there's very little fire support there, too, ” says Riley Yesno, a member of Eabametoong First Nation, also known as Fort Hope, and a distinguished fellow at the Yellowhead Institute.

The remote Ojibway community, located about 360 kilometres north of Thunder Bay, declared a state of emergency on Wednesday. More than 1,600 people live in Eabametoong; about 600 of them are being flown out by military aircraft, with help from the Royal Canadian Air Force and Canadian Rangers.

Evacuation flights began over the weekend, after the federal minister of emergency management and community resilience, Eleanor Olszewski, approved a request from Ontario Regional Chief Abram Benedict for assistance from the Canadian Armed Forces. Some 460 evacuees have already arrived in Niagara Falls.

CBC News has contacted Eabametoong’s Chief Solomon Atlookan for more details and is awaiting his availability for an interview.

Most of the nearly 190 wildfires burning across the province are in northwestern Ontario. There are about 1,800 evacuees from the region from well over a dozen communities.

Amid all this, there have been more calls for government action, including from First Nations themselves.

WATCH | Ford warns people refusing to evacuate are hindering wildfire response: Ford warns people refusing to evacuate are hindering wildfire response | Duration 3:56 A new evacuation centre has opened in Thunder Bay for people displaced by northern Ontario wildfires. Premier Doug Ford warned that people refusing evacuation orders are hindering firefighting efforts.

Yesno has been in close contact with her friends and family amid the Eabametoong evacuation and has been helping sort donations for evacuees in Thunder Bay.

It's not the only challenge faced by the First Nation. It has been under a boil-water advisory since 2001 that's been considered as long term since 2002.

“It's always just so difficult when the infrastructure that we have there, like in so many remote northern communities, is just so insufficient to deal with the level of crisis that they are experiencing or could very soon be experiencing,” Yesno said regarding the wildfires.

“The conditions in which they are dealing with, just in terms of air quality, are already poor — and there's very little fire support there, too.”

According to Indigenous Services Canada (ISC), about 80 per cent of Indigenous communities in Canada are in areas susceptible to wildland fire, spokesperson Jacinthe Goulet said in an email to CBC News on Saturday.

“Indigenous communities are also more vulnerable due to factors like remoteness, community size, inadequate infrastructure, socio-economic conditions, limited access to emergency management resources and community capacity,” they wrote.

About 600 wildfire evacuees from Eabametoong First Nation, also known as Fort Hope, in northwestern Ontario are being transported out of the community by the Canadian Armed Forces. They will be staying in Niagara Falls. (Eabametoong First Nation/Facebook)

“They are also significantly more likely to be evacuated than those off-reserve and take longer to recover due to their location and remoteness. Emergencies like this highlight the critical need for equitable and co-ordinated support.”

Goulet said the federal department “is working closely with First Nations leadership, Ontario and emergency management partners to support the immediate and evolving needs of impacted communities.”

However, First Nation leaders, including from Nishnawbe Aski Nation (NAN) and Anishinabek Nation, have criticized the provincial and federal governments for not responding to the wildfire situation quickly enough. Namaygoosisagagun First Nation (Collins First Nation) completely burned to the ground Monday and leaders say they weren’t warned of the wildfire in advance.

WATCH | Thunder Bay wildfire evacuees receive urgent housing and essential relief: Thunder Bay wildfire evacuees receive urgent housing and essential relief | Duration 4:10 Vicky Woodbeck of the Ontario Native Women’s Association (ONWA) discusses the wildfire situation in Thunder Bay, Ont. She outlines how the fires are affecting local residents, their anxieties about returning home and the ONWA's efforts to support evacuees with critical needs such as housing, food and baby supplies.

NAN Grand Chief Alvin Fiddler said First Nation leaders were not told about Ontario Premier Doug Ford's visit to Thunder Bay on Saturday ahead of time and that he did not schedule meetings with them.

“The premier came up to meet local people co-ordinating Ontario’s wildfire response. That’s fine, but he also needs to engage with First Nations leadership managing this situation,” Fiddler wrote on Facebook on Saturday.

“I would like to remind Doug Ford that it’s our people that are being impacted the most by these wildland fires. If you are going to make the effort to come up, it can’t just be for a photo-op."

It's very shameful that we are living in a country where Indigenous people are made to be climate refugees in their own homelands. - Riley Yesno, Eabametoong First Nation member

Yesno said the lack of engagement speaks to “a colonial legacy that essentially sets Indigenous communities up to be disposable.”

“I'm really extremely angry with not just this government, but all levels of government, and the generations of underfunding that communities like mine have experienced, that emergency services have experienced,” Yesno said.

“It's very shameful that we are living in a country where Indigenous people are made to be climate refugees in their own homelands.”

Yesno said remote communities need more long-term, sustainable funding for emergency management services.

As well, she wants the federal government to set more ambitious climate targets to prevent Canada’s wildfire seasons from becoming increasingly severe.

“That’s a big ask and it feels like an insurmountable one, but if our summers are only going to get hotter, then the fires that have always happened are only ever going to get bigger.”

World.title: 2 boys missing, believed to have drowned in Manitoba's Nutimik Lake
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Two brothers from Winnipeg, aged 10 and 13, are believed to have slipped into the fast-moving rapids near Sturgeon Falls Trail in Manitoba's Nutimik Lake on Saturday.

RCMP say a search is underway involving their underwater recovery team and the Hutterian Emergency Aquatic Response Team (HEART).

Officers were called just after 12:30 p.m. Saturday about the possible drowning in Whiteshell Provincial Park after the boys fell into the rapids and had not resurfaced, RCMP said in a news release on Sunday.

Police and local firefighters and other emergency responders searched the water and along the shorelines using boats and drones, but the boys have yet to be found, the news release stated.

Staff Sgt. Cory Meyers with Lac du Bonnet RCMP said the search is focused on an area surrounding the falls and its current.

"We've had success in that general area in the past. But as we keep searching here, we'll slowly keep expanding a bit more into Nutimik Lake," he told CBC News on Sunday afternoon.

While police are still fairly early in the investigation, Meyers said there are "strong indications" that the two boys may have drowned.

The search is ongoing.

A search is underway for two boys believed to have drowned in Nutimik Lake. The RCMP underwater recovery team and the Hutterian Emergency Aquatic Response Team (HEART) are involved. (Submitted by RCMP)

Meyers said the two boys and their father had travelled from Winnipeg to visit the park with friends on Saturday.

Meyers said the boys' parents have been on scene with police and are "devastated by the situation."

"There's some hope here [that] we can get some closure for them," he said.

A 38-year-old woman drowned at the same location in June 2025 and a 12 -year-old boy drowned there in May 2023.

The falls are a wide set of rapids between Numao and Nutimik lakes, which are wide parts of the Winnipeg River, about 135 kilometres east of Winnipeg near the Manitoba-Ontario border.

Meyers said the rocks around the falls are very slippery and the current is very dangerous.

"If folks … get too close to the edge or they get caught by the water, they'll enter the water very quickly and it's very difficult, just with the current, to get back out," he said, encouraging people to keep a safe distance away from the water near the falls.

Wearing personal flotation devices, like life jackets, can also help keep people safe in and around the water, he said.
