World.title: All-Women ‘Shaolin Soccer’ Tribute Scores Big, Divides Fans
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018769/All-Women ‘Shaolin Soccer’ Tribute Scores Big, Divides Fans
World.content:
Renowned Hong Kong actor-filmmaker Stephen Chow’s new kung fu football comedy, “Kung Fu Soccer,” has generated a wave of nostalgia in China and grossed over 660 million yuan ($100 million) at the box office in just four days.

Released Saturday, the film is the best-attended and highest-grossing summer film debut in China in the last five years. Chow’s first film in seven years is considered a tribute to his 2001 comedy “Shaolin Soccer” and follows the Emei women’s football team, a modest group named after the famous wuxia martial arts sect. The players employ classic kung fu moves, often flying through the air to beat their rivals.

The film attracted significant investment. According to ticketing platform Maoyan, it was backed by 18 production companies and six co-producers, with a reported total investment of 380 million yuan.

Renowned for his signature mo lei tau, or “illogical,” comedy style, featuring exaggerated performances, absurd elements, underdog stories, and unpredictable twists that often satirize social conventions, Chow is widely regarded as having played a defining role in the development of on-screen Chinese comedy.

Unlike Chow’s previous football film, which centers around an all-male team, “Kung Fu Soccer” features female protagonists. It also explores how its characters reconcile with winning and losing, rather than how ordinary people rise to prominence through hard work, as was often the focus in Chow’s earlier films.

Prior to the release of “Kung Fu Soccer,” anticipation was high on social media. Many reposted the phrase “I owe Stephen Chow a movie ticket,” an apologetic reference to the prevalence of piracy of Chow’s past films in the Chinese mainland.

However, after watching the film, many reneged on their promise, posting instead that it was not viewers who owed Chow tickets, but rather the director who owed them tickets — in part because they were let down by the comedy.

Many complained that the film’s jokes felt outdated, with exaggerated performances, abrupt character development, and disjointed transitions between plot points that reminded some of “short-video compilations.” Others criticized the film for its jarring and distracting visual effects, including glowing football fields and players transforming into tigers, leopards, and dragons mid-match.

And without Chow himself performing his signature mo lei tau comedy, as he has previously done, many said the actors’ attempts to imitate his style come across as awkward and failed to capture its essence.

Beyond its comedic shortcomings, some viewers also critiqued the film for sexism. On multiple occasions, female players use sexually suggestive moves to distract the male referees, while one of the Emei footballer’s special skills is triggered after seeing her toxic ex-boyfriend kissing another woman.

As of Tuesday, the film holds a score of 6.6 out of 10 on Chinese review platform Douban. In a highly upvoted comment, one user wrote, “Chow’s fascination with social outsiders is still present in the film, as is his fondness for eccentric characters. The film sometimes even offers glimpses of the magic that once defined his work.”

“The problem is that these moments are all too brief. Just as they begin to rekindle your expectations, they are quickly interrupted by an outdated meme, an over-the-top performance, or an overly sentimental scene,” they added.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A poster for “Kung Fu Soccer.” From Douban)

World.title: The fight over Sara Duterte’s bank and tax records, explained
World.content:
MEET. Vice President Sara Duterte arrives at the Senate on July 7, 2026, to meet with her lawyers but did attend her impeachment trial.

What are the three obstacles that the prosecution must overcome to follow Sara Duterte's money trail?

MANILA, Philippines – To examine whether Vice President Sara Duterte accumulated wealth she failed to disclose or could not explain, prosecutors want to compare what she declared in her Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN), what moved through bank accounts linked to her, and what income she reported to tax authorities.

Senator-judges are expected to continue deliberation on Monday, July 20, whether to issue subpoenas for the financial records of Duterte and her husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

The court held oral arguments on Wednesday, July 15, but emerged from a closed-door caucus lasting more than an hour without a ruling. The postponement suggests they haven’t reached a common position on whether the subpoenas are necessary fact-finding tools or an excessively broad “fishing expedition,” as Duterte’s defense argues.

What prosecutors want

The prosecution wants nine bank branches ordered to produce records relating to Duterte and Carpio, including accounts, deposits, investments, trusts, loans, safe-deposit boxes, and transactions allegedly maintained, controlled, beneficially owned, or held by the couple or their representatives, nominees, and signatories from 2007 to 2025.

It also wants the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) to turn over covered transaction reports and suspicious transaction reports involving the couple, along with related investigation documents and electronic database extracts. (LIST: Sara Duterte’s bank accounts, AMLC records covered by subpoena request)

The tax records are the subject of a separate subpoena request. During the House impeachment inquiry, the Bureau of Internal Revenue (BIR) produced a sealed box containing records involving Duterte, Carpio, and businesses linked to them.

The same box later traveled to the Senate before it was returned to the BIR unopened.

A subpoena would compel the BIR commissioner to appear and bring Duterte’s tax records, although separate presidential authority may still be required before they can be disclosed.

So, what are the obstacles standing in the prosecution’s way?

Obstacle 1: Getting Senate approval

Senator-judges must first authorize the subpoenas. Monday’s action could result in approval, rejection, or an order narrower than what prosecutors requested.

The defense says the proposed period extends years before Duterte became Vice President and sweeps in records involving her spouse, businesses, representatives, and nominees without sufficient specificity.

Prosecutors counter that allegedly undisclosed wealth accumulated earlier could continue benefiting an impeachable official, and that integrity is a continuing qualification for public office.

If the motions are rejected, the banks, BIR, and AMLC would not be compelled under these requests to produce the material. But does that mean tax records are completely beyond reach? Perhaps not.

“The President’s authority under Section 71 of the Tax Code exists independently of a Senate subpoena. In principle, the BIR Commissioner could seek that authority if disclosure is legally warranted,” global tax policy expert Mon Abrea told Rappler.

Getting these records released is, of course, one thing. But their admissibility as evidence in an impeachment proceeding is another matter.

“However, whether those records would later be admitted as evidence in an impeachment trial is a separate matter for the Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, to determine under the Constitution,” he added.

Obstacle 2: Getting the actual records

Even if the Senate approves both subpoena requests, bank and tax records won’t be equally easy to obtain.

The Bank Secrecy Law generally protects bank deposits but expressly provides an exception “in cases of impeachment.” Consequently, though requests may still face legal challenges, bank secrecy isn’t an absolute barrier during impeachment proceedings.

The Tax Code, by contrast, has no comparable impeachment exception. Section 270 imposes criminal penalties on BIR personnel who unlawfully disclose confidential taxpayer information, including imprisonment of two to five years, a fine, or both.

That gives BIR officials an even stronger reason to withhold records unless the legal basis for disclosure is crystal clear.

“The different treatment under the Bank Secrecy Law and the Tax Code is precisely why I believe Congress should revisit these laws,” Abrea told Rappler. “The Bank Secrecy Law expressly recognizes impeachment as an exception, while the Tax Code generally protects taxpayer confidentiality and, under Section 71, requires presidential authority before income tax returns may be opened for inspection.”

The closest precedent is the 2012 trial of then-chief justice Renato Corona. The Senate obtained tax information covering Corona, his wife, children, and son-in-law. It also examined bank records that senators later compared with his SALNs.

To obtain these, the Senate first subpoenaed then-BIR commissioner Kim Henares. She then sought and received authority from then-president Benigno Aquino III before producing the requested tax information.

In a recent interview on ANC’s Headstart, Henares said the same process could be followed in Duterte’s case, with the BIR commissioner needing to seek presidential authority before releasing the records.

“The BIR Commissioner still has to get the authority [from the President,]” Henares said in the interview. “Ngayon, kung hindi niya makuha ‘yung authority, pupunta siya sa Senado at sasabihin niya, hindi ako makaka-release kasi hindi ako binigyan ng authority ng Presidente. (Now, if they were unable to get authority, they will go to the Senate and say that they cannot release the records because they weren’t able to get authority from the President.)”

That could put President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. in an awkward position. He has previously distanced himself and the executive department from the impeachment proceedings, saying, “I do not give guidance to Congress. We are independent of each other.”

But if the BIR commissioner seeks presidential authority to open Duterte’s tax records, Marcos may still be required to make a decision with direct consequences for the evidence available to the Senate.

Malacañang said on July 13 that no request had yet reached the President, but that any request would be studied before he decides what action to take.

Abrea agreed that the commissioner doesn’t have blanket discretion to release confidential tax records. But he cautioned against treating presidential authorization as the end of the legal question.

“The real issue is not whether President Marcos signs or refuses to sign,” Abrea told Rappler. “The real issue is whether the Constitution gives the Senate, sitting as an impeachment court, powers that prevail over the statutory confidentiality of taxpayer records.”

Under the ordinary procedure set out in the Tax Code, presidential authority is required, Abrea said. But if the Senate insists that its constitutional powers as an impeachment court allow it to compel disclosure anyway, the dispute could become a constitutional question.

“If that conflict arises, the final answer should come from the Supreme Court — not from politics,” Abrea said.

Obstacle 3: Connecting the dots

Once the records have been released, the final and most important challenge would be proving the Vice President’s wealth is truly unexplained.

For example, bank and AMLC documents could reveal the amounts, dates, counterparties, and patterns behind transactions that prosecutors may want banks and witnesses to explain. But their existence doesn’t by itself establish that any wrongdoing was committed. Covered transactions may be reported because they exceed regulatory thresholds, while suspicious transactions could be flagged because of their circumstances, regardless of their value.

“Bank and tax records are among the most important pieces of the puzzle, but they are only part of the financial picture,” Abrea told Rappler.

“Investigators would typically compare tax returns, bank records, SALNs, property acquisitions, corporate interests, and other assets and liabilities to determine whether there is a substantial disparity between declared income and accumulated wealth. That was essentially the approach taken during the Corona impeachment,” he added.

Henares, who testified during the Corona trial, explained that each layer of evidence obtained would serve a different purpose for the prosecution.

“‘Yung SALN at ‘yung bank record, ang pinag-uusapan diyan is kompleto ba ‘yung sinabi mo sa SALN. So ngayon, naghahanap ka ng asset na hindi niya ni-report sa SALN,” Henares said during the Headstart interview.

(When it comes to the SALN and bank record, the question is whether what was declared in the SALN is complete. So now, you’re looking for assets that weren’t reported in the SALN.)

For instance, if bank records showed that total deposits exceed the amount declared in the SALN, prosecutors may have evidence of an inaccurate or incomplete SALN. A possible next step would be to compare this with income declared to the BIR.

“Ngayon dahil in-adjust mo ‘yung asset niya based on sa mga evidence mo, i-cocompare mo sa income na dineclare mo. Ngayon kung ‘yung income dineclare mo hindi ma-explain – kunwari ang dineclare mong income for the whole period is P20 million lang, biglang ang asset mo P1 billion – may difference siya. So, unexplained wealth ‘yan,” Henares added.

(Now because you adjusted the asset based on the evidence, you compare them with the declared income. If you can’t explain that declared income – for example, you only declared an income of P20 million for the whole, and your assets suddenly amount to P1 billion – then there’s a difference. That’s unexplained wealth.)

The analysis could become more complicated if Duterte argues that money in a joint or linked account belonged to her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte.

Henares said that once such a defense is formally raised, prosecutors would have a stronger basis to seek his SALNs and tax returns without it appearing to be a fishing expedition. Rodrigo Duterte’s detention in The Hague could also complicate efforts to obtain his testimony.

Monday’s decision is therefore just the first step in what could become a months-long journey to settle the unexplained-wealth charge. – Rappler.com

World.title: [FIRST PERSON] An afternoon with Frank Drilon
World.content:
'Many politicians overstay their welcome, but Drilon seems to know how — and when — to say goodbye'

When former Senate president Franklin Drilon told us one afternoon that he had no plans of returning to his old life in politics, my mind immediately wandered to Hamilton: The Musical.

One of my favorite parts of that Tony Award winner is the song “One Last Time,” depicting an imaginary conversation — though historically grounded — between first US president George Washington and his secretary of treasury Alexander Hamilton. Even though he faced no constitutional term limits and was expected to win a reelection bid easily, Washington refused a third term.

The song in that musical goes:

(Hamilton) Why do you have to say goodbye?

(Washington) If I say goodbye, the nation learns to move on. It outlives me when I’m gone.

I asked Drilon that afternoon: “But don’t you miss it?”

“Let other leaders do their share. I think I have done my share. I leave my fate to history,” he said.

Many politicians overstay their welcome; Drilon seems to know how — and when — to say goodbye.

A Rappler+ event

Drilon — or Sir Frank as I called him — was our guest at the Rappler office on July 17 for our quarterly town hall with our Rappler+ members. Events like this one allow our loyal subscribers to meet movers of our nation, and even throw questions at them.

Belle, our Rappler+ lead, asked me last month to do the interview, and facilitate the open forum that came after. Even though one-on-one interviews (and with an audience!) are not a journalistic skill that I have mastered, I reluctantly agreed: it meant achieving a KPI, and opportunities to interview someone who has occupied so many of the country’s most important offices don’t often come around.

I knew I had to find time to read his memoir that had been gathering dust in my bedroom since our executive editor Glenda Gloria lent me her copy three or four months ago. Drilon has been a staple in Philippine politics even before I was born in 1996, but I haven’t met him in person since I entered the media profession in 2017. To read his book is to understand the complexities of a man who survived turmoil after turmoil in our young, fragile democracy.

Brush-ins with higher office

In his book and in our conversation, what struck me was a sense of delicadeza that has guided the statesman throughout his career.

Drilon told us a story of how he had been asked by the late former president Noynoy Aquino, after the conclusion of the Renato Corona impeachment trial in 2012, to apply for the vacant chief justice position, but he declined the offer.

“I refused because I said I was perceived to be defending the administration in that proceeding and therefore, for me, to accept the nomination and be appointed, people would say, the reason why you were asking those questions is because you wanted to be chief justice, which was completely not called for, but that would have been the result,” Drilon said.

It’s not the first time this man — who has worn so many hats in government as labor, justice, and executive secretary, as well as the longest-serving Senate president — walked away from a path to higher office.

In his memoir, he talked about the time he came close to becoming president in 2004.

After the national elections that year, there was intense pressure for him as co-presiding officer of the joint session of Congress to delay the proclamation of the winner of the presidential race amid allegations of widespread election cheating. He noted that had no president been proclaimed by June 30, he would have been acting president for 60 days.

“Ultimately, I made the decision to proclaim Mrs. (Gloria Macapagal) Arroyo as president. My reasoning was clear: as acting president, I would lack a popular mandate, and critically, the authority to command the armed forces,” he wrote.

“I never wanted (the presidency). Even when it was practically handed to me, as in 2004, I felt no compelling urge to reach for it,” he added. “The immense burdens of the presidency would remove me from a position of control over the areas that matter most to me as a public servant: lawmaking, representational and constituent service, and addressing ethical and governance issues.”

AUTOGRAPH. After the town hall, the writer asked Drilon to sign his copy of the former senator’s book, which was gifted by former tourism chief Narzalina Lim through Rappler head of community Pia Ranada.

Resisting dynasties

The former senator takes pride in being the only Drilon in politics. It is striking how a man who has all the political infrastructure to establish a dynasty chose not to.

Curbing the concentration of political power in a handful of families remains one of the unfulfilled promises of the 1986 EDSA People Power Revolution. The 1987 Constitution prohibits political dynasties, but in the absence of an enabling law, elective office has largely remained a family affair.

It’s a hot-button issue these days as the House passes a bill defining dynasties. Its loose provisions, however, raise fears that the proposal will legitimize dynasties instead of regulate them. Given the composition of Congress, it’s unsurprising that proposals to regulate political dynasties stop short of meaningfully limiting them.

I think — and I say this with all due respect to the lawmakers I have been covering for a number of years now — that politicians, including those who truly believe they are some of the few good ones, should disabuse themselves of the notion that the country’s future rests solely in their hands.

No single family has the monopoly on good governance. Democracies are sustained by institutions and their people, not by messiahs.

Play Video

Finding hope

Drilon’s retirement does not mean complete disengagement from politics. These days, he makes media appearances to speak his mind about the country’s affairs.

He’s monitoring Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial, but admits even he gets “bored” by the very technical nature of the proceedings. He called on Senate President Win Gatchalian and presiding officer Chiz Escudero to “exercise more authority” so people won’t be fatigued by trivialities, such as the lengthy debate over the legitimacy of Duterte’s video threat which the entire country already knew happened.

Drilon also said he’s part of a group of 10 people trying to convince former vice president Leni Robredo to give the presidency another shot.

“At a certain point, (former) vice president Leni was no longer responding to my text messages. We respect her for that. We have not at this point identified any other candidate because, as I said, one week is too long in politics,” he said.

Much of that Rappler+ town hall revolved around today’s political actors: who should be held accountable, who should run, what the Senate should be doing. Before we wrapped up, I asked him something broader. How can a man — who first entered government in 1987 as deputy labor minister and with an optimism to do his share in rebuilding democracy — not give in to the cynicism that has struck other Filipinos?

The family that was ousted by the 1986 revolution, after all, has returned to Malacañang.

“I keep on telling my friends, my children, we should not give up because this is our country. I must admit that there are times when I myself get disillusioned. But you wake up to the fact that this is your only country,” he said.

“We can’t rely on anybody else. At the end of the day, this is our country and we face and we suffer the consequences of erroneous decisions that we make as a people.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Spain silences Messi, Argentina to win FIFA World Cup crown
World.content:
Super-sub Ferran Torres delivers the winner in extra time as Spain captures its second FIFA World Cup crown and denies Lionel Messi and Argentina a title repeat

NEW JERSEY, USA – Ferran Torres scored in the 106th minute to lift Spain to its second FIFA World Cup title with a 1-0 win in extra time over gutsy, 10-man Argentina in the final on Sunday, July 19 (Monday, July 20, Manila time).

Torres’ deserved winner came 16 years and eight days after Andres Iniesta also scored in extra time to lift the Spaniards to their first world championship with a 1-0 victory over the Netherlands.

Goal l 🇪🇸 Spain 1-0 Argentina 🇦🇷 l Ferran Torres pic.twitter.com/foXWHXpG2y — Goals Highlights (@GoalsHighlight_) July 19, 2026

It came on La Roja’s 20th shot on the contest against defending champion Argentina, which failed to manage any to that point and struggled to wrest possession away from its superior Iberian opponents.

That was true at even strength and became more difficult when the Albiceleste’s numbers were reduced when Enzo Fernandez’s late challenge of Pau Cubarsi left referee Slavko Vincic no choice but to produce a second caution just before the end of normal time.

Spain remains the only nation ever to win a European Championship and World Cup in successive tournaments, having now done so a second time. It is also the first World Cup champion ever to concede only once across an entire tournament.

Lionel Messi’s Argentina failed to earn a title for the first time in three major tournaments, having also captured the 2021 and 2024 Copa Americas either side of their 2022 World Cup triumph.

The 39-year-old, eight-time Ballon d’Or winner Messi finished the competition with eight goals and four assists, but had little time on the ball until Spain finally took the lead and never seriously looked like lifting his side to another great moment as he has so many times in the last two World Cup cycles.

Emi Martinez made 11 saves for the Albiceleste, who fell short in their bid to be the first consecutive World Cup champions since Brazil won the 1958 and 1962 titles.

What had felt so difficult for the first 105 minutes suddenly looked easy after 37 seconds of play in the second period of extra time.

Pedro Porro curled in an outswinging cross from the left to the back post, Nico Williams won the header and nodded it back into space, and Torres hammered a half-volley at last past the flailing Martinez. It was his only goal of the tournament, making him the seventh player to score during a tournament in which his side never trailed. – Rappler.com

World.title: France star Kylian Mbappe breaks FIFA World Cup career goal record
World.content:
SCORER. France's Kylian Mbappe reacts after their bronze-medal match against England in the 2026 FIFA World Cup.

France's Kylian Mbappe ends the 2026 FIFA World Cup with 10 goals, two ahead of Argentina's Lionel Messi in the competition for the Golden Boot

France didn’t get the win but Kylian Mbappe got the record on Saturday, July 18 (Sunday, July 19, Manila time). For now.

The French star became the all-time leading goal scorer in FIFA World Cup history with 22 after two goals in his club’s third-place match against England in Miami Gardens, Florida.

Despite Mbappe’s efforts, France lost 6-4 as its attempted comeback from a 4-0 halftime deficit fell short.

Mbappe scored goals in the 48th and 66th minutes to move one ahead of Argentina great Lionel Messi.

“I’m just trying to help my team score every time,” Mbappe said after the match. “It’s for sure that when you score that many goals in the World Cup, it elevates you to certain levels but I would have liked to not be the top scorer in history and play tomorrow’s (championship) match.”

“So, I think it’s good for legacy and when we stop (playing) to say that I was one of those players. But today, it’s not the first thing crossing my mind.”

Mbappe also has 10 goals in this World Cup, two ahead of Messi in the competition for the Golden Boot. Messi’s squad meets Spain in the final in East Rutherford, New Jersey, on Sunday, meaning the Argentine star has a chance to surpass both marks Mbappe set.

Mbappe is the first player with 10 goals in a World Cup since West Germany’s Gerd Muller in 1970. – Rappler.com

World.title: Who is Lorna Kapunan, private prosecutor in Sara Duterte impeachment trial?
World.content:
The celebrity lawyer is no stranger to handling high-profile cases and lawyering for controversial public figures

Lorna Kapunan is perhaps the most recognizable name on the list of private lawyers who make up the prosecution panel in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Her first major appearance in the high-stakes affair happened on Tuesday, July 14, when the lawyer manifested the prosecution’s intent to withdraw Office of the Vice President chief of staff Zuleika Lopez from their witness list.

Kapunan is one of the first people enlisted by the House in their team. When the House first impeached Duterte in 2025, Kapunan expressed her desire to participate in what she had described then as the “trial of the century.”

“It is our duty to stand for what is right. It is our duty as lawyers to stand for justice, and we see that this whitewashing, we see that this burying of evidence, we see that this brazen violation of the Constitution, and the principle of accountability is being violated,” Kapunan said in an interview with DZMM at the time.

Play Video

There’s no surprise that Kapunan chose a career in law. After all, she is the daughter of Lino Mejia Patajo, a former Supreme Court associate justice, whom Kapunan fondly remembers as her “anchor and moral compass in life and in law.”

A political science and law graduate from the University of the Philippines, Kapunan began her career as senior associate at ACCRALAW in 1978. She stayed there until 1986, after which she began managing her own firms. Today, it is known as the Kapunan and Castillo Law Offices, which she founded in 2011.

She is the widow of former trial court judge Eduardo Ronen Kapunan, whom she lost to cancer in 2001. Her son died from leukemia two years later, a tragedy that inspired her to co-found a support group for mothers who lost their children.

Kapunan prides herself as a women’s rights advocate, and was even chairperson of the United Nations Development Fund for Women. But she also once drew criticism for representing controversial male clients, such as Dr. Hayden Kho, and Kris Aquino’s ex-husband James Yap.

The celebrity lawyer is no stranger to handling cases that captured national attention. These include:

The West Tower Condominium vs. First Philippine Industrial Corporation (FPIC) case: Kapunan served as counsel for the petitioners who complained about a pipeline causing hazardous leakage. The case is known for triggering the Supreme Court’s first ever writ of Kalikasan.

Pork barrel scam queen Janet Lim Napoles’ serious illegal detention case, which Kapunan withdrew from as lead counsel in 2013 due to “difference in opinion” with another lawyer on Napoles’ team.

A class suit where she represented Philippine Airlines flight stewardesses, who sued the airline for compulsorily retiring them at 55 years old while their male counterparts could retire at 60.

The fatal hazing case of Horacio Castillo III, whose family she represented. A Manila court convicted her for unjust vexation over remarks she made while working on the case.

The missing cockfighters case, in which she briefly lawyered for businessman Charlie “Atong” Ang.

Kapunan also cultivated political ambitions. She ran for senator in 2016 as part of the slate of then-senatorial aspirant Grace Poe, but only placed 29th after receiving over a million votes.

Kapunan’s legal career brought her beyond the courtroom and into the broadcast studio, as she also served as a television host for various shows, such as Aliw23 TV’s “Laban Para sa Karapatan”, DZRJ TV’s “Legally Speaking,” and TV5’s “FACE 2 FACE.”

On Wednesday, July 15, Senator Pia Cayetano called out Kapunan for offering a lengthy explanation on why the prosecution dropped Lopez from the witness list. Some senator-judges claimed such statements could affect the impeachment court’s impartiality.

“When we talk about balance and when we talk about impartiality, that same standard should apply not only to the prosecutors, not only to the defense, but to the senator-judges,” Kapunan later said. – Rappler.com

Isabel Victorino is a fourth year AB Communication student at Ateneo de Manila University and a writer for its school publication The GUIDON. She is currently a Rappler intern.

World.title: Users of Meta’s Facebook, Instagram report suffering some outages
World.content:
FACEBOOK. Facebook app icon is seen on a smartphone in this illustration taken October 27, 2025

Some Facebook and Instagram users experience intermittent access to the two social media platforms

Meta’s Instagram and Facebook social networks appeared to suffer some outages on Sunday, July 19, with users reporting issues with the app and website.

According to website downtime monitoring service Downdetector, there were 4,808 reports filed by Facebook users in the United States as of 0746 GMT, with 63% of users facing issues accessing the website.

Another 2,829 reports were filed by Instagram users in the US who faced issues with the app as of 0818 GMT on Sunday.

Checks by Reuters also found that access to Facebook and Instagram was intermittent in Singapore.

Meta did not immediately reply to a request for comment sent by email. – Rappler.com

World.title: [Inside the Newsroom] Why you need to help independent newsrooms
World.content:
Unlike lies — which you can pull out of thin air — ‘the best obtainable version of the truth’ takes time, talent, resources, and courage

We totally get it.

People are so used to getting content for free that it’s hard to imagine why you would need to pay for it. Why shell out money for content when Facebook, Tiktok, and YouTube are teeming with creators who repurpose stories and share their “analysis” of current events for free, at the drop of a hat?

The attention economy is a cutthroat space that newsrooms cannot win now — unless we succumb to ridiculous antics, screaming headlines, and short “analyses” that many content creators of today resort to just to get eyeballs.

The traditional way by which newsrooms earn revenue to support themselves is through advertising. But that model has long gone down the drain. Nearly 80% of global media advertising is now cornered by the top 10 tech companies: Google, Facebook, Amazon, etc. To get to the remaining 20%, newsrooms from all over the world have to fight tooth and nail with each other, with an ever growing number of influencers and content creators, and — more recently — with an avalanche of AI slop.

Yet, most Rappler stories remain free. We are committed to our public mission to deliver verified information on matters of public interest.

Only select Rappler exclusives require a paywall. But we also produce short video derivatives from them to serve for free on TikTok and YouTube. It’s a constant source of joy to see these videos on corruption and geopolitics watched by millions of viewers.

We require people to register (via their emails) — for free — for two reasons: We want to make sure that humans, not bots, are on our site (and even then this has become uphill battle because of the sneaky ways of AI) AI companies steal our content as training data — without seeking permission and without paying. They then deploy information to readers who would otherwise find them in news sites.

For fact checks that Rappler makes, readers are not even required to register.

It is when we publish investigative stories and premium analyses that we ask the public to help us sustain this kind of work by joining our Rappler + membership program. And we appreciate that they do, because this simple act of citizenship inspires us further to tell stories that those in power prefer not to be told.

Rappler + members believe that journalism is vital to making governments and communities work, and they part with their hard-earned money to help ensure that this work continues.

We grant, however, that it’s not a small ask if one takes into account the shrinking personal and household income of Filipinos. That said, we used to pay for newspapers. We also paid for cable news.

As of 2022, the Philippine Statistics Authority even estimated that one in 10 Filipino families are already subscribed to streaming services like Netflix.

Estimates peg the amount Filipinos spend on mobile games at roughly US$1.5 billion.

We also pay for more frivolous things online. Lazada, Shopee, and Temu are flourishing here. Even Amazon has found it lucrative enough to enter the Philippine market.

If you find value in the investigations and in-depth reporting that Rappler has been delivering, surely you will not find the small amount of P247 a month or P3,500 a year prohibitive?

Yet, when we release exclusive, well-researched, original content on disinformation narratives or anything of public interest, we get comments like these: “Galit kayo sa disinformation pero yung information, lalagyan nyo ng paywall.”

As one fellow journalist said, this is how journalism dies: when people think it always needs to be given away for free.

It is as if Rappler does not have to pay for what goes through the process of researching, investigating, editing, publishing, and keeping a workforce. The meter for our hosting server does not stop when the subject matter of an article a user is accessing is a public interest issue.

The inconvenient truth here is this: unlike lies and conjecture — which you can pull out of thin air — ”the best obtainable version of the truth” takes time, talent, and resources. And, yes, courage.

Thus, Rappler and other newsrooms are facing the challenge of coming up with multiple revenue streams to sustain the business — through membership programs and other revenue pillars.

It’s a battle we won’t win without our public.

We ask that you will pass on this message so more people will support independent journalism.

Thank you. – Rappler.com

Inside the Newsroom is a newsletter delivered straight to your inbox every week. Visit rappler.com/newsletters to manage your newsletter subscriptions.

World.title: Democratic Taiwan must not become ‘China’s Taiwan,’ president says
World.content:
LAI CHING-TE. Taiwan President Lai Ching-te speaks at the annual congress of the ruling Democratic Progressive Party in Taipei, Taiwan, July 19, 2026.

Lai Ching-te says Taiwan must remain vigilant in times of peace, pointing to China's 'legal warfare,' such as its new ethnic unity law which gives Beijing the basis to take action against people outside its borders

Taiwan must work together to protect its democracy and not become part of China, President Lai Ching-te said on Sunday, July 19, calling on members of his Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) to oppose the “red terror” coming from Beijing.

Lai, who won election two years ago, and his ruling DPP, champion Taiwan’s separate identity from China, a position that frequently angers Beijing which views the island as an inviolable part of Chinese territory.

Speaking to the DPP’s annual convention, Lai said Taiwan must remain vigilant in times of peace, pointing to what he said was China’s “legal warfare”, such as its new ethnic unity law which gives Beijing the basis to take action against people outside its borders.

That has alarmed Taiwan, because it could give Beijing another legal basis to try and prosecute or arrest Taiwanese it views as separatists. China has rejected all criticism of the law. China’s legal system has no jurisdiction in Taiwan.

“I also expect comrades within the party to stand on the front lines, unite as one, and jointly oppose the threat posed by China’s ‘red terror’ to Taiwanese society,” Lai added, speaking in Taiwanese, also known as Hokkien or Hoklo, rather than the main language of government, Mandarin.

“We must work together to protect our democratic and free way of life, and absolutely never allow ‘democratic Taiwan’ to turn back and become ‘China’s Taiwan’,” he said.

China’s Taiwan Affairs Office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. China has rebuffed Lai’s repeated calls for talks, calling him a “separatist”.

Lai, who is also DPP chairman, reiterated that Taiwan is already an independent country, whose constitutional name is the Republic of China, and it is not subordinate to the People’s Republic of China.

“Regardless of ethnic group, regardless of who came earlier or later, anyone who identifies with Taiwan is a master of the country. Taiwan’s future must be decided jointly by the 23 million people of Taiwan,” he said.

The defeated Republic of China government fled to Taiwan in 1949 after losing a civil war with Mao Zedong’s communists, who formed the People’s Republic.

To this day neither government formally recognizes the other and no peace treaty to end the civil war or armistice has ever been signed.

Over the past decade of DPP government, Lai said Taiwan had not backed down in the face of “authoritarian expansion,” disinformation attacks, military threats, and diplomatic pressure.

“Taiwan has shown the world that democracy is not a weakness; democracy is strength,” he added. – Rappler.com

World.title: Bomb threat forces class suspension at 2 schools in Pateros
World.content:
.

LUCENA CITY – Face-to-face classes at two public schools in Pateros were suspended on Monday, July 20, following an alleged bomb threat.

In a public advisory posted on its Facebook page at around 5:30 a.m., the local government of Pateros announced the cancellation of in-person classes at Pateros National High School and the nearby Pateros Elementary School.

“As a precautionary measure and to ensure everyone’s safety, face-to-face classes are suspended today following the receipt of a security threat (bomb threat) at Pateros National High School (Main Campus),” read the advisory, written in Filipino.

Article continues after this 

READ: Police: No bomb at Mandaluyong High School after alleged threat

As an added safety measure, face-to-face classes at the adjacent Pateros Elementary School were also suspended to protect the welfare of students, teachers, and school personnel.

“The public is encouraged to remain calm, follow the advisories issued by the appropriate authorities, and refrain from spreading unverified information,” the local government said.

Despite the suspension of onsite classes, both schools will shift to online instruction through the Alternative Delivery Mode of Learning, in accordance with the directive of the Department of Education–Schools Division Office of Taguig and Pateros, to ensure that students’ education continues uninterrupted.

World.title: Romblon yacht fire: 4 crew members rescued
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

CALAPAN CITY, Oriental Mindoro — Four crew members were rescued after a private yacht caught fire while sailing through the Sibuyan Strait off San Fernando, Romblon, on July 19, authorities said.

The Mimaropa police said personnel from the San Fernando Municipal Police Station immediately coordinated with the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG), the Municipal Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Office (MDRRMO), and Bantay Dagat volunteers after receiving reports of a burning vessel off Barangay Mabini.

The approximately 20-meter-long yacht, MY JAYSON, was traveling from Subic, Zambales, to Cebu for repairs when it caught fire at around 11 a.m., forcing its crew to abandon the vessel.

Article continues after this 

READ: Motor yacht catches fire off Tingloy, Batangas; 7 crew rescued

Before government rescue teams arrived, four crew members were rescued by local fishermen who responded to the emergency. They were later turned over to the San Fernando municipal government for assistance.

Authorities said responding personnel continued coordinating with the PCG and other concerned agencies to secure the area while waiting for the fire to be fully extinguished and for investigators to determine its cause.

“The safe rescue of all four crew members reflects the value of preparedness, rapid coordination, and strong partnerships during emergencies,” said Police Brig. Gen. Christopher R. Dela Cruz, Mimaropa police regional director.

He also recognized the efforts of the Philippine Coast Guard, MDRRMO, Bantay Dagat volunteers, and local fishermen, saying their immediate response helped save lives. /mcm

World.title: Baguio circumferential road crash injures 3
World.content:
INQUIRER FILES

BAGUIO CITY, Philippines — Three people were injured after a private van carrying 14 passengers crashed into a concrete barrier along the Balacbac Circumferential Road here on Sunday afternoon, July 19, during heavy rains, police said.

The accident occurred at around 4:30 p.m., according to the Baguio City Police Office (BCPO). The white Kia van, bound for Nueva Ecija, was carrying eight adults and six minors who had attended activities at the Baguio Cathedral.

The driver and two passengers sustained minor injuries in the crash. The identities of the van’s occupants had not been released as of presstime.

Article continues after this 

READ: 1 dead, 6 injured in Baguio City highway mishap

Initial police investigation showed that the van was descending the road when the driver failed to shift to a lower gear and could not stop the vehicle’s acceleration with the brakes due to its weight and the rain-slicked road.

Police officers and emergency medical responders immediately assisted the victims at the scene.

However, the injured individuals declined to be taken to a hospital for further medical evaluation and treatment. It was not clear whether they chose to commute out of Baguio.

World.title: Green ribbon drive fights tree cutting in Pangasinan
World.content:
DEFENDING NATURE Members of the Pangasinan People’s Strike for the Environment (PPSE) and partner groups hold a ribbon-hanging activity at the Urdaneta City People’s Park in this phototaken on July 16 to call for a halt to large-scale tree cutting in Pangasinan, particularly at the Capitol Complex in Lingayen. —Photo courtesy of PPSE

LINGAYEN, PANGASINAN, Philippines — Green ribbons carrying messages urging people to “save the trees before the province loses another piece of its natural heritage” fluttered along Maramba Boulevard here on Saturday as environmental advocates staged a symbolic protest against continued tree cutting in Pangasinan.

Members of the Pangasinan People’s Strike for the Environment (PPSE), a grassroots environmental network, tied the ribbons to roadside trees with the support of youth organizations, local councils and other environmental groups from across the province.

The activity was intended to protest what the groups described as development projects that prioritize infrastructure and profit over environmental protection and public welfare.

Article continues after this 

READ: Caritas: Tree cutting direct assault on poor

For the organizers, each green ribbon symbolizes a commitment to protect trees that serve as natural defenses against extreme heat, flooding and the worsening impacts of climate change.

“This is a pledge to protect trees that serve as natural shields against scorching heat, floods and the worsening effects of climate change. Destroying nature is not genuine development. The loss of our public green spaces is not progress,” the group said in a statement.

READ: DENR defends mass cutting of trees in Manila for road project

The environmental advocates also urged authorities to hold accountable those responsible for the continued removal of trees and called on government planners to pursue development that is environmentally sustainable and responsive to the needs of communities.

Article continues after this 

On July 16, PPSE and its partner organizations held a similar campaign at the Urdaneta City People’s Park, renewing their call for the immediate suspension of large-scale tree cutting in Pangasinan, particularly the ongoing removal of trees within the Capitol Complex in Lingayen.

The ribbon-hanging campaign forms part of the group’s broader effort to protect the province’s remaining tree cover and public green spaces.

Article continues after this 

The provincial government said the removal of invasive tree species, including mahogany, at the Capitol Complex is part of the redevelopment of the park.

Cebu campaign

In Cebu, environmental and civic groups recently asked Oslob town officials to release documents on the proposed Oslob Sports and Cultural Center, citing concerns over the conversion of the town’s public plaza and the cutting of century-old trees.

World.title: Marcos’ trust rating at 34%, Sara Duterte at 57% in SWS June poll
World.content:
President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and VP Sara Duterte —Marianne Bermudez/Niño Jesus Orbeta

MANILA, Philippines — Ahead of his fifth State of the Nation Address (Sona) next week, President Marcos’ trust rating dropped by a percentage point to a new record-low in the second quarter of the year, according to the latest Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey.

Vice President Sara Duterte maintained a stronger level of public confidence amid her impeachment trial.

Commissioned and released on Sunday by think tank Stratbase Group, the SWS survey conducted from June 20 to 29 showed that 34 percent of Filipinos said they had “much trust” in Marcos—down from 35 percent in the previous survey in March.

Article continues after this 

This was the lowest trust rating received by Marcos since July 2024 when he had enjoyed his highest confidence among Filipinos at 64 percent.

READ: Marcos’ net satisfaction rating rises to -7 in June

The other 45 percent said they had “little trust” with the President—the highest level of distrust Marcos had received since getting 41 percent in November 2025.

The remaining 19 percent of the respondents were undecided.

Trust in VP

Marcos’ trust rating had steadily dropped since July 2024, when he and his estranged ally Duterte, his running mate in 2022, started on equal footing, with the Vice President enjoying a high 65 percent.

Article continues after this 

READ: Analyst tracks why Marcos ratings sank most in Mindanao

The President’s numbers briefly recovered in May and June last year (at 38 and 48 percent of high trust, respectively), before dropping in the succeeding months until his new low in the latest survey.

Article continues after this 

Duterte sustained a comparatively high level of public trust among Filipinos, despite the controversies thrown at her, which led to her being impeached twice in two years.

The survey found that 57 percent of Filipinos said they had much trust in the Vice President in June 2026, a figure that remained unchanged from March this year.

Twenty-seven percent said they had little trust in her, while 15 percent were undecided.

Marcos is set to deliver his penultimate Sona a week later on July 27.

Unfazed by poll numbers

The House of Representatives has yet to confirm if Duterte will attend this year’s Sona after skipping it in the past two years since her fallout with the President in 2024.

Malacañang on July 16 said Marcos is already finalizing his Sona speech but declined to disclose specific details or key themes to be highlighted by the President.

According to Palace press officer Claire Castro, Marcos remains unfazed by his recent trust and public approval ratings. She said his priority is to work for Filipinos rather than improving his survey numbers.

‘Wake-up call’

Castro also said members of the Cabinet should use the survey to improve services to Filipinos.

For Stratbase Institute president Victor Andres “Dindo” Manhit, the latest survey results should be seen as a key opportunity for the Marcos administration to respond to growing public concerns and outline its priorities for the remainder of its term.

While Malacañang had chosen to repeatedly dismiss every survey result, Manhit said the latest findings should already serve as a “wake-up call” for Marcos.

“As President Marcos prepares to deliver his fifth Sona, Filipinos will be looking not for rhetoric but for a clear plan to address the issues that affect their daily lives,” Manhit said.

He urged the President to “demonstrate stronger political will in bringing down the cost of food and other basic commodities, ensuring stable prices, creating quality jobs, and improving the delivery of essential public services.”

‘Public confidence’

Manhit also advised the President to use the Sona to reassure the public that the government is serious about strengthening accountability and good governance.

“Recent controversies, including questions surrounding flood control projects and the ongoing impeachment proceedings against the Vice President, have heightened public demand for transparency and responsible leadership,” he said.

“The President has an opportunity to show that no one is above accountability and that public resources will be protected. Restoring public confidence begins with delivering meaningful solutions to the everyday concerns of the Filipino people,” he added.

The survey, which polled 1,200 respondents, had an error margin of ±3 percent for national percentages, and ±6 percent for Metro Manila, Luzon outside Metro Manila, the Visayas and Mindanao, at a 95-percent confidence level. It utilized face-to-face interviews using a structured questionnaire with visuals. —WITH A REPORT FROM INQUIRER RESEARCH

World.title: Cops probe online activities of slain pro-Marcos vlogger
World.content:
PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. —Photo from Office of the Chief PNP/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The online activities of pro-Marcos vlogger Alicia Lipata is one of the angles being examined by the Philippine National Police, which ordered on Sunday a full investigation into her killing.

Lipata, popularly known online as “Mima Alicia,” had 362,000 subscribers on YouTube through her channel “Alicia Comments.”

In a statement, PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said he would expect investigators to conduct a thorough probe, particularly into the possibility that the attack was connected to the victim’s activities as a political vlogger.

Article continues after this 

READ: Pro-Marcos vlogger shot dead, partner hurt

The National Capital Region Police Office (NCRPO) was directed to cover all possible angles, including Lipata’s presence and engagements on social media.

Earlier, NCRPO spokesperson Maj. Hazel Asilo said the vlogger was a “BBM (Bongbong Marcos) loyalist” based on her social media posts.

READ: Davao Oriental political vlogger shot dead

Initial police reports showed that two motorcycle-riding suspects shot Lipata and her partner outside her residence in Caloocan City on Friday morning.

Article continues after this 

PNP commitment

Neighbors rushed both to a hospital, but only the vlogger’s partner survived.

“Violence has no place in a society where freedom of expression is honored and respected,” Nartatez said in a statement.

Article continues after this 

“There may be differences in beliefs and opinion, but we in the PNP commit to uphold and protect the right to express them — and this includes aggressively running after those responsible in this case,” he added.

In a statement on Sunday, the Northern Police District (NPD) also expressed its condolences to Lipata’s family and said the Special Investigation Task Group “MIMA” remains active in efforts to swiftly resolve her killing.

The Caloocan City Police Station is spearheading the investigation, with authorities carrying out intelligence and investigative operations to identify and track down the suspects.

“The victim has undergone an autopsy, the findings of which will form part of the evidence being evaluated,” said the NPD, led by acting district director Brig. Gen. Benliner Capili.

The NPD added that it continues to coordinate with the victim’s family to keep them informed of developments and provide assistance.

To protect the integrity of the case, the NPD said it would withhold additional details for now.

Authorities urged individuals with relevant information to contact the investigation officer-on-case, Police Staff Sgt. Romnick Laceda, through the Caloocan police station or the nearest police station, assuring them of confidentiality.

World.title: LTFRB revives fixed pickup rates for ride-app services
World.content:
File photo

MANILA, Philippines — The Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) on Sunday announced it was reviving fixed pickup fares for transport network vehicle service (TNVS) to prevent the charging of unauthorized fees to commuters.

LTFRB Chair Vigor Mendoza II said the revival of Memorandum Circular (MC) 2025-058 aims to provide a “middle ground” for the TNVS sector and commuters.

“While commuters’ welfare is a priority, part of our mandate is also to ensure that the concerns of those from the public transportation sectors are heard. In this case, the revival of the pickup fare implementation will serve both ends,” Mendoza said in a press release.

Article continues after this 

READ: LTFRB imposes price cap on online taxi booking fees

The circular, dated Dec. 17, 2025, allowed the ride-hailing services to charge passengers once a booking was accepted, instead of from the pickup point. The LTFRB attributed this to the TNVS drivers’ operational challenges in configuring the platform and dealing with the traffic situation in Metro Manila.

READ: DOTr orders halt on onboarding new TNVS drivers, motortaxi riders

The circular, which was first implemented from Dec. 20, 2025, to Jan. 4, 2026, provided the following fixed rates:

—For hatchback/subcompact: price cap of P24 within a one-kilometer radius; P72 (3 km); P96 (4 km); and P120 (5 km).

Article continues after this 

—Sedan type: P26 (1 km); P52 (2 km), P78 (3 km), P104 (4 km), and P130 (5 km).

—AUV/SUV type: P29 (1 km); P58 (2 km); and P145 (5 km).

Article continues after this 

‘Availability of rides’

The new MC 2026-059 states that the revival was found reasonable “to prevent service shortages, ensure the availability of rides across all areas, and protect the riding public from unauthorized or improvised pick-up charges.”

The LTFRB also directed transportation network companies (TNCs) “to limit the matching radius to five (5) kilometers to minimize passenger waiting time and operational costs.”

“No Pick-Up Fare beyond the five (5)-kilometer radius amounts above shall be imposed or collected,” it stated.

It further instructed TNCs to:

• Clearly and separately show the pickup fare in the fare breakdown displayed to the passenger prior to confirmation of the booking;

• Inform the passenger of the total fare, including the pickup fare, before acceptance of the ride; and
