Should Abkhazia’s MPs be required to speak Abkhaz?

World.title: Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from Council of Europe: sovereignty strategy and possible consequences
World.content:
Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from the Council of Europe

On 13 July, speaking at the opening ceremony of the 4th Global Media Forum in Shusha, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev said the country was considering a complete withdrawal from the Council of Europe (CoE). His remarks came after the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE) decided in January 2024 not to ratify the credentials of the Azerbaijani delegation, effectively suspending its voting rights.

Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe voluntarily in 2001. According to the government’s official position, it sought membership to make use of international mechanisms and secure support for resolving the Karabakh conflict. Relations between Baku and the organisation, however, gradually deteriorated. After Azerbaijan restored full control over its internationally recognised territory in 2023, the authorities described PACE’s decisions as unfair and politically motivated. Aliyev’s latest statement reflects a broader reassessment of sovereignty in Azerbaijan’s foreign policy and its approach to international organisations.

This article draws on official statements, independent analysis and international sources to examine Azerbaijan’s position, the criticism it has faced, and the potential consequences of leaving the Council of Europe.

Official position and arguments

Speaking at the 4th Global Media Forum in Shusha, President Ilham Aliyev said Azerbaijan was seriously considering leaving the Council of Europe altogether.

“I openly say that Azerbaijan is considering the possibility of completely withdrawing from the organisation. This is not about suspending or freezing our membership. We are definitely considering leaving this institution.”

Aliyev also argued that if Azerbaijan were to leave the Council of Europe, ordinary citizens would not notice any significant changes and the situation could even improve. State officials and pro-government media framed the issue as one of protecting national sovereignty and accused international institutions of treating Azerbaijan unfairly.

According to the government’s official position, Azerbaijan joined the Council of Europe in 2001 in the hope of securing international support for resolving the Karabakh conflict. Officials argue that those expectations were never fulfilled. They also describe PACE’s January 2024 decision not to ratify the credentials of the Azerbaijani delegation and suspend its voting rights as punishment for Azerbaijan’s restoration of its territorial integrity in 2023.

“We did not take part in the vote on the election of judges and have been subjected to discrimination for the past two years,” Aliyev said.

The Council of Europe’s leadership, including Secretary General Alain Berset, has contacted Aliyev and urged Azerbaijan not to leave the organisation, while calling for a way to resolve the dispute.

Baku maintains that the next step should come from the Council of Europe. According to the government, PACE should first restore the Azerbaijani delegation’s voting rights, after which the delegation could return to its work in the Assembly. Officials argue that leaving the organisation would have little impact on the country’s domestic situation because Azerbaijan already has its own institutional mechanisms in place and regards sovereignty as a top priority. Analysts close to the government have echoed this position, saying Azerbaijan should reject what they describe as bias by international organisations and put national interests first.

Critical assessments and the international perspective

In reports and video coverage published on 13 July, Meydan TV argues that Aliyev’s statement signals preparations for Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from both PACE and the jurisdiction of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR). The outlet published its coverage under the headline: “Aliyev is preparing to withdraw Azerbaijan from PACE and the ECtHR – who will lose out?” It focuses primarily on the risk that Azerbaijani citizens could lose their right to file individual applications with the ECtHR.

According to Meydan TV, such a move would weaken human rights protections, particularly against the backdrop of cases involving the arrests of journalists from AbzasMedia and Meydan TV, as well as the broader state of media freedom. In contrast to the government’s position, the outlet argues that withdrawing from the Council of Europe and ending the ECtHR’s jurisdiction would have significant consequences for ordinary citizens. It notes that the ECtHR dealt with 2,180 cases involving Azerbaijan in 2025 alone, arguing that this reflects the large number of people who turned to the international court after failing to obtain justice in the country’s domestic courts.

RFE/RL places the issue in a broader context. It notes that PACE imposed sanctions on Azerbaijan amid a wave of arrests that began in 2023, a growing number of political prisoners and continued concerns over media freedom. The outlet also points to Azerbaijan’s refusal to invite PACE observers to monitor the presidential election held in February 2024.

RFE/RL also recalls that, as part of the process of joining the Council of Europe between 1996 and 2002, Azerbaijan introduced a number of reforms, including abolishing the death penalty, reforming its penitentiary system and acceding to the European Convention on Human Rights.

The outlet further compares Aliyev’s claim that “little will change, and things may even improve” after withdrawal with Russia’s departure from the Council of Europe in 2022. It argues that Russia’s experience suggests such a move can deprive citizens of access to international human rights protection mechanisms. According to RFE/RL, any Azerbaijani withdrawal from the Council of Europe would primarily affect people seeking justice for human rights violations.

From an international perspective, the possible consequences of Azerbaijan’s full withdrawal from the Council of Europe include greater international isolation and reputational damage, although the Azerbaijani authorities reject this assessment. At the same time, the Council of Europe’s leadership has publicly expressed its desire for Azerbaijan to remain a member of the organisation.

Alternative platforms and a long-term strategy

Azerbaijan’s foreign policy has traditionally been based on a multi-vector approach that seeks to balance relations with different international partners. This strategy allows the country to engage selectively with international organisations in line with its national interests. According to the government’s official position, regional and international bodies such as the Organization of Turkic States, the Organization of Islamic Cooperation and the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation offer forms of cooperation that place greater emphasis on sovereignty and equal partnership. Officials argue that these organisations provide opportunities to expand cooperation in areas including the economy, energy, culture and security.

At the same time, Azerbaijan continues to deepen its energy partnership with European countries. Projects such as the Southern Gas Corridor and natural gas exports operate independently of the country’s membership in the Council of Europe. As a result, Baku argues that a stronger focus on sovereignty can coexist with pragmatic economic and energy cooperation with Europe.

In the longer term, this diversification is intended to give Azerbaijan greater flexibility in its foreign policy and allow it to maintain balanced relations with different partners. Critics warn that leaving the Council of Europe could weaken international human rights safeguards available to Azerbaijani citizens. The government, however, argues that alternative international platforms can offset any gaps in economic and political cooperation. Overall, officials present this strategy as part of a broader effort to pursue an independent foreign policy based on Azerbaijan’s national interests.

Azerbaijan’s withdrawal from the Council of Europe

World.title: Russian MFA spokeswoman: ‘West cannot stomach Georgia’s independence’
World.content:
Maria Zakharova on Georgia and OSCE

Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Georgian Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze‘s assessment of Western institutions required no further confirmation from Moscow, adding that the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly had long pursued a course of “aggression, aggressive rhetoric and destructive actions”.

Zakharova’s remarks came in response to a question at a news conference on whether the Russian Foreign Ministry shared Kobakhidze’s assessment. Kobakhidze had earlier accused the OSCE and European institutions of involvement in attempts to bring about a violent change of government in Georgia.

Maria Zakharova: “The Georgian prime minister’s remarks require no confirmation from us. We are talking about the leader of a sovereign state who knows and loves his country and represents its people.

Modern Georgia is a clear example of brazen, and at times unprecedented, external interference in the affairs of a state that possesses all the attributes of sovereignty

Tbilisi’s determination to pursue an independent and nationally oriented policy — meaning one focused on its own people, who are themselves multi-ethnic — is perceived by the ‘collective West’ as a direct challenge. To put it in plain Russian, it sticks in their throat.

This irritates Western representatives so much that they are prepared to use every lever at their disposal to remove the current government simply because it serves the interests of its own people, thinks about them, understands them and their history, and builds the country’s future on that basis, rather than serving those who have nothing to do with the Georgian people or their history.

The Georgian prime minister’s remarks apparently relate to the adoption of the Hague Declaration at the annual session of the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly. The declaration includes a number of resolutions, including one concerning Georgia’s ‘undemocratic’ elections.

Such destructive activity by the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly comes as no surprise to us. The assembly long ago chose the path of aggression. A number of states use the OSCE platform to launch unrestrained criticism not only of Russia but also of other countries, including through the use of the ‘Moscow Mechanism’ — an outdated, pseudo-human-rights and non-consensual instrument.

Everything they allege against Georgia, including the accusations you have asked about, is false.”

OSCE resolution

On 8 July, the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly adopted a critical resolution on Georgia calling on the country’s authorities to release political prisoners, repeal legislation restricting civil liberties and uphold democratic standards.

The resolution, entitled Protecting Electoral Integrity and Fundamental Freedoms in Georgia, forms part of the Hague Declaration, the final document adopted at the assembly’s 33rd annual session, held in the Netherlands from 4 to 8 July.

Representatives of Georgia’s ruling Georgian Dream party attended the session but walked out in protest at the adoption of the resolution.

World.title: Armenia begins ratifying TRIPP agreement with US: foreign minister outlines key details
World.content:
Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

Armenia has begun the process of ratifying the framework agreement on strategic cooperation with the United States under the TRIPP project.

The agreement concerns the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), a transit route linking Azerbaijan with its exclave of Nakhichevan. The project forms part of the Armenian government’s Crossroads of Peace initiative, which aims to reopen regional transport links.

The government has approved the agreement and submitted it to the Constitutional Court. The court must now determine whether it complies with Armenia’s constitution.

“If the Constitutional Court finds that the obligations set out in this international agreement are compatible with Armenia’s constitution, we will submit it to the National Assembly in accordance with the established procedure and bring it before parliament for discussion,” Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said, outlining the next steps. Parliament must ratify the agreement before it can take effect.

Mirzoyan said Armenia must also finalise two more documents before it can complete the TRIPP project. They include a shareholders’ agreement and the charter of the TRIPP Development Company.

The foreign minister also commented on reports about the TRIPP+ fund. Britain’s The Guardian reported on the fund a day earlier, prompting questions in Armenia about the new structure. Mirzoyan said it was an American investment fund and would have only “an indirect connection” with the company that Armenia plans to establish.

Armenia and the United States initialled the framework agreement on strategic cooperation under the Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity project on 26 May 2026. Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio took part in the initialling ceremony in Yerevan. They signed the agreement shortly afterwards through a remote procedure. Rubio signed it in Washington on 1 June, while Mirzoyan signed it in Yerevan on 4 June. “To dispel any possible questions, I would like to note that international practice and Armenian legislation both provide for the signing of such non-simultaneous, remote agreements, and this is a widely accepted practice,” Ararat Mirzoyan said during today’s government meeting. On 8 August 2025, the leaders of Armenia, Azerbaijan and the United States signed a joint declaration at a summit in Washington, marking the launch of the regional connectivity project. The declaration mentioned the Trump Route project for the first time. Before that, Armenia and Azerbaijan had failed to reach agreement on the issue. Azerbaijan had demanded a route it called the “Zangezur Corridor”. Armenia said it was ready to reopen all transport links. At the same time, it firmly rejected the term “corridor”, arguing that it implied the loss of sovereign rights over its territory. The parties reached a compromise only in Washington. They agreed that Armenia would retain sovereign control over the route, while the United States would join the project as a business partner.

“Armenia and the US will help strengthen peace in the South Caucasus”

According to Armenia’s foreign minister, the TRIPP project will help bring peace, stability and prosperity to the South Caucasus. He said it would achieve this by promoting:

transport connectivity;

infrastructure development; and

regional and global trade.

Under the framework agreement, Armenia and the United States will establish the TRIPP Development Company. The company will have the authority to create special purpose entities and bring in additional partners to implement individual projects in Armenia.

“The entire process, from the establishment of the development company to its future operations, will fully respect Armenia’s sovereignty, jurisdiction and territorial integrity,” Ararat Mirzoyan said.

He recalled that the development company would receive land use and development rights for the relevant areas. The parties have set the initial term at 49 years. The United States will hold a 74% stake in the company, while Armenia will own the remaining 26%. If the partnership continues for another 50 years, Armenia’s share will automatically increase to 49% after the first 49-year term.

“If the term is extended, Armenia will not need to take any additional steps to obtain its 49% stake,” the minister said.

Armenia will retain control over border, customs and migration procedures

The foreign minister again stressed that, in line with Armenia’s domestic legislation and international agreements, the Armenian authorities will continue to oversee:

security and the protection of rights;

border control and border security;

customs and migration procedures;

the collection of taxes and customs duties for the state budget;

state information systems; and

public administrative functions.

He said these guarantees should address public concerns about Armenia retaining its sovereign rights over the territory.

What is the link between the TRIPP Development Company and TRIPP+?

Britain’s The Guardian reported that the US State Department had appointed Konstantin Sokolov to lead the TRIPP+ trade fund. Sokolov is a US investor who was born in the Soviet Union and now lives in Chicago.

Armenian media quickly picked up the report. However, questions remained about the nature of the fund and its relationship with the company that Armenia plans to establish to implement the Trump Route project.

Journalists raised the issue during the government meeting. Ararat Mirzoyan replied that the agreement between Yerevan and Washington provides for the creation of the TRIPP Development Company.

“Its founders will be the Armenian government and the TRIPP Development Company-USA, which will be established in the United States,” Mirzoyan said.

As for TRIPP+, he said it is an American company established under the TRIPP Development Company-USA. Its role will be to attract investment for the project.

“From a legal perspective, TRIPP+ has only an indirect relationship with the TRIPP Development Company that will be established in Armenia,” the minister said..

Armenia begins ratifying the TRIPP agreement

World.title: A quick breakdown of the offside rule
World.content:
Spain has just won the FIFA World Cup 1-0 in a match against Argentina that ran down to the wire.

During extra time, it looked as though Ferran Torres had scored a goal that would have brought Spain's lead to two and sealed a victory.

It was the second goal disallowed for Spain, this time for offside.

So what is the offside rule?

It's an infamous question asked by millions of football newbies every tournament.

If you've jumped on the World Cup bandwagon and found yourself trying to wrap your head around this section of the rule book, we're here to help.

Here's a quick breakdown of the rule.

Why does it exist?

The offside rule aims to prevent players from lingering next to the opponent's net to wait for a pass.

It forces teams to build up play carefully and use complex tactics to score goals.

Without the rule, teams would be incentivised to constantly launch long balls, making the game less dynamic.

So how does it work?

If a player is called for an offside offence, the referee will stop the play and award an indirect free kick to the opposing team.

The free kick is taken from the spot where the offside player had been located when their teammate passed them the ball.

What is a free kick? Read more A free kick is awarded when a player on one team does something wrong, with the referee giving the other team a chance to kick the ball while play has stopped. A penalty is essentially the same thing, except the kick is taken inside the penalty box, which is directly in front of the goal, and opposing players aren't allowed to interfere until after the shot is taken. Goals can be scored from either a free kick or a penalty kick, but they are more easily achieved from penalties.

When is a player offside?

A player is in an offside position if:

they're standing in their opponent's half; and

they're nearer to the goal than both the ball and the last line of defenders at the exact moment the ball is passed to them by a teammate.

However, an offside player is only penalised if they become involved in play.

And there's no offside offence if a player receives the ball directly from an opposition player, a goal kick, a throw-in or a corner kick.

Test your knowledge

World.title: Why the Tate brothers were arrested and what they are charged with
World.content:
Influencer brothers Andrew and Tristan Tate have been arrested in Miami after UK prosecutors said they had brought further rape and sex trafficking charges against them.

These charges are on top of previous accusations of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain, between 2012 and 2015, in the UK.

One of the brothers, Andrew Tate, is also facing charges for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.

Britain's Crown Prosecution Service said the new charges related to four further victims and were brought after authorities received evidence from Bedfordshire Police in south-eastern England.

The charges include rape, assault, trafficking and offences relating to "indecent images of a child and extreme pornography".

The case against the Tate brothers in Romania has not been closed. (Reuters: Inquam Photos/Eduard Vinatoru)

The charges bring the total number of alleged victims in the UK to seven and are the latest in a long-running international legal saga involving the brothers that has spanned the US, Britain and Romania.

The brothers have denied wrongdoing.

An attorney for the brothers, Joseph McBride, blasted the latest charges as "filth and slander". In a phone interview Sunday, he said he was confident the extradition request would be denied.

Here are some things to know about the Tate brothers.

Who the Tate Brothers are

Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, are dual US-British citizens known for their social media empire promoting wealth, male dominance and misogyny.

The new charges against Andrew Tate relate to rape, sex trafficking, assault and extreme pornography. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist who has amassed more than 10 million followers, most of them boys and young men, on X.

He has been banned from platforms YouTube, TikTok and Instagram for violating hate speech guidelines.

He also runs an online academy where he says he teaches young men how to get rich and attract women.

Tristan Tate is also a former kickboxer.

The brothers are avid supporters of US President Donald Trump.

What the Tates are charged with

Andrew Tate and his brother have faced multiple charges in the UK and Romania, where they moved to in 2016.

British prosecutors said the new charges related to alleged offences between 2010 and 2017.

They said Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault and 19 charges for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography.

Tristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating sex trafficking.

Andrew Tate is a former professional kickboxer and self-described misogynist. (Reuters: Inquam Photos/Octav Ganea)

The Crown Prosecution Service said in a statement it "has requested the extradition of the Tates from the US".

"They have been arrested and await extradition proceedings to the UK," it said.

The Tates already face previous charges of rape, bodily harm, human trafficking and controlling prostitution for gain relating to three other alleged victims in the UK between 2012 and 2015.

In June, a UK High Court judge threw out a legal bid by the Tates to be told the names of their accusers.

In Romania, the siblings were arrested in late 2022 along with two Romanian women.

The four were accused of participating in criminal schemes to lure women for sexual exploitation.

The issues dividing Trump's base The release of the Epstein files followed some of Donald Trump's dedicated supporters launching a rare revolt against the US president. Here are six more issues that could also divide Republicans.

They denied those allegations, and the Romanian case hasn't gone forward because of legal and procedural problems.

The case hasn't been closed, and there is also a separate legal case against the brothers in Romania.

Andrew Tate has repeatedly claimed that prosecutors in Romania have no evidence against him and that there is a political conspiracy to silence him.

How the extradition process could work

The brothers are expected to appear before a magistrate judge in Miami, where they are currently being held in federal detention.

Bail is rarely granted to those held for international extradition, and their lawyer said he expected they would remain jailed for the time being.

In the coming weeks, a US district judge will consider whether they meet the conditions for extradition.

The ultimate decision about whether to order the extradition will fall to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

While the State Department has discretion to deny extradition requests from the UK, it has granted almost every British request since ratifying a strengthened extradition treaty in 2007.

One exception came during Trump's first term, when the US declined an extradition request for the wife of a former American diplomat involved in a fatal crash in England, citing diplomatic immunity.

The rejection prompted an international outcry.

Why the Tates were in the US

British police previously sought the Tates' extradition to the UK once their legal proceedings in Romania concluded.

But in February 2025, they were allowed to leave Romania after authorities lifted travel restrictions, and they flew to Florida on a private jet.

Romania's foreign minister said at the time that a US official in the Trump administration had expressed interest in the brothers' legal case in Romania.

Trump said he knew "nothing about" the case when asked if his administration pressured the Romanian government to release the Tates.

World.title: Decade of work helps remote island's native wildlife 'return to 1616'
World.content:
For the first time in more than a century, a pint-sized native marsupial is bouncing through the brush of a remote island off Australia's remote west coast.

Dirk Hartog Island, or Wirrawunna, sits about 850 kilometres north of Perth in the renowned Shark Bay World Heritage Area.

After years of damage by invasive species, the past decade has seen a slow but steady process of environmental repair.

Bettongs, or "rat kangaroos", are the latest creature to benefit from that work.

According to wildlife expert Rebecca Quah, they might not have without researchers getting their hands a little "dirty".

"There's so much you can do with poop," she said.

" You just gotta get in there. "

The tiny marsupials are part of a series of reintroductions on the WA island. (Supplied: DBCA)

A new study, published in the journal Ecosystems, has shone a light on the complex and often unglamorous tasks faced by scientists when translocating species from one place to another.

In the case of the mouse-like bettong, the job quite literally began from the ground up.

Ms Quah analysed the fungal contents of bettong faeces to determine if the animal's former home was fit for habitation.

While not for the squeamish, their findings have fed a tangible conservation outcome: guiding one of the final animal reintroductions in an ambitious effort to restore WA's largest island to pre-colonial times.

Return of the 'rat kangaroo'

Bettongs were once widespread in Australia before being hunted to the brink of extinction by invasive predators.

The boodie, or burrowing bettong, gets its name from Noongar language. (Supplied: Rebecca Quah)

Feral cats and European foxes preyed upon the nocturnal foragers and decimated their numbers across the country's desert landscapes.

"They are very sweet animals," said Ms Quah, a PhD student at Edith Cowan University.

"They're [like] a really small kangaroo; [a] hoppy macropod sort of animal.

" That's how they got their nickname, rat kangaroo. "

Today, bettongs live under the close eye of conservationists and mostly in fenced-off sanctuaries.

In 2025, WA's Department of Biodiversity, Conservation and Attractions (DBCA) set about reintroducing one type of bettong, an endangered, brushtail variety called a woylie, to Dirk Hartog Island.

Feral animals have largely been eliminated from the national park off Shark Bay as part of the Return to 1616 project.

The Return to 1616 project seeks to restore Dirk Hartog Island's pre-colonial ecosystem. (Supplied: Samille Mitchell, DBCA)

The DBCA initiative hopes to wind back the ecological clock at the erstwhile pastoral station to the moment Dutch explorer Dirk Hartog set foot on its shores.

Bettongs round out a long list of native fauna in the program, but park managers first had to be sure there was enough food to support a new population.

Mushrooms on the menu

Feral goats ravaged much of Dirk Hartog Island's native vegetation, so meeting the bettongs' dietary requirements was far from guaranteed.

"Firstly, I had to decipher what sort of fungi the bettongs were eating … and specifically I was looking through their poop," Ms Quah said.

"Poop is so useful for understanding so much about animals, not just their diets. You can do so much with it, like studying hormones, stress levels, reproduction."

Rebecca Quah in the field. (Supplied)

By scrutinising the scat left behind by mainland bettongs, Ms Quah could paint a clear picture of what they ate.

She crafted the menu down to the molecule and extracted fungal DNA from samples gathered in WA and the Northern Territory

These produced a "meta-barcode", or a fingerprint-like impression of DNA sequences in the waste, for easy comparison with soil taken from Dirk Hartog Island.

"The results were really encouraging actually," Ms Quah said.

"Dirk Hartog Island is home to 75 different types of fungi that produce those larger, more visible fruiting bodies that animals are likely to go for.

"More importantly, approximately 50 per cent of those fungi that boodies and woylies eat are also present on the island."

Loading...

Island brought back to life

Early monitoring of the reintroduced woylies has been encouraging.

DBCA plans for a group of boodies, woylies' burrowing bettong relatives, to join them in the springtime.

"[Ms Quah's] work has been really crucial in helping understand how the two bettong species coexist at other sites," Return to 1616 senior project officer Colleen Sims said.

"There's going to be a good food source and a good variety of foods … that both these bettongs will be able to turn to."

Early signs suggest the woylies are eating and breeding well on Dirk Hartog Island. (Supplied: Ian Wheeler, DBCA)

The boodies are the penultimate species slated for Dirk Hartog Island, a decade after the Return to 1616 project began.

Dr Sims said a native mammal predator would be brought to the island in the next five years to cap off the restored ecosystem.

But positive changes were already taking hold.

"You can see those animals around, you can see the digging and the changes that they shift in the soil and the effect they have on the vegetation," Dr Sims said.

" It's really bringing the island to life. "

For Ms Quah, even a small part in the project affirmed her many hours of research.

"To see these animals living and thriving in a place that they used to be, that's very special," she said,

World.title: Ken Hinkley to be announced as inaugural Tasmania Devils coach
World.content:
Former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley will be formally unveiled as the inaugural coach of the Tasmania Devils this morning.

It completes a year-long hunt for a senior coach for the AFL's newest club, that included strong interest from high-profile candidates John Longmire and Nathan Buckley.

It is understood Hinkley will join the club on a five-year deal, that will take him through until the end of the 2031 season.

The 59-year-old was whisked into Hobart yesterday morning for a final presentation to the Devils' coaching selection panel, which included chair Grant O'Brien, CEO Brendon Gale, football director Alastair Lynch and culture boss Lauren Jauncey.

Devils coaching choice both a blessing and a curse The Tasmania Devils need to pick a coach to get them ready for their AFL entry.

It was Jauncey who accompanied Hinkley into Hobart yesterday.

Following a presentation to the panel at Hobart's Tasman Hotel yesterday afternoon, the decision to sign Hinkley was ratified by the board.

The appointment is the most consequential in the Devils' short history, surpassing that of inaugural CEO Brendon Gale in 2024, with Hinkley now charged with building the Devils into an on-field force and acting as the club's public face and spokesperson.

Tasmania had made no secret of securing a "people person" as its inaugural coach, with the JackJumpers NBL club's appointment of now championship-winning coach Scott Roth serving as inspiration.

Tasmania Devils chief executive Brendon Gale was part of the Devils' coaching selection panel. (ABC News: Mackenzie Heard)

On Friday, CEO Brendon Gale spoke of the successful candidate having a "real intrinsic motivation" to coach the club.

"The people we're speaking with have the ability, and the experience and a track record but this is a big job," he said.

" You've got to really want this job and be prepared to embrace all the challenges and opportunities that come with it. "

One of those challenges will be uniting Tasmania behind the Devils, whose popularity is strong but has been tarnished by at-times vicious debate over the construction of the estimated $1.13 billion Macquarie Point Stadium in Hobart.

Hinkley will also be confronted by the task of galvanising the state's three regions behind the team, which is seen by some as Hobart centric.

Former Port Adelaide coach Ken Hinkley coached the team across 12 seasons, but has never coached a team to the finals. (ABC News: Ben Pettitt)

His coaching record will also be brought into sharper focus in the coming days, as the decision is analysed by the football public.

Across 12 seasons at Port Adelaide, Hinkley coached 282 home and away matches, winning 116 and losing 114 at a record of 59.6 per cent.

But in finals, that winning percentage dipped to just 40 per cent, with six wins coming from 15 appearances.

Hinkley has never coached a team to a grand final.

Fellow candidates John Longmire and Nathan Buckley — who had signalled his strong desire to coach the team more than 12 months ago — were informed yesterday they had been unsuccessful in their pursuit of the role.

World.title: Five-year wait for much-needed housing in WA's holiday hotspot
World.content:
A housing charity trying to build prefabricated, small homes for the homeless in one of Western Australia's premier tourist towns says red tape has proven a significant obstacle.

The development application for the long-vacant railway barracks area has finally been submitted after years of negotiations with the state government over use of the land.

The project was initially proposed by the local Rotary club five years ago as a way to provide social housing on disused land for an increasing number of homeless people across the region.

Julian Sanderson and Gordon Temby were among those who first proposed building tiny houses at the old railway barracks site. (ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia)

MyHome founder Michelle Blakeley said the ongoing process to secure the peppercorn lease of the crown land from the state government had been lengthy, despite broader community support for more social and alternative housing.

"I think everyone from the shire president down would love to see more social housing in Margaret River, right through the South West and Great Southern," she said.

Michelle Blakeley says the process of providing small social housing can be lengthy. (Supplied: Michelle Blakeley)

"Because there's a high demand for holiday rentals, the [rents] in that area are very high, and a lot of people living in that area, even if they are employed, even as key workers, they just can't afford the rents in the area, because they are paying a premium."

Ms Blakeley said the charity had already delivered 30 small social homes on leased vacant land in North Fremantle and Albany, and 24 homes in Carlisle.

Margaret River's old railway barracks date back to the 1920s. (ABC South West WA: Anthony Pancia)

She said the process of obtaining land leases, checking, and securing government funding needed to be streamlined to ensure housing charities could help the homeless.

"We really do have to jump through hoops in a very elongated red tape procedure," she said.

" So that side of it is very frustrating, particularly when we get to winter. "

Small homes built by charity MyHome on leased land in North Fremantle.

She said the Department of Planning indicated negotiations would have to take place with local Aboriginal corporation Karri Karrak.

Karri Karrak chief executive Abby Phillis said while the land was initially intended to form part of the Noongar Land Estate, the corporation was broadly supportive of social and affordable housing being provided on the site.

Shire of Augusta Margaret River chief executive Andrea Sevley said the project would now be assessed.

"The shire has a long history of supporting initiatives that increase access to safe, secure, and affordable housing," she said.

The Margaret River proposal would be similar to these small homes built in North Fremantle. (Supplied: MyHome )

Process not to blame: government

A state government spokesperson rejected suggestions its processes were behind the project's slow progress, saying MyHome had only re-engaged with planning officials this year.

"MyHome advised that their own due diligence investigations concluded the site was not viable for a residential development," the spokesperson said.

"The land is eligible for inclusion in the Noongar Land Estate; however, it has not been offered to Karri Karrak Aboriginal Corporation.

"Its eligibility has not caused a delay."

Should the project be approved, the spokesman said DPLH would consider appropriate tenure to facilitate the development.

Tiny homes can struggle to find a space

Ms Blakeley stressed the project could best be described as small social homes, as separate from mobile "tiny homes", which are placed on a trailer and are privately owned.

Both have been touted as ways to ease the housing crisis, but getting necessary approvals can prove frustrating.

Earlier this year, the Shire of Capel gave a privately owned permanent tiny-homes-on-wheels community the green light. It is believed to be the first of its kind in Western Australia.

In New South Wales, Shellharbour Council has approved a trial of new planning rules to allow tiny homes on residential lots without a development application.

Modular homes on wheels have proven increasingly popular across Australia. (Supplied: Strive Homes )

NSW tiny home builder Brenden Morrissey said people who had purchased tiny homes sometimes struggled with legislative requirements governing where they can be placed.

"It's always a challenge," he said.

"We've got one lady that her tiny home is here, ready, and she's living in South Australia and is still looking for her spot."

Social housing provider Accordwest maintains a mix of housing types is needed to solve housing issues across Regional WA.

Chief executive Danelle Milward said there was no singular solution.

"We need a mix of social housing, affordable housing, crisis accommodation and innovative approaches, including modular housing and other models that can be delivered more quickly," she said.

World.title: Fears massive US private lending market sinking
World.content:
The muddy world of private lending has Australia's corporate regulator on high alert.

Wall Street is ground zero for the alternative investment market and there are fears this massive, risky US private lending ship is sinking and investors are jumping out.

And there are unique risks for Australia too.

"If the Australian property is overvalued, and we see those practices emerging and it happens at scale, you get gaps," ASIC commissioner Simone Constant told The Business.

"And when you get those gaps, you get problems with liquidity, you get lagging in data, you get the risk of default, for example.

"And of course, investors putting their money into things that don't stack up."

Simone Constant is concerned Australian investors could lose money if there is a private credit financial shock. (ABC News: John Gunn)

US private credit firm Blue Owl had to limit the amount of money investors could withdraw this year as the company bled value from souring software investments.

The firm's two private credit funds again faced elevated redemptions — investors seeking to withdraw cash — in the June quarter.

Its shares have plummeted 40 per cent this year as investors have fretted about the lender's exposure to ailing software companies.

US auto lender Tricolor Holdings and UK mortgage lender Market Financial Solutions have already collapsed.

Central banks and regulators watching closely

It has caught the attention of global central banks.

In December, the Bank of England launched a system-wide exploratory scenario exercise to enhance its understanding of broader risks and dynamics in private markets, according to Reserve Bank Freedom of Information (FOI) documents.

Bank of England governor Andrew Bailey told Bloomberg in May: "There are some signs of strain in the market."

The Bank of England, led by Andrew Bailey, wants to better understand the risks and dynamics in private markets. (AP: Toby Melville/Pool)

"We are seeing some increase in requests," he said.

"Quite a big increase in requests for outflows, to take liquidity out."

The results of the UK central bank's review are expected to be published in early 2027.

Documents obtained under FOI, originally requested by Nine, reveal the Reserve Bank has also been making inquiries into financial and economic risks for Australia related to the opaque private credit sector.

ASIC's November 2025 private credit surveillance report noted the "market is growing rapidly, but there are some areas where improvement is needed — and in some cases, materially so".

Wave of money moves out of software

Private credit refers to lending outside the banking sector.

Software companies received much of this non-bank funding earlier this decade, but the flow of funds has since moved towards AI.

Verdad Adviser managing partner Dan Rasmussen has been warning of major global financial stability risks from an eventual implosion of US private credit.

Loading...

"We're going to see more and more pain," he warned.

Mr Rasmussen is worried about a negative feedback loop in which software companies default on their debt and lead to further panic in private credit markets.

"Now what's happening is that there's $100 billion of loans outstanding and there's only $50 billion of new fundraising and private credit," he said.

"Well, that's going to force defaults on itself because there is no-one else who's willing to lend to these companies.

"No bank is going to lend to them, so either the private credit lends to them or they go bankrupt."

Global credit crunch risk

Australia's corporate regulator is bracing for the rising risk of another global credit crunch.

"Private credit is now at a size and at a breadth that hasn't been seen before and certainly hasn't been tested in a downturn," ASIC's Simone Constant said.

"So, there would be bumps."

Locally, there is currently $250 billion worth of private credit loans, up from roughly $35 billion a decade ago.

Nick Kelly thinks the Austrailan market will face challenges in the future. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"It's not just been the retail investors in the market. The institutional investors, superannuation funds and others have piled into this asset class," Wilson Asset Management portfolio manager Nick Kelly said.

"I think the Australian market will face its own challenges in the future, just given the amount of capital that's being deployed into this market, into assets that I don't think are as safe as some people perceive them to be."

And Australia's $4.5 trillion superannuation sector is high on the regulator's worry list.

"So increasingly, every working Australian, investing Australian does have exposure to private credit," Ms Constant said.

Over half of all private lending in Australia is concentrated in property development and construction.

ASIC says it is monitoring loans in this space, but it does not have as much information as it would like.

Australian financial shock

ASIC is concerned a property market crash could trigger a private credit financial shock.

Australian private credit provider Brett Craig, who is Aura Group's director of private credit, said investors in Australian property finance needed to be careful.

"Lending against property construction transactions is a good way to make money if you know what you're doing and you can actually step in should the borrower default," he said.

Brett Craig warns investors in Australian property finance need to be careful. (ABC News: John Gunn)

"But it is a very good way to lose money if you don't have that ability to step in and complete a project as an example."

The concern for regulators, ultimately, is that private investors and superannuants end up footing the bill for weak investments.

"We want there to be confidence in private credit," Ms Constant said.

"What could go wrong? Investors could lose money.

"Investors [may not] understand they're going to lose money, and that could happen at some scale."

Dan Rasmussen said every Australian should know if they were exposed to private credit.

"What we don't know yet is who owns it, to what extent [big US companies own it], and what the downstream consequences are when they find out how bad it's going to be, right?" Mr Rasmussen said.

"And the biggest risk I'd be worried [about] if I was in Australia is how much the superannuation schemes own of it.

"How exposed are they?

"And what happens if this stuff turns out to be materially worse than it looks now?"

World.title: Boxing community mourns death of rising US star Hannah Rapp
World.content:
American boxer Hannah Rapp has been killed in a collision with a car while she was cycling in Brazos, Texas.

The 26-year-old rising boxing star had won eight and drawn one of her first nine professional bouts, capturing the North American Boxing Federation featherweight title.

Last month she challenged Tiara Brown for the World Boxing Council (WBC) featherweight championship, losing by unanimous decision.

Ms Brown paid tribute to Rapp online saying she was "the best dance partner I have ever faced as a pro".

WBC president Mauricio Sulaiman also shared a statement in the wake of the tragedy, describing Rapp as "an exceptional boxer, but above all, an invaluable member of our boxing family".

"We join in the grief that overwhelms her loved ones, her team, and all those who had the privilege of knowing and supporting her throughout her brilliant career," he said.

Internet personality and founder of boxing and mixed martial arts promotion company Most Valuable Promotions, Jake Paul, called Rapp a "warrior" in a tribute posted on X.

"Gone too soon. Condolences to her entire clan," he said.

The Brazos County sheriff's office said it had identified the driver of the vehicle as 31-year-old Charles Medina, who has been charged with manslaughter.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Police release suspect's image after alleged kidnapping attempt
World.content:
Police have released images of a woman they believe was tasked to kidnap another woman in the regional Victorian town of Warrnambool earlier this month.

Police say a 33-year-old woman was walking home from work on Willow Tree Lane on July 7 about 4.30pm when another woman grabbed her from behind and pushed her into a car.

The victim managed to fight off her attacker, but the offender stole her phone and drove south away from the scene.

Authorities have established that the 2016 Hyundai i30 used in the attack was a hire car.

Victoria Police said they believe the woman was tasked with the crime by a man who lives overseas and is known to the victim.

Police say the attacker was a blonde woman aged in her 20s or 30s. (ABC News: Abbey Haberecht)

The female offender is described as Caucasian, aged between 20 and 30 years old with blonde curly hair.

She was wearing a black hoodie and pink hiking pants during the incident.

"We've done a lot of work and progressed our investigation; however, we're now at a stage where we need assistance from the public," Detective Acting Sergeant Joe Fisher said.

" This was a targeted incident in which we believe the woman involved was tasked by a man linked to the victim. "

Detective Acting Sergeant Fisher said he couldn't go into detail on who they believe the individual who ordered the kidnapping may be.

"We believe we know who he is, and he appears to be offshore," he said.

"Our aim today is to identify the woman involved, and we believe someone will know who she is.

"The victim was very brave, and I thank goodness she was able to get away. Luckily, she was not seriously injured."

Investigators have released CCTV of the vehicle driving on Koroit, Hyland and Giffen streets, and Raglan Parade in the hour following the incident.

Detectives are appealing for more CCTV and dash cam vision from motorists who might have been in the street or the surrounding area at the time.

World.title: ASX advances while oil prices climb as Middle East hostilities escalate
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX advances while oil prices climb as Middle East hostilities escalate Stan Choe Updated July 20, 2026 — 10:11am ,first published July 20, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has made a positive start to the week while oil prices have climbed after tensions escalated in the Middle East. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, in early trade. Oil prices advanced over the weekend and jumped more than 2 per cent this morning as the United States launched more airstrikes at Iran in response to the killing of US troops, and Iran fired missiles toward Jordan that risked widening the conflict into neighbouring Israel. On Friday, a fresh selloff in artificial intelligence stocks sent Wall Street lower. The S&P 500 fell 1 per cent to finish its first losing week in the last three and only its third since the end of March. Just a couple of days earlier, it had climbed within 0.5 per cent of its all-time high. Chip stocks and other AI darlings once again were at the centre of the shaky trading on Wall Street. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 406 points, or 0.8 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1.4 per cent. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.71¢.



Chip stocks and other AI darlings once again were at the centre of the shaky trading. They’ve been under pressure for weeks on worries that their prices shot too high and that voracious demand for computer memory and processors may be unsustainable if AI ends up producing less profit and productivity than promised. Nvidia was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 after dropping 2.2 per cent. Its recent losses forced it to briefly cede the No. 1 ranking as the most valuable company on Wall Street Friday, but it finished the day back above Apple. Related Article Private banking ‘Real harm’: Record $830m in fines against banks, financial firms Applied Materials sank 5.6 per cent to trim its surge for the year to 106 per cent. Micron Technology swung between a loss of 5.8 per cent and a gain of 3.2 per cent before slipping 0.5 per cent. Earlier in the morning, tech sold off worldwide. Indexes tumbled 6.5 per cent in Taipei, 4 per cent in Tokyo and 3 per cent in Shanghai as stocks like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. dropped 7.3 per cent.



South Korea’s stock market was closed for a holiday, offering some respite, if only temporary. It’s been at the centre of the AI swings because it’s dominated by two huge tech companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. This past week alone, Seoul’s Kospi stock index had one day where it surged 6.2 per cent and two others where it sank 6.4 per cent and 8.9 per cent. News of a powerful Chinese AI model by startup Moonshot, Kimi K3, further shook markets. Similar to when China’s DeepSeek announced its AI model in early 2025, another low-cost rival to big Western AI models like ChatGPT and OpenAI could potentially hurt demand for computer chips and other components. European stock indexes, which have less of an emphasis on AI and tech, had milder moves. Adding to the pressure on Wall Street were drops for several stocks following their latest earnings reports. Companies are under pressure to deliver big growth for the spring to justify the big moves upward their stock prices have already made. Netflix sank 7.3 per cent after its revenue for the latest quarter fell just short of analysts’ expectations, even though its profit was bigger than expected. Its forecasts for upcoming revenue and profit in the summer also fell below expectations.



Intuitive Surgical, a maker of robotic surgical systems, dropped 14.1 per cent despite topping expectations for the latest quarter. Analysts pointed to worries about slowing procedure growth because of the expiration of enhanced tax credits that helped lower the cost of health insurance for many Affordable Care Act enrollees. Related Article Opinion

Medicare I ended up in a Medicare urgent care clinic … and I liked it Millie Muroi Economics Writer Elon Musk’s SpaceX fell 5.4 per cent and touched its lowest level since its stock began trading on the Nasdaq just over a month ago. The owner of the xAI business has been swept up in the swings for AI stocks, and it also had to abort a test flight of its mega Starship rocket Thursday within a second or so from blasting off. All told, the S&P 500 fell 76.08 points to 7,457.69. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 406.55 to 52,146.42, and the Nasdaq composite sank 361.70 to 25,520.24. The United States expanded its airstrike campaign against Iran early Friday by hitting more bridges and collapsing a tower at a key Iranian port. That raised further worries about whether oil tankers will be able to use the Strait of Hormuz to carry crude from the Persian Gulf to customers worldwide.



High oil prices have sent Treasury yields upward in the bond market, which threaten to slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and all kinds of other investments. Higher yields have already sent the average 30-year mortgage rate to its highest level in nearly a year. But longer-term Treasury yields eased Friday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.55 per cent from 4.57 per cent late Thursday. A report suggested sentiment among U.S. consumers is improving more than economists expected, while expectations for upcoming inflation eased. That’s important for the Federal Reserve, which is considering hikes to interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. If expectations for inflation remain anchored, it could prevent a vicious cycle where people make moves in anticipation of higher inflation, which only worsen it. With AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football Vince Rugari July 20, 2026 — 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The word of the day is suffer. In football, it means to endure under sustained and intense pressure, to remain resilient and disciplined throughout prolonged difficulty. To stay dialled in while the opponent is on top, and to hang in there until the pendulum swings. It is a concept borrowed from the Hispanosphere; in Spanish, the term is sufrir, and for them, it is one half of the game. A duty. Coaches say: “You have to know how to suffer.” It’s what you have to do sometimes, when you’re not doing what you’d prefer to be doing, which is keeping the ball, going on the attack, and making the other team suffer. Spain captain Rodri celebrates winning the World Cup. Getty Images In the World Cup final, both teams suffered. Argentina suffered without the ball, Spain suffered with it. But only one tried to suffer its way to victory. The other tried to win, and won. There can be no arguments: this 2026 model of La Roja is the most deserving World Cup-winning team in history, at least based on the football played in the final. Only one team even played football in this final.



The numbers say it all: 1-0, but also 20 shots to two, almost double the amount of passes (852 to 464). In this match, Argentina’s goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez faced more shots on target (12) than Spain allowed throughout the entire tournament (nine); in this match, they allowed zero. The domination was total, definitive and unprecedented. Anything other than a Spanish victory would have been a profound injustice. In contrast, Argentina took the concept of suffering to its ultimate extreme, and discovered that suffering alone can only take you so far. Specifically, it can take you 105 minutes and 37 seconds deep into a World Cup final – but no further than that. You’re not supposed to suffer for that long. For Lionel Messi and Argentina, the match ended in sadness. AP Argentina became the first team in a World Cup final to go without a single shot in regulation time, the only two thereafter coming in a desperate chase for an equaliser. Evidently, their manager Lionel Scaloni watched Spain’s phenomenal shutout of France in the semi-final and reached the conclusion that his team had no chance of going toe-to-toe with them. So they elected not to bother.



From minute one, they played to defend, they sought to frustrate, they tried to deceive the referee - hoping that at some point, their captain and inspiration Lionel Messi would conjure something to win it for them and end their suffering. It’s often said that Messi is capable of making something out of nothing. But not even he can make something out of less than nothing, or work from negative space. The Spanish are about control, suffocation, overwhelming the opponent. You cannot hurt them if you don’t have the ball. Celebrations are under way in Madrid following Spain’s World Cup win. Getty Images In the end, this was a decisive triumph for the collective over the individual. No single star won them this World Cup; it was a squad of 26, and a national playing pool of thousands. As a country, Spain has built arguably the most complete and effective football ecosystem ever seen. Their methodology is almost faultless. They are now the first nation to hold the men’s and women’s World Cup trophies simultaneously – along with everything else they’ve won. And they will continue to win until someone figures out how to stop them, assuming there is a way to interrupt this machine.



Argentina, in contrast, have for years been a team (and a country) organised around and geared towards the service of Messi. Tactically, physically, spiritually. You can surely understand why: even at 39, the guy is a freak, and continues to win games off his own boot. He did it only a few days ago. If you have that kind of legendary superpower on your team, you have to try to maximise it. But that sort of strategy, when matched against the ultimate team unit, does have its limits. Spain’s Ferran Torres celebrates scoring the winner. AP Photo/Julio Cortez In a way, we all suffered, because this was such a tough watch. As a spectacle, it was unworthy of the early Australian alarm. All those who think football is a boring game would have felt justified for thinking so after seeing La Roja probe unsuccessfully for openings so long, their blunt play evoking the famous Simpsons parody, which still holds up: “Half-back passes to the centre, back to the wing, back to the centre … centre holds it. Holds it! Holds it!” Indeed, there is another kind of suffering: the agony of domination without reward. Of creating chance after chance, only to find an outstretched palm, leg or thigh in the way, or to hear a referee’s whistle stopping the action. Martinez made a staggering 11 saves, yet many of the shots he faced came directly at him. But for some sharper finishing, we all would have been put out of our misery much sooner – Argentina included.



Related Article Live

FIFA World Cup FIFA World Cup 2026 LIVE updates: Spain win 2026 World Cup final after defeating Argentina 1-0 in extra time Credit to them, though, for some phenomenal scrambling defence, which continued despite losing both of their starting centre-backs, Lisandro Martinez and Cristian Romero, to injury, and after being reduced to 10 men with Enzo Fernandez’s second yellow card in the 93rd minute. This frustration could have driven Spain mad; it did, for a while, feel like it was going to be one of those games where the ball refuses to go in. To silence that little voice of doubt, you have to actively resist negative thoughts and persist in the belief that the ball will fall for you, sooner or later. Eventually, it did. Argentina kicked off the second half of extra time but lost possession. From deep in defence, near the corner flag on the left-hand side, Spain pieced together a glorious move, shifting the ball in six passes to the opposite corner, where Pedro Porro’s cross was headed back inside by Nico Williams and then thumped in by Ferran Torres. Pure ecstasy. No more suffering; not for them. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Son of All Blacks great – and Shane Warne’s mate – breaks 63-year hoodoo at British Open
World.content:
SportGolfBritish Open Son of All Blacks great – and Shane Warne’s mate – breaks 63-year hoodoo at British Open Tom Decent Updated July 20, 2026 — 9:54am ,first published 4:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Southport: Ryan Fox’s against-the-odds triumph at Royal Birkdale on Sunday, becoming the first New Zealander in 63 years to win the British Open, was made all the more remarkable by a conversation with his famous father 13 years ago when he was on the verge of walking away from golf. The year was 2013, and Fox was in his second season on the Australasian tour. He wasn’t winning, wasn’t enjoying himself and certainly wasn’t making much money. Ryan Fox with the Claret Jug after winning The 154th Open Championship at Royal Birkdale. Warren Little He arrived at the Australian Masters at Royal Melbourne after “badly” missing the cut at the Australian PGA, wondering whether professional golf was really for him. His father, New Zealand rugby royalty Grant Fox, who won the inaugural Rugby World Cup in 1987, was on the bag as a caddie and asked him one simple question.



Why do you play? “I said, well, it’s supposed to be fun. But it wasn’t really very fun at the time,” Fox recalled. “He goes, ‘Let’s just go out this week and try to have some fun’. Fox celebrates on the 18th green after winning the British Open. AP Photo/Jon Super “I think I finished fifth that week, and that made enough to keep my card for the year. It took the pressure off the rest of the year, and I came back the following year and played really, really well. “I was very close to giving it up at that point.”



With a nerveless 3.5-metre birdie putt on the 18th green in front of a packed grandstand on Sunday, Fox finally shook the tag of being Grant Fox’s son by winning the British Open. The 39-year-old, who began the day in the final group after a brilliant third round 62, closed with a two-under 68 to finish at 10-under, one shot clear of American Cam Young. Australia’s great hope Lucas Herbert briefly threatened before fading with a one-over 71 to finish six-under in a tie for sixth, one shot ahead of Adam Scott. As Herbert addressed reporters afterwards, he watched Fox’s winning putt disappear into the cup on a television nearby.



“I guess I’m chopped liver now,” Herbert joked. “It is what it is. It was a great experience. I can’t be too upset. A lot of positives to take. This is my best finish in a major. I genuinely contended. I was up around the lead for the last, what, 45 holes? There’s a lot to take away from that.” The crowd celebrates with the popular player as he holded a birdie putt on the 18th green to secure victory on day four of the British Open. Getty Images Fox’s victory was built on resilience as the pressure intensified on the back nine. A horror lie in a bunker on the par-three 15th forced him to chip backwards towards the tee box, before salvaging a bogey with a superb up-and-down. After making birdies on the 13th, 14th and 16th holes, he needed one more for glory on the 18th. Fox promised himself he wouldn’t die wondering, telling his caddy he could live with the consequences for the rest of his life if he produced a bad drive on the most difficult hole on the course.



He smashed a perfect drive and fired in a nine-iron from 160 metres. Fox then stayed true to his reputation as one of golf’s quickest players by sinking the winning putt almost before the crowd had time to process the moment. He became the first New Zealander to lift the Claret Jug since Sir Bob Charles in 1963, marking one of the unlikeliest major triumphs in modern golf. His previous best finish in a major was a tie for 16th at the 2019 Open, making him just the second player to win a major without previously recording a top-10 finish. Fox kisses the Claret Jug trophy after winning the British Open. AP Photo/Jon Super “I was a rookie on the DP World Tour at 30. I was a rookie on the PGA Tour at 37 and now a major champion at 39,” Fox said. “The Aussie tour was the first tour I played on. It’s a really underrated tour. “If you’d have given me my career up until yesterday when I first turned pro, I would have jumped at it. Now I probably would have killed people for it.”



Nic Dastey, a close friend of Fox and PGA Australia’s general manager of tournaments, was beaming with pride watching on. Related Article British Open Wonder shot keeps Herbert’s Open hopes alive; McIlroy goes after DeChambeau “The greatest thing I could say about Ryan is he hasn’t changed from the moment he first turned professional. This won’t change him either,” Dastey said. “He’s just a fantastic human being. He’s someone that if you could model the professional golfer on, and someone we would want as a tour member, he’s it. He’s brilliant, and he will always continue to give back to Australian and New Zealand golf.” Fox also forged a close friendship with Shane Warne and dedicated his 2022 Alfred Dunhill Links Championship victory on the Old Course at St Andrews to the spin king. Warne would have been proud of Fox’s poise.



Sunday’s celebrations reflected just how unexpected the moment was. Fox had won twice previously on the PGA Tour, yet when he was asked to crack a champagne bottle for a photo, those nearby could hear him laughing that he had never done it before. “I don’t really know what to think at the moment,” Fox said. “I spoke to my kids last night, and they said, ‘bring back a trophy’. I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them. My family back in New Zealand and all my supporters back there, I know it’s been a long night for them, but I’m glad it was worthwhile. “It’s something you dream of. I used to get up in the middle of the night to watch this tournament back home. It’s unbelievable, surreal, crazy. I don’t have enough words in my vocabulary to explain it, to be honest.” News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: ‘Like a bad trip’: Oasis legend joins roast of World Cup final half-time show
World.content:
Analysis CultureMusicFIFA World Cup ‘Like a bad trip’: Oasis legend joins roast of World Cup final half-time show Robert Moran July 20, 2026 — 7:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The World Cup final delivered the game’s first half-time show ever – and hopefully the last, judging by reactions from pundits and celebrities. Former England striker Wayne Rooney, broadcasting for BBC Sport, said the best part of the performance – which featured Madonna, Justin Bieber and the Muppets – was when it finished. “I like a lot of them artists but I thought it was crap,” he said. What a way to begin! Madonna on the big screen during the half-time show. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher approved of Bieber’s set – “Justin rules,” he posted on X – but he wasn’t so fond of the rest of it. “This is like a bad trip,” he posted. “It’s a good job I’ve got my spiritual socks on or that half-time entertainment could have tipped me over the edge.”



After a nervy first half, viewers were given a fever dream of a half-time performance – one that lasted a record 27 minutes and 22 seconds – to relieve the tension. But this was no Super Bowl level extravaganza. View post on X Madonna opened up the show singing her hit Music from an underground rollerskating rink, in a car being driven by Brazilian legends Ronaldinho and Ronaldo. Before you could even crack a joke about their tracksuits, the action whiplashed elsewhere. Then it was a sudden shift to the Muppets, with composer Gustavo Dudamel doing the White Stripes’ iconic Seven Nation Army. It must’ve had Jack White turning in his grave (because he sleeps in a coffin, probably). Miss Piggy, Kermit the Frog and other Muppets performed during the half-time show. Getty Images



The Ted Lasso cast join the performance. AP Photo/Reed Hoffmann K-pop icons BTS, in all red, slipped into their smash Dynamite, before they got interrupted by Ted Lasso stars Jason Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt, who subbed in edgy Hillsong priest Justin Bieber and his acoustic guitar for a chilled out Everything Hallelujah. Colombian star Shakira brought some appropriate World Cup energy, performing the tournament’s anthem Dai Dai with Burna Boy. What would FIFA do without Shakira? Probably a whole show with the Muppets. Tom Cruise addresses the crowd before the game. Getty Images It’s no Beauty and a Beat, but it’s Justin Bieber we got. Getty



Post Malone donned a cheeky shirt for the opening ceremony: “I just hope both teams have fun”. Getty Images Before the game, Tom Cruise, dressed like a backstage roadie, delivered a stirring speech from the middle of the pitch like he was the Gandalf of futbol. “Football is a language spoken without words, a force that unites people, that turns strangers to friends,” he said, before announcing the teams – “Espana y Argentina” – with all the cultural respect of an SBS commentator. Shakira dances on the stage. Getty Images Post Malone also popped up in a cowboy hat and the tightest Canadian tuxedo you’ll see, performing his new song Chrome Heartbreaker, a return to his rap roots after going country, before bringing out Swae Lee for the Spiderverse hit Sunflowers.



It all made about as much sense as the phrase “New York New Jersey”. Let us never revisit this again. Spotted in the stands for the game were A-listers including Will Ferrell, Pharrell Williams, Adrien Brody, Matt Damon (with his Argentinian wife Luciana Barroso), Trevor Noah in a Spain shirt, and San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama. World.title: ASX advances while oil prices climb as Middle East hostilities escalate
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX advances while oil prices climb as Middle East hostilities escalate Stan Choe Updated July 20, 2026 — 10:11am ,first published July 20, 2026 — 5:22am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket has made a positive start to the week while oil prices have climbed after tensions escalated in the Middle East. The S&P/ASX 200 was up 35 points, or 0.4 per cent, in early trade. Oil prices advanced over the weekend and jumped more than 2 per cent this morning as the United States launched more airstrikes at Iran in response to the killing of US troops, and Iran fired missiles toward Jordan that risked widening the conflict into neighbouring Israel. On Friday, a fresh selloff in artificial intelligence stocks sent Wall Street lower. The S&P 500 fell 1 per cent to finish its first losing week in the last three and only its third since the end of March. Just a couple of days earlier, it had climbed within 0.5 per cent of its all-time high. Chip stocks and other AI darlings once again were at the centre of the shaky trading on Wall Street. AP The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 406 points, or 0.8 per cent, and the Nasdaq composite sank 1.4 per cent. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.71¢.



Chip stocks and other AI darlings once again were at the centre of the shaky trading. They’ve been under pressure for weeks on worries that their prices shot too high and that voracious demand for computer memory and processors may be unsustainable if AI ends up producing less profit and productivity than promised. Nvidia was the heaviest weight on the S&P 500 after dropping 2.2 per cent. Its recent losses forced it to briefly cede the No. 1 ranking as the most valuable company on Wall Street Friday, but it finished the day back above Apple. Related Article Private banking ‘Real harm’: Record $830m in fines against banks, financial firms Applied Materials sank 5.6 per cent to trim its surge for the year to 106 per cent. Micron Technology swung between a loss of 5.8 per cent and a gain of 3.2 per cent before slipping 0.5 per cent. Earlier in the morning, tech sold off worldwide. Indexes tumbled 6.5 per cent in Taipei, 4 per cent in Tokyo and 3 per cent in Shanghai as stocks like Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. dropped 7.3 per cent.



South Korea’s stock market was closed for a holiday, offering some respite, if only temporary. It’s been at the centre of the AI swings because it’s dominated by two huge tech companies, Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix. This past week alone, Seoul’s Kospi stock index had one day where it surged 6.2 per cent and two others where it sank 6.4 per cent and 8.9 per cent. News of a powerful Chinese AI model by startup Moonshot, Kimi K3, further shook markets. Similar to when China’s DeepSeek announced its AI model in early 2025, another low-cost rival to big Western AI models like ChatGPT and OpenAI could potentially hurt demand for computer chips and other components. European stock indexes, which have less of an emphasis on AI and tech, had milder moves. Adding to the pressure on Wall Street were drops for several stocks following their latest earnings reports. Companies are under pressure to deliver big growth for the spring to justify the big moves upward their stock prices have already made. Netflix sank 7.3 per cent after its revenue for the latest quarter fell just short of analysts’ expectations, even though its profit was bigger than expected. Its forecasts for upcoming revenue and profit in the summer also fell below expectations.



Intuitive Surgical, a maker of robotic surgical systems, dropped 14.1 per cent despite topping expectations for the latest quarter. Analysts pointed to worries about slowing procedure growth because of the expiration of enhanced tax credits that helped lower the cost of health insurance for many Affordable Care Act enrollees. Related Article Opinion

Medicare I ended up in a Medicare urgent care clinic … and I liked it Millie Muroi Economics Writer Elon Musk’s SpaceX fell 5.4 per cent and touched its lowest level since its stock began trading on the Nasdaq just over a month ago. The owner of the xAI business has been swept up in the swings for AI stocks, and it also had to abort a test flight of its mega Starship rocket Thursday within a second or so from blasting off. All told, the S&P 500 fell 76.08 points to 7,457.69. The Dow Jones Industrial Average dropped 406.55 to 52,146.42, and the Nasdaq composite sank 361.70 to 25,520.24. The United States expanded its airstrike campaign against Iran early Friday by hitting more bridges and collapsing a tower at a key Iranian port. That raised further worries about whether oil tankers will be able to use the Strait of Hormuz to carry crude from the Persian Gulf to customers worldwide.



High oil prices have sent Treasury yields upward in the bond market, which threaten to slow the economy and undercut prices for stocks and all kinds of other investments. Higher yields have already sent the average 30-year mortgage rate to its highest level in nearly a year. But longer-term Treasury yields eased Friday. The yield on the 10-year Treasury fell to 4.55 per cent from 4.57 per cent late Thursday. A report suggested sentiment among U.S. consumers is improving more than economists expected, while expectations for upcoming inflation eased. That’s important for the Federal Reserve, which is considering hikes to interest rates to keep a lid on inflation. If expectations for inflation remain anchored, it could prevent a vicious cycle where people make moves in anticipation of higher inflation, which only worsen it. With AP The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.
