World.title: Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football
World.content:
Analysis SportSoccerFIFA World Cup Spanish domination shows the limitations of ‘suffering’ in football Vince Rugari July 20, 2026 — 10:02am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The word of the day is suffer. In football, it means to endure under sustained and intense pressure, to remain resilient and disciplined throughout prolonged difficulty. To stay dialled in while the opponent is on top, and to hang in there until the pendulum swings. It is a concept borrowed from the Hispanosphere; in Spanish, the term is sufrir, and for them, it is one half of the game. A duty. Coaches say: “You have to know how to suffer.” It’s what you have to do sometimes, when you’re not doing what you’d prefer to be doing, which is keeping the ball, going on the attack, and making the other team suffer. Spain captain Rodri celebrates winning the World Cup. Getty Images In the World Cup final, both teams suffered. Argentina suffered without the ball, Spain suffered with it. But only one tried to suffer its way to victory. The other tried to win, and won. There can be no arguments: this 2026 model of La Roja is the most deserving World Cup-winning team in history, at least based on the football played in the final. Only one team even played football in this final.



The numbers say it all: 1-0, but also 20 shots to two, almost double the amount of passes (852 to 464). In this match, Argentina’s goalkeeper Emiliano Martinez faced more shots on target (12) than Spain allowed throughout the entire tournament (nine); in this match, they allowed zero. The domination was total, definitive and unprecedented. Anything other than a Spanish victory would have been a profound injustice. In contrast, Argentina took the concept of suffering to its ultimate extreme, and discovered that suffering alone can only take you so far. Specifically, it can take you 105 minutes and 37 seconds deep into a World Cup final – but no further than that. You’re not supposed to suffer for that long. For Lionel Messi and Argentina, the match ended in sadness. AP Argentina became the first team in a World Cup final to go without a single shot in regulation time, the only two thereafter coming in a desperate chase for an equaliser. Evidently, their manager Lionel Scaloni watched Spain’s phenomenal shutout of France in the semi-final and reached the conclusion that his team had no chance of going toe-to-toe with them. So they elected not to bother.



From minute one, they played to defend, they sought to frustrate, they tried to deceive the referee - hoping that at some point, their captain and inspiration Lionel Messi would conjure something to win it for them and end their suffering. It’s often said that Messi is capable of making something out of nothing. But not even he can make something out of less than nothing, or work from negative space. The Spanish are about control, suffocation, overwhelming the opponent. You cannot hurt them if you don’t have the ball. Celebrations are under way in Madrid following Spain’s World Cup win. Getty Images In the end, this was a decisive triumph for the collective over the individual. No single star won them this World Cup; it was a squad of 26, and a national playing pool of thousands. As a country, Spain has built arguably the most complete and effective football ecosystem ever seen. Their methodology is almost faultless. They are now the first nation to hold the men’s and women’s World Cup trophies simultaneously – along with everything else they’ve won. And they will continue to win until someone figures out how to stop them, assuming there is a way to interrupt this machine.



Argentina, in contrast, have for years been a team (and a country) organised around and geared towards the service of Messi. Tactically, physically, spiritually. You can surely understand why: even at 39, the guy is a freak, and continues to win games off his own boot. He did it only a few days ago. If you have that kind of legendary superpower on your team, you have to try to maximise it. But that sort of strategy, when matched against the ultimate team unit, does have its limits. Spain’s Ferran Torres celebrates scoring the winner. AP Photo/Julio Cortez In a way, we all suffered, because this was such a tough watch. As a spectacle, it was unworthy of the early Australian alarm. All those who think football is a boring game would have felt justified for thinking so after seeing La Roja probe unsuccessfully for openings so long, their blunt play evoking the famous Simpsons parody, which still holds up: “Half-back passes to the centre, back to the wing, back to the centre … centre holds it. Holds it! Holds it!” Indeed, there is another kind of suffering: the agony of domination without reward. Of creating chance after chance, only to find an outstretched palm, leg or thigh in the way, or to hear a referee’s whistle stopping the action. Martinez made a staggering 11 saves, yet many of the shots he faced came directly at him. But for some sharper finishing, we all would have been put out of our misery much sooner – Argentina included.



Related Article Live

FIFA World Cup FIFA World Cup 2026 LIVE updates: Spain win 2026 World Cup final after defeating Argentina 1-0 in extra time Credit to them, though, for some phenomenal scrambling defence, which continued despite losing both of their starting centre-backs, Lisandro Martinez and Cristian Romero, to injury, and after being reduced to 10 men with Enzo Fernandez’s second yellow card in the 93rd minute. This frustration could have driven Spain mad; it did, for a while, feel like it was going to be one of those games where the ball refuses to go in. To silence that little voice of doubt, you have to actively resist negative thoughts and persist in the belief that the ball will fall for you, sooner or later. Eventually, it did. Argentina kicked off the second half of extra time but lost possession. From deep in defence, near the corner flag on the left-hand side, Spain pieced together a glorious move, shifting the ball in six passes to the opposite corner, where Pedro Porro’s cross was headed back inside by Nico Williams and then thumped in by Ferran Torres. Pure ecstasy. No more suffering; not for them. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

Analysis CultureMusicFIFA World Cup ‘Like a bad trip’: Oasis legend joins roast of World Cup final half-time show Robert Moran July 20, 2026 — 7:49am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The World Cup final delivered the game’s first half-time show ever – and hopefully the last, judging by reactions from pundits and celebrities. Former England striker Wayne Rooney, broadcasting for BBC Sport, said the best part of the performance – which featured Madonna, Justin Bieber and the Muppets – was when it finished. “I like a lot of them artists but I thought it was crap,” he said. What a way to begin! Madonna on the big screen during the half-time show. AP Photo/Frank Franklin II Oasis frontman Liam Gallagher approved of Bieber’s set – “Justin rules,” he posted on X – but he wasn’t so fond of the rest of it. “This is like a bad trip,” he posted. “It’s a good job I’ve got my spiritual socks on or that half-time entertainment could have tipped me over the edge.”



After a nervy first half, viewers were given a fever dream of a half-time performance – one that lasted a record 27 minutes and 22 seconds – to relieve the tension. But this was no Super Bowl level extravaganza. View post on X Madonna opened up the show singing her hit Music from an underground rollerskating rink, in a car being driven by Brazilian legends Ronaldinho and Ronaldo. Before you could even crack a joke about their tracksuits, the action whiplashed elsewhere. Then it was a sudden shift to the Muppets, with composer Gustavo Dudamel doing the White Stripes’ iconic Seven Nation Army. It must’ve had Jack White turning in his grave (because he sleeps in a coffin, probably). Miss Piggy, Kermit the Frog and other Muppets performed during the half-time show. Getty Images



The Ted Lasso cast join the performance. AP Photo/Reed Hoffmann K-pop icons BTS, in all red, slipped into their smash Dynamite, before they got interrupted by Ted Lasso stars Jason Sudeikis and Brendan Hunt, who subbed in edgy Hillsong priest Justin Bieber and his acoustic guitar for a chilled out Everything Hallelujah. Colombian star Shakira brought some appropriate World Cup energy, performing the tournament’s anthem Dai Dai with Burna Boy. What would FIFA do without Shakira? Probably a whole show with the Muppets. Tom Cruise addresses the crowd before the game. Getty Images It’s no Beauty and a Beat, but it’s Justin Bieber we got. Getty



Post Malone donned a cheeky shirt for the opening ceremony: “I just hope both teams have fun”. Getty Images Before the game, Tom Cruise, dressed like a backstage roadie, delivered a stirring speech from the middle of the pitch like he was the Gandalf of futbol. “Football is a language spoken without words, a force that unites people, that turns strangers to friends,” he said, before announcing the teams – “Espana y Argentina” – with all the cultural respect of an SBS commentator. Shakira dances on the stage. Getty Images Post Malone also popped up in a cowboy hat and the tightest Canadian tuxedo you’ll see, performing his new song Chrome Heartbreaker, a return to his rap roots after going country, before bringing out Swae Lee for the Spiderverse hit Sunflowers.



It all made about as much sense as the phrase “New York New Jersey”. Let us never revisit this again. Spotted in the stands for the game were A-listers including Will Ferrell, Pharrell Williams, Adrien Brody, Matt Damon (with his Argentinian wife Luciana Barroso), Trevor Noah in a Spain shirt, and San Antonio Spurs superstar Victor Wembanyama. News, results and expert analysis from the weekend of sport sent every Monday.

World.title: Authorities had 'concerns' with LynnMall terrorist five years before attack
World.content:
The Coroners Court has heard details about the LynnMall terrorist's first interaction with New Zealand authorities.

Ahamed Samsudeen stabbed six people in a West Auckland supermarket in 2021, before being shot dead by police.

Phases two and three of a coronial inquest into his death are underway in Auckland, looking at Samsudeen's path to violent extremism as well as the time leading up to the attack, and his attitudes towards women.

The court heard on Monday from Detective Superintendent Sean Hansen, who was part of the police's National Security Group at the time. He provided details of the first interaction Samsudeen had with police.

Authorities were alerted to Samsudeen after finding an account on social media in March 2016 under the name Aathill Al-Ceyloni Al-Moori.

The account had posted photographs and videos of graphic violence against Muslims on its public page, along with comments supporting violent extremism and ISIL (Islamic State, or ISIS) terrorist attacks overseas.

That prompted a visit from police to assess Samsudeen's level of risk, as well as give him a verbal warning.

"The first visit, it was assessed that we had some concerns about him and his responses didn't give us a sense that he was likely to stop having those views," Hansen said

"He presented somewhat of a threat."

But a second visit in May that year, Hansen said, appeared more successful.

"He gave the staff that dealt with him at the time a sense that he had acknowledged that what he was doing was wrong, and that he was pulling away from that, and gave them some confidence that we didn't need to undertake any further follow-up with him," he said.

"It was a judgement call by the staff at the time."

Ahamed Samsudeen visiting the New Lynn Woolworths about a month prior to the attack. Supplied

That success was short-lived however, with police learning in October that Samsudeen had reopened his Facebook account and posted more material.

He was finally arrested in 2017 at Auckland Airport, with the Security Intelligence Service believing he was travelling to Syria to join ISIL fighters there.

While in prison, Hansen said Samsudeen was obstructive towards staff.

"When we went to visit him in prison, he refused to come out of his cell," Hansen said. "He called obscenities, he really refused to engage with us at all."

As a result, police started pulling back from attempts to physically see Samsudeen, to see if there were other ways they could work with or around him.

Police were still trying to engage with Samsudeen when he was released from prison in 2018 and bailed to a mosque, Hansen said.

"We had some, probably call them transactional visits in terms of getting a passport. We assisted Corrections at times in terms of finding him accommodation.

"Really, what our efforts throughout this period - and they continued through - was to do as much as we could to put him in an environment where he would then cooperate and engage with us so we could start some disengagement work."

But Samsudeen was back in prison by August 2018, where he would stay until his release seven weeks before the attack.

Hansen said shortly before his release, Samsudeen stopped engaging with police altogether.

He was asked by the lawyer representing police, Alysha McClintock, if the mosque Samsudeen stayed at in the time before the attack in 2021 had been told about his level of risk.

"As I understand from the staff, the degree of risk that he posed was conveyed, and why he had been in prison had been conveyed."

Hansen said the best outcome for the country was a preventive one, but did not know if prevention should sit with any one agency.

"We are firmly of the view the best long-term outcome for New Zealand in terms of violent extremism and terrorism is a preventive one.

"I've seen the carnage in Australia and the UK in particular with the impact of imprisoning people for long periods of time - it presents them with some very difficult issues when they come out of prison."

World.title: 'Everyone trips over the acronym': Name change considered for giant free trade pact
World.content:
A change of name for the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership is on the agenda for a senior officials meeting taking place in Vietnam this week.

The 12 nation free trade agreement featuring the likes of New Zealand, Australia, Japan and the UK, has its origins in the Trans Pacific Partnership, or TPP, formed back in 2016.

It evolved into the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership or CPTPP when Donald Trump withdrew the US from the original TPP agreement in 2017.

The change of name was long overdue, according to a global trade expert, who has put forward some ideas for officials to ponder, as the widely used acronym of CPTPP was more than a mouthful for many and made little sense given the global trade organisation's expansion to include non-Pacific nations, such as Uruguay and Britain, with others set to join.

"Everyone trips over the acronym. No one can remember what it actually stands for. It was always too complicated," head of trade policy at the Heinrich Foundation in Singapore Deborah Elms said.

She said a recent poll asking members for suggestions for a change of name,came back with a range of suggestions, with most along the lines of international or global trade partnership.

"You can imagine people's ideas. Acronyms that were things like FART, you know, all sorts of crazy suggestions."

However, she said there were other priorities for the organisation that covered goods, services, investment, intellectual property rights, standards, labour, environment, but had not been updated since 2015.

"There are folks who say, do we really want to spend our time and energy on a name change that could actually turn out to be a very long and convoluted process. And while we're doing that, we are not doing things like upgrading the digital rules. So you have to, you know, everything is a trade-off, and you have to say what are the most important priorities."

She said the agreement was currently about 600 pages of legal rules and thousands of pages of separate schedules for all of the members, which provided a level of certainty and lowered risks for businesses operating between CPTPP countries.

"There are some provisions in the original agreement that were put in because of requests of members at the time that no longer appear to apply. Those could be adjusted.

"We have some new chapters that you could usefully add. For example, we've all learned that trade in times of crisis is difficult. We could add a chapter on trade in times of crisis. We could add a chapter on supply chain resilience. We could potentially add a chapter on artificial intelligence as part of the accompanying upgrade to the digital rules, anyways."

Elms said she had also been "arguing strongly" for the creation of a secretariat to manage the organisation, which continued to grow, with 12 members, with Costa Rica about to join, and a queue of eight more countries interested.

"Four more are starting accession. And once you start to get to that level of membership, you really need to have people focused on this full time," Elms said.

World.title: Listen: Christopher Luxon slams Shane Jones over India FTA comments, brushes off poll slump
World.content:
Weekly interview with Prime Minister, Christopher Luxon Morning Report Download MP3 8m

The prime minister says comments made by New Zealand First's deputy leader about the free trade agreement (FTA) with India were "crass and unprofessional", saying his coalition partner is on the wrong side of history.

At NZ First's annual convention over the weekend, deputy leader Shane Jones criticised supporters of the deal, saying his party was "nationalist" and was speaking up for New Zealanders' interests.

NZ First does not support the deal, citing concerns over immigration and whether the clause to promote investment of $34 billion is actually a firm investment commitment with repercussions if New Zealand fails to reach that target.

Jones said he would "call out" the levels of Indian migration into New Zealand "every day, every week, every month".

"It is not foundational Kiwi culture to have foreigners running slave gangs in our kiwifruit industry, never paying tax, owing more to the IRD than the GDP of Kaitaia. Put them on the first plane and send them home."

Referring to the visit of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi the weekend prior, Jones then addressed the leaders of other parties.

"Labour Party, National Party, ACT Party, Green Party: the next time you go to an ethno-nationalist rally to receive a foreign leader, take off your knee pads. You represent the New Zealand Parliament."

AUCKLAND, NEW ZEALAND - July 11: Official photography coverage of the visit to New Zealand by the Prime Minister of India Narendra Modi. Auckland, New Zealand. (Photo by Mark Tantrum/ http://marktantrum.com) Mark Tantrum

Asked about Jones' comments on Morning Report, Christopher Luxon said he remained proud of the deal.

"Pretty crass and unprofessional comments. I'm actually super proud of our India FTA, I'm actually proud of the team and all the efforts that went into hosting a significant world leader in Prime Minister Modi, and I would have thought that we actually want all of New Zealand presenting well out on the global stage."

Similarly to comments made by ACT last week, Luxon pointed out the irony of NZ First opposing the deal while one of its ministers visited India to promote New Zealand wool.

"Frankly, it's a bit hypocritical from NZ First to be against the Indian FTA while they've got their colleague, the Associate Agriculture Minister Mark Patterson, out there in India trying to sell tariff-free New Zealand wool under the FTA to Indians.

"So at least he realises the massive economic benefits of the FTA for the people in the regions."

'I don't talk about your poll' - Luxon dismisses polling slump

Luxon was also asked about the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll result, which put National on its lowest result since he became leader.

National was at 28.7 percent, a fall of 2.1 percentage points and its fourth consecutive decline in this poll.

But Luxon dismissed the result, saying there were lots of polls and his focus was on fixing the "gnarly, hard problems" facing the country.

"I don't talk about your poll. What I can tell you is, though, that even just having come back from the States, is I reckon the US, Australia, places like that are on an economic downswing. I think New Zealand's on an economic upswing.

"We see that 14 percent growth in Kiwis coming back home from Australia last year. We've got good economic growth. You saw manufacturing expanding last week, services expanding, good levels of exports, investor-farmer confidence, and business confidence actually on the improve.

World.title: Fiji police arrest man over alleged social media threat to burn Suva
World.content:
Fiji police say a man in his 50s has been taken into custody after he "allegedly issued a threat on social media" to remove the country's 2013 Constitution or "burn the nation's capital".

In a statement on Monday, police added that investigations are continuing.

"The suspect in his 50s was questioned by investigators from the Cybercrime Division at the Criminal Investigations Department Headquarters on Sunday 19 July 2026, and remains in custody," the statement read.

This comes as the Fijian government's dual and parallel constitutional review and truth and reconciliation processes are underway.

Fijian social media users have been warned that "inciteful posts or the practice of sharing such posts" can result in them being taken to task under Fiji's criminal laws for offences such as urging political violence, criminal intimidation and malicious acts.

World.title: Tears and excitement as Spain win Football World Cup
World.content:
"Vamos" was heard from both of those cheering for Argentina and Spain.

But Spain came out on top, winning the Football World Cup final 1-0.

Inside central Auckland's Wynyard Pavilion, the whole crowd was singing, stamping.

Hundreds of people, dressed in red, knew their team were just minutes away from being world champions.

Finally, the ball found the back of the net, and the bar erupted. The loud cheering was accompanied by a person banging on a drum.

People hugged and kissed. A couple even threw their dog in the air. A man went outside to video call a family member, tears streaming down his face. The crowd of Spain supporters sang, danced, exalted.

They had watched for long, long minutes as their team had done everything bar beat Argentina.

Spain fans in Auckland CBD. RNZ / Jeremy Rees

Wearing the Iberian red of the Spanish strip, they had been exuberant, excited, then tense and silent as minutes ticked by.

"This is a team that can do everything except we don't have a Messi," said one red shirt at 80 minutes.

That was true. There were still three quarters of an hour of tension and worry to go as the game ticked down to injury time, then extra time.

It was heart stopping stuff. Endless Spanish attacks had the crowd on their feet. Then seconds later that exhalation, "Oooooh" as the shot was wide or blocked.

"España! España!", they chanted to will their team to victory.

But football is a terrible stark game. All that beauty and passing the ball through the eye of the needle means nothing when the score stands at 0-0.

And then, in minute 106, it came.

And the crowd erupted in relief, in joy, in fury, in pent up energy.

An Argentina fan reacts to Spain's game-winning goal. RNZ / Nick Monro

Up on the North Shore, there were also tears - but for a different reason at the Argentina watch party.

About 200 supporters crammed into a warehouse at Pachamama Latino Store in Glenfield to watch the game.

Proudly sporting blue and white and their Argentina kits, they cheered on their team all throughout the nail-biting game.

Fans earlier said they were confident Argentina had what it took to become back-to-back men's World Cup champions after winning the competition in 2022.

But it was not their day.

Football fans packed out Locker Room in Queenstown. RNZ / Katie Todd

Many in the crowd burst into tears at the result and embraced each other to cope with the loss of not only the title but Lionel Messi, who has indicated this would be his last World Cup match.

In Queenstown, the Locker Room sports bar erupted into scenes of equal elation and devastation as Spain locked in the win.

More than 280 fans from both sides had arrived as early as 6am, equipped with face paint and flags.

Spanish fans told RNZ they could not be more relieved or happy, while Argentinian fans said they felt their team had given it all.

World.title: Law Association says move on bill ' needs some adjustment'
World.content:
Why the Law Association is opposing planned 'move-on' orders Nine To Noon Download MP3 9m

The Law Association is raising concerns the move-on orders bill would need adjustments, saying it may risk "unfairly criminalising" what is not criminal behaviour.

The Summary Offences (Move-On Orders) Amendment Bill, whci is currently before a select committee, would give police power to ask people begging or rough sleeping to move elsewhere.

The association's Convener of the Criminal Law Committee, Julie-Anne Kincade KC, told Nine to Noon the committee was not against the intent behind the bill but felt changes were needed.

"It needs some adjustment to ensure that the right balance is struck between enabling the police to respond to disorderly behaviour without encroaching on basic human rights."

She said more importantly the bill should not be "unfairly criminalising what is currently non-criminal behaviour".

Last week Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith defended the bill on RNZ's Morning Report saying it covered behaviour that is not already in existing legislation.

He gave examples not currently covered such as people "shouting or swearing" at others on the street, people "lying in a sleeping bag on the ground, on a bench or in a doorway" and putting up a "makeshift dwelling" on a public street.

Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

Kincade referenced Goldsmith's example of a person in a sleeping bag saying the committee believed such behaviour should not be criminalised, unlike shouting or being aggressive which was disruptive.

"We just need to be careful that we don't go too far in unfairly criminalising people that actually are not causing a public disorder."

She said there should be other ways in place to deal with homelessness rather than " criminalising someone because they are lying in a sleeping bag on the street."

Kincade said there were often complex factors behind rough sleeping such as mental health issues, addiction or family violence.

The committee had also said there are currently no limitations to the distance a person can be asked to move.

"If someone is homeless and without resources, they may not be able to move the distance imposed. That may be being set up to fail."

She said the committee had also raised a concern that the current threshold for allowing police to issue a move on order is very low and should be raised.

Kincade said this would avoid the "potential for inadvertent misuse of the power" by the police and encourage them to "take care" when issuing an order.

While there is no possibility of imprisonment if a person were to refuse a move on order there is a penalty fine, something Kincade said was a "very impractical solution" in the eyes of the committee.

"It does seem nonsensical as we can imagine that there are people that they're not in a position to pay any sort of fine".

She said the committee had actually suggested the penalty be raised to imprisonment as that would then allow the court and the judge more flexibility and reflection.

"The flexibility is it allows the judge to think about something like supervision or even community work."

She said this was often the process undertaken when a person is unable to pay their fines, but it was "administratively heavy".

World.title: All Blacks shine at Eden Park while Fiji, Samoa and Tonga suffer on the road
World.content:
All Blacks captain Ardie Savea jetted out to Samoa on Sunday morning, hours after leading his team to a 40-21 win over Ireland at Eden Park.

The former Rongotai College First XV captain and head boy touched down at Faleolo International Airport less than 24 hours after ensuring the All Blacks' record at Eden Park remained intact. The All Blacks have lost at the ground since 1994.

Savea and his wife, Saskia, are in Samoa with their three children and will travel on to Fiji before returning to rejoin the All Blacks squad for the upcoming tour of South Africa.

Samoa Observer reported the family was met by Krista Liu of local car rental company Lulu, where they had arranged a vehicle for their stay. They were accompanied by Savea's parents.

Savea is originally from Suimu village.

The tough looseman is part of the new All Blacks management and leadership team, that has now recorded a clean sheet in their first Test series of 2026.

Having created history in New Zealand because of their Pasifika heritage, head coach Dave Rennie and his team won three out of three in the first leg of the Nations Championship.

Rennie, whose mother is from the Cook Islands, is the first with Pasifika heritage to be head coach of the All Blacks.

He has Fa'alogo Tana Umaga, who is of Samoan origin and the first Pasifika to be captain of the premier New Zealand side, as one of his assistants.

Savea is part of the 12 players in the current squad who have Pasifika heritage as well.

The side have recorded wins over France, Italy and Ireland in their first three home matches.

While there were some questions around how the side performed against both France and Italy, Rennie believes Saturday night's win over Ireland in front of more than 48,000 fans in Auckland showed promise of what the team can do moving forward.

Although it was a was a tense start to the match, with both teams having periods on attack, it was the All Blacks who were the most enterprising and they were rewarded with the first try, with lock Patrick Tuipulotu scoring near the posts after several phases.

Savea said post-match he was proud of the team's performance against Ireland, and applauded the squad as a whole, especially those who did not get game time, for pushing the players at trainings.

"I think for us we only can control what we can control, and that's our preparation," he said. "We knew what was at stake and the best way to prepare for them was how we turned up each day and prepared."

"Thought the lads prepared well, especially our guys that didn't get a chance. They really pushed us to the limit at trainings and when you get that and then we get a performance like that tonight, just proud of everyone in the squad."

Savea scored a try in the clash, showing his power when he picked up from the base of a scrum, following a penalty option, and bulldozed his way to the line despite tacklers hanging on to him.

All Blacks hooker Asafo Aumua scores next to the posts. Brett Phibbs / www.photosport.nz

Aumua: We're always ready'

Tough hooker Asafo Aumua was thrust into the game earlier than planned, when Cody Taylor had to leave the field in the first spell through injury.

Aumua said captain Savea had always reminded the players that as an All Black they have to be ready for the call all the time, which he said was a practical lesson for him on Saturday.

"It was tough," he said at the post-match conference. "Obviously, didn't expect to come on there early, but as All Blacks, Ardie always says we're always ready. So, yeah, just happy to get the win.

"Focusing on the next job, obviously a lineout and just took it moment by moment."

Aumua was one of the six try-scorers in the match, getting that shortly after he took the field.

"I looked at the big screen my eyes were open, but I could just see black. I did definitely put it down. I just didn't know if it was on the line or not."

He said the message from Savea was for the team to keep going, keep the ball moving and keep the opposition guessing.

"Just try and keep keep the ball moving, keep it alive, try not to give the opposition rest. It's pretty hard fitness-wise."

All Blacks head coach Dave Rennie. © Photosport Ltd 2026 www.photosport.nz

Rennie happy

Rennie said post-match the players had put in the hard work and that is beginning to show.

It was a big jump from the close two points win over France at the One New Zealand Stadium in Christchurch in the first game.

But as the first three wins wrapped up the first international calendar for the year Rennie and his team were also looking forward to the seven-match tour of South Africa, including three tests against the Springboks in South Africa and a fourth in the United States.

The reigning world champions will host matches in Johannesburg, Cape Town, Johannesburg again in Baltimore.

"They're such a good side, Ireland, as we saw tonight," Rennie admitted at the post-match conference after the Eden Park dust had settled.

"We asked a lot of questions of them and they defended really well for big parts. If you give them access into your end of the field, they can hurt you, but I thought the balance of the game was really good tonight.

"We looked after the ball really well. Our big men carried and went a little bit more direct and [we had] smarter kicking that created opportunities for us."

Rennie said the team defended well, especially on their line as Ireland had them on the backfoot time and time again during the match.

Ireland had arrived in New Zealand with two good wins under their belt - beating Australia 33-31 and Japan 36-20 in their first two Nations Championship tests.

"They came here with a lot of confidence," Rennie said.

"They have won a series here last time and they are a very experienced squad who have played a lot of footy together. We're quite a new group. These guys played the Six Nations a few months ago.

"I would have taken a one-point win, but I thought we were pretty clinical when it mattered. A lot of the hard work that we've been putting in, on and off the field, we saw it on the park today."

Blair confident

All Blacks attack coach and one of Rennie's assistants, Mike Blair said he's confident they can make history against the Springboks.

New Zealand ran in six tries off the back of some high-tempo and expansive rugby.

"Still some bits that we can do better, definitely," he told journalists after the game.

"It sounds strange to say when you put 40 points on the board, but some really pleasing stuff, some good ball movement, some good decision making.

"Once we get into the 22, I think we've got some growth there. You need variety. You've got to have the ability to play through a team, but also to manipulate a team."

South Africa have also won three first three matches in the series, beating Six Nations teams England, Scotland and Wales.

But Blair is confident the All Blacks can win the upcoming four-test series against the World Champions, which starts next month, if they keep growing and stay consistent.

Rennie will announce the 44-member tour squad next week, with at least 10 more players added to the current squad.

"It's going to be a big step up for us, so we're going to have to evolve and improve again," Blair added.

In other Nations Championship matches at the weekend, Australia managed their first win, a 57-10 win over Italy in Perth on Saturday night.

France beat Japan 42-15, South Africa thrashed Wales 43-0 while England beat Argentina 31-24.

Pacific trio lose again

Meanwhile, Fiji, Samoa and Tonga all lost their games at the weekend.

Fiji led Scotland 17-7 at halftime, following tries from captain Tevita Ikanivere, Selesitino Ravutaumada and Elia Canakaivata.

But Scottish side came back hard in the second spell and scored three of their own tries.

Flying Fijians head coach Senirusi Seruvakula said it was another tough loss, following earlier defeats at the hands of Wales and England.

He said despite preparing well during the week their bench could not function as planned.

"It showed in the first half. Our bench was not good, they did not come and lift the game and that's what the last 20 minutes showed.

"[Scotland's] bench was good and they carried the momentum of the game until the end and they never let down their pace."

Fiji finished the Nations Championship without a win.

Samoa and Tonga also gave away leads in their matches to lose in their World Rugby Nations Cup matches.

Manu Samoa led Romania 17-14 at halftime, but ended up losing by a point in Uruguay.

The Miracle Fai'ilagi captained team scored tries through Alamanda Motuga, Abraham Papali'i, Iakopo Petelo-Mapu and Fai'ilagi himself.

Romania scored five tries, one including that from Fiji-born Iliesa Lesumaitaiti Tiqe in the first half.

Tonga also suffered the same fate against Portugal, going down 32-28 to Portugal in Canada.

The Tongans managed tries through Otunuku Jr Pauta, Taniela Filimone, Telusa Veainu and captain Solomone Kata.

Portugal scored five tries, including a double to Raffaele Storti.

Both Samoa and Tonga had won a game each and lost two on the road out of their three matches.

The second round of both the Nations Cup and the Nations Championship will be held in November.

World.title: Vingegaard forced out of Tour after fracture in 'devastating' crash
World.content:
Jonas Vingegaard will undergo surgery on a fractured collarbone after his Tour de France ended abruptly with a crash near the end of the 15th stage.

The 2022 and '23 Tour champion was among a few riders who fell close to a kerb some 20 kilometres from the end of the stage. After a few moments, Vingegaard's Tour was over as he limped into an ambulance with his right arm in a sling.

"Jonas sustained a fractured collarbone and multiple abrasions," his Visma–Lease a Bike team said in a statement posted on X. "Due to the severity of the collarbone fracture, surgical intervention has been recommended and will be performed in the coming days. Join us in wishing Jonas a smooth recovery."

Vingegaard had been in second place overall behind defending champion Tadej Pogačar heading into Stage 15, which finished with a big climb.

"It is devastating that Jonas has had to leave the Tour de France," the team's sporting director, Marc Reef, said. "It was quickly clear that Jonas could not continue. He was in a lot of pain."

The 29-year-old Danish rider became one of only eight male riders to have won all three Grand Tours this year.

"I'm really sad to see Jonas crash out," the four-time Tour champion Pogacar said.

" Without him, the Tour will not be the same. "

Vingegaard's teammate Sepp Kuss and Pogačar's UAE Emirates XRG teammate Isaac Del Toro also fell but were able to continue.

Pogačar's yellow jersey group slowed down after hearing news of the crash — perhaps unsure whether he would continue or not — but resumed racing normally after a few moments when it became clear Vingegaard was out.

Before crashing, Vingegaard looked poised to attack in the 11-kilometre final climb up Plateau de Solaison in the French Alps.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"We had two riders in the breakaway and controlled the peloton," Reef said. "Jonas felt extremely good, and we wanted to go for the victory today. Unfortunately, cycling can be very cruel at times."

Del Toro finished the stage in third place behind Pogačar and stage winner Remco Evenepoel.

Evenepoel climbed to second in the standings, five minutes behind Pogačar, with Del Toro 5:58 back in third place.

Pogačar said after the stage that he and Vingegaard were woken in the early hours of Sunday morning by officials conducting unannounced anti-doping tests.

Pogačar said his test was carried out at 5am and that Vingegaard's was at 2am.

AP

World.title: Fox takes out British Open, denies Aussie after 'two perfect shots'
World.content:
Golf has been left saluting tough New Zealander Ryan Fox after the son of an All Black gun delivered the round of his life, growing ever stronger as his rivals crumbled, to lift the Claret Jug as the British Open champion.

Feeling so nervous he was barely able to hold his putter on the final green at Royal Birkdale, the popular Kiwi still managed to play the perfect 18th hole, birdieing the brute with a 12-foot putt to win the title by one shot from American Cameron Young in Monday morning's thrilling finale.

Behind the 39-year-old was a host of tales of near-misses, including Australia's Lucas Herbert, who was still hanging tough in the hunt for the crown at the famous Lancashire links as he teed off at 17, still requiring two birdies to match clubhouse leader Young on nine-under.

But an untidy penultimate hole, where the 30-year-old drove into the bushes, got bunkered with his third shot and ended up with a bogey six, followed by a par at the last, ensured Herbert could only finish on six-under, tied for sixth, four shots behind the winner.

But up ahead, Fox, son of World Cup-winning All Black flyhalf Grant Fox, proved unbreakable in his mentality, looking, as he had all afternoon, like the one golfer out there ready to dare to attack for glory.

Fox, who became only the second New Zealander ever to lift the Jug after Bob Charles 63 years earlier, had endured bad luck during the round, coming up against a bunker lip on 15 and just trickling into a fairway sand trap after a fine drive on 17, but he refused to be daunted.

After missing a 10-footer on 17 to take the lead, he drove off on 18 tied with Young, who had earlier given all the field a severe target to match after a 64, the best round of the entire day.

Australia's Lucas Herbert (pictured) fell short of the British Open title despite a gallant effort. (Getty Images: Kate McShane)

Sam Burns was also in a position to match Young's total if he could hole his birdie putt at the last, but it slid by for the overnight leader to finish third on eight under.

But Fox played a glorious approach on the final hole, the popular Aucklander, who never wastes any time on the course, then quickly knuckling down to sink the winning putt for a 68 and a winning total of 10-under, before pumping his arms in joy.

"With me, it's always been 'see a shot, hit a shot'. As soon as I start thinking about it too much, then some bad stuff creeps in," smiled Fox.

"On the last, I hit two perfect shots. I'm not sure how I hit the putt. My hands were all over the place; I was just trying to get it towards the hole somewhere. It's surreal that it went in. Yeah, 'Champion Golfer of the Year' has a pretty good ring to it."

His wife and two children were in Florida. "I spoke to my kids last night, and they said, 'Bring back a trophy'. I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them!"

Ultimately, as the sea breezes kicked up to make Birkdale a real test on the final day, with Fox being one of only three players in the final 12 groups to shoot under par, all his main rivals were far too error-prone.

That included Herbert, who, like Fox, had earlier in the week recorded a record-equalling all-time low round in a men's major championship, with a landmark eight-under 62. His four bogeys on Sunday eventually sank him.

"I can't be too upset," shrugged the Victorian, who shot a final-round 71 but just missed out on the top-five finish which would have earned him a place in all the majors next season.

"A lot of positives to take. It's my best finish in a major. I genuinely contended. I was up around the lead for the last 45 holes. There's a lot to take away from that. I've learned so much this week."

World No.1 Scottie Scheffler (67) finished tied for fourth on seven under, alongside local hero Tommy Fleetwood (68), while South African Casey Jarvis (66) and Korean Si Woo Kim (72) were alongside Herbert in fourth.

Evergreen Australian Adam Scott, at the age of 46 and in his 101st consecutive major, earned his seventh top-10 finish in an Open, with a final round 66 earning him joint-ninth position on five under.

Like everyone else, though, Herbert was delighted for Fox, who's one of the most popular performers in golf. "His manager and my caddie are really close. Yeah, the Aussies and the Kiwis tend to stick together out there, familiar breed," smiled Herbert.

AAP

World.title: Spain will receive championship rings — but they'll also be for sale
World.content:
Spain was playing for more than the World Cup trophy. They were playing for rings as well.

For the first time, FIFA is awarding rings to commemorate a championship. Title-winning teams receiving rings is a tradition in North American sports that dates back to the late 19th century, but something that isn't commonplace in other parts of the world.

With this final in the US, the move by FIFA seems to be a nod to that tradition. Players on the World Cup-winning team will get gold medals, as usual, and the captain and coach of the winning team will get temporary rings as well shortly after the title match.

Eventually, Spain will get 30 customised rings. The World Cup trophy will be on one side, while the other side will be created "to reflect the identity of the winning team," FIFA said.

Only 2,026 rings — a nod to the year — will be made, and each will be individually numbered, custom-fitted and delivered with its own certificate of authenticity. The 1,996 rings that will not go to the winning team will be on sale to the public.

FIFA has not said how much those rings will cost.

The tradition of championship rings is believed to go back to at least 1893 when the Montreal Hockey Club was awarded the Dominion Hockey Challenge Cup, the precursor to what is now called the Stanley Cup. That team also commissioned simple bands with tiny hockey sticks attached at the top.

Major League Baseball teams began giving out championship rings in the 1920s, while NBA champions have received them basically since that league's inception in the late 1940s and NFL teams have gotten them throughout the entirety of the Super Bowl era that dates to the 1960s.

Some Halls of Fame give rings out to their members, and US Olympians and Paralympians have received rings as part of the perk package that comes with representing their country on the world stage.

Rings are now commonly awarded in all US pro sports — along with a number of college, high school and even youth sports — to commemorate championships.

World.title: 'Open door to fraud': European body slams FIFA's World Cup integrity
World.content:
Europe's top human rights body has questioned the integrity of the World Cup and urged FIFA to help build a stronger framework for the 2030 edition, which will be played mostly in Spain and Portugal.

"The next crisis has already begun. It has two names: money and power," the head of the 46-nation Council of Europe wrote in an open letter to its formal working partner, FIFA, hours before the final between Spain and Argentina in East Rutherford, New Jersey.

Swiss politician Alain Berset cited FIFA suspending a ban for United States forward Folarin Balogun while under pressure from US President Donald Trump and the risk of fraud in the soccer body signing a prediction market as a World Cup sponsor.

"When the rules bend under pressure, every result is open to doubt," Berset wrote about Balogun being freed from a mandatory one-game ban to face Belgium with a quarterfinals place at stake. Belgium won 4-1.

"Political influence has also moved onto the field," said Berset, who was twice a president of FIFA's home country, Switzerland.

Folarin Balogun was allowed to play after a red card following pressure from Donald Trump. (Getty Images: Maja Hitij)

"The sanction suspended mid-tournament came after a head of state called the president of FIFA."

FIFA signed a prediction market sponsor deal in April worth a reported $US150 million ($215 million) with ADI Predictstreet, one week after the Abu Dhabi-backed company was formally created. FIFA also has other commercial deals with the gambling industry for this World Cup.

Prediction betting has been criticised as rewarding insider trading, and Berset noted that in soccer it allowed wagers to be won on "moments a single player can produce without changing the score".

"It is an open door to fraud," he wrote.

"And this World Cup has opened the door wider."

The Council of Europe (CoE) aired its concerns publicly despite having a formal working agreement with FIFA signed by its president, Gianni Infantino, in 2018.

The intergovernmental body that created the European Convention on Human Rights has a stated mission: "To promote democracy, human rights and the rule of law across Europe and beyond."

When signing the FIFA-CoE memorandum of understanding eight years ago, Infantino said: "It is a natural relationship, as we share common values and goals: transparency, accountability, integrity, safety in sport and respect for human rights, for children's rights."

Infantino and Berset met in 2024 on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.

FIFA's disciplinary ruling on Balogun was fiercely criticised by European soccer body UEFA, which said the decision "crossed a red line" in soccer's rule of law and transparency. FIFA has yet to publish documents explaining the reasoning of its disciplinary judge from the United Arab Emirates.

"A sanction suspended under pressure, within days, with no reasons given," Berset wrote, before adding other concerns about the first 48-team, 104-game World Cup.

The authority of referees is called into question. Racist abuse of players, some of it from elected officials. Betting on every pass, every card, every corner."

The next men's World Cup will be staged mostly in Europe, with Morocco also co-hosting. Three South American neighbours, Argentina, Paraguay and Uruguay, are currently scheduled to host one game each at the start of the centenary edition in June 2030 to mark the original 1930 World Cup host, Uruguay.

"So here is my proposal to FIFA," Berset wrote.

"A working dialogue that starts tonight, to build the integrity framework of the 2030 World Cup before it is played."

World.title: World Cup final ends in glory for Spain and heartache for champion Messi
World.content:
Spain has beaten Argentina 1-0 to win the 2026 World Cup, with Ferran Torres coming off the bench to score the winner in extra-time against 10-man Argentina.

Torres's goal came at the start of the second period of extra time, after a furiously tense final at the New York/New Jersey stadium in Meadowlands ended goalless after 90 minutes.

The extra time win gives Spain its second men's World Cup title, echoing the extra time goal scored by Andrés Iniesta in 2010 that gave them their first title.

And it is impossible to say the European champions didn't deserve it.

Enzo Fernández was sent off for a second yellow card in stoppage time at the end of normal time, clattering young player of the tournament Pau Cubarsí with an ugly challenge that sent the 19-year-old star flying.

The 10 men of Argentina could not hang on against the increasingly relentless attack of the Spanish.

Fernández's first yellow card was for dissent just 11 minutes prior, one of six bookings the Argentinians received in the game.

He became the sixth player ever to be sent off in a World Cup final. Argentina account for half of those dismissals, with Pedro Monzón and Gustavo Dezotti both sent off in the 1990 decider.

Spain made all the running in the game, with Argentina failing to have a single shot in the opening 90 minutes of the contest.

The level of Spain's dominance can be illustrated by the fact they completed 235 passes in the final third of the pitch, while Argentina completed just 47.

By the time the referee blew full time at the end of normal time, Spain had 15 total shots, 10 of them on target.

Emi Martínez was by far the more active of the goalkeepers, making a series of stops to deny Lamine Yamal from a free kick and a glancing header from Nico Williams.

But he could do nothing to stop Torres's strike just 37 seconds into the final 15-minute period of extra time.

That was Spain's 20th attempt on goal in the match and, up until then, Argentina had offered none.

After going behind, the defending champions attempted to bring some pressure, Lionel Messi fashioning a number of chances from the right as Spain sat back and defended.

But even the Argentine magician could not conjure a late miracle, with Argentina only finishing with two attempts at goal for the entire game, the first of which came 26 minutes into extra time, a woeful return when the trophy was on the line.

Argentina was far more intent on niggly fouls than playing football — their 25 fouls the most in a World Cup game since their 2022 victory in the final against France.

After full time, Leandro Paredes disgraced himself by starting a scuffle with celebrating Spanish players, the 32-year-old shown a posthumous red card.

The scrappy game was not helped by a 27-minute half time, the longest ever at a World Cup, to accommodate an underwhelming and poorly received Super Bowl-style show.

US President Donald Trump presented the trophy to the winners, hovering awkwardly at the side of the stage as Spain captain and player of the tournament Rodri lifted the trophy.

Look back at how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Antonelli extends F1 championship lead, heartbroken Russell crashes out in Belgium
World.content:
Kimi Antonelli has extended his lead at the top of the F1 championship standings with victory in the Belgian Grand Prix, with George Russell crashing out in the first lap and Oscar Piastri overcoming an early knock to finish fifth.

Piastri suffered minor damage to his car in the incident which saw him collide with the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc, who was cleared of wrongdoing by race officials and went on to claim second place.

And Piastri, who won this race last year, recovered well to ensure he finished in the scoring places behind Antonelli, with Max Verstappen third behind Leclerc.

Lewis Hamilton was placed fourth, but his Ferrari team are under investigation for an unsafe release, so there could yet be a change of order.

The incident followed another early controversy when Russell was forced to retire on the first lap after a prang with fellow Briton Hamilton to deal a huge blow to the Mercedes man's title hopes.

Russell, who had started third on the grid was attempting to overtake Hamilton when his rear wheel was tagged by the Ferrari driver, sending him spinning into the gravel and forcing the arrival of the safety car.

Russell drops to third in the drivers' championship and was fuming with the outcome having lost further ground on title leader Antonelli, and was once again left baffled by a mystery engine issue causing a speed deficit.

"I just got totally swallowed up down the straight, I lost three positions down the straight, down into turn five, then the incident was a racing incident," Russell told the host broadcaster.

"Maybe I could have gone a bit wider, maybe he could've braked a bit more.

"The incident shouldn't have happened if I had the speed down the straight.

"Very, very disappointing … felt like I was in a position to fight for the lead after turn one and suddenly no power and it's all gone."

Russell was bitterly disappointed with his early exit from the race. (Getty Images: Clive Mason)

The victory was the sixth of the season for teenage driver Antonelli and the first since last month's Monaco Grand Prix, which leaves him 45 points clear of Russell in the championship.

"Let's go!" he screamed to the Mercedes team over the radio.

"Thank you so much, guys, thank you."

Piastri's McLaren team-mate, Lando Norris, started 13th due to a grid penalty but he still finished seventh after a pit-stop delay.

Frenchman Isack Hadjar finished sixth behind Piastri for Red Bull, despite starting at the back of the field because of a penalty.

AAP/ABC

World.title: Brondello suspended by WNBA for inappropriate comment
World.content:
Australian coach Sandy Brondello has been suspended for one game by the WNBA for an inappropriate comment she used during a Toronto Tempo game against the Atlanta Dream.

Brondello, who coaches the Tempo as well the Opals, will miss Tuesday's AEST game against the Las Vegas Aces.

"The WNBA expects all coaches and team personnel to uphold the highest standards of professionalism and respect that are fundamental to our league," the league said in a statement announcing the suspension.

During the 111-92 loss to the Dream on Saturday AEST, the broadcast picked up Brondello addressing officials after Tempo player Nyara Sabally went down with an injury following contact with Angel Reese.

Sabally was called for the foul and Brondello could be heard saying Reese was a "protected species".

The "protected species" phrase is commonly used in Australian sports to express frustration for a lack of calls against a player.

In the US, however, the phrase can be considered derogatory towards black people.

Angel Reese took to social media in response to Sandy Brondello's comment. (Getty Images: Mark Blinch)

Brondello posted an apology on social media.

"Angel, I'm sorry," Brondello wrote on X.

"Last night, in the emotion of the moment after Nyara's injury, I used a phrase that I shouldn't have used, and I take full responsibility for that. My frustration was with the officiating, but my words unfairly put the focus on you."

How Brondello hopes to topple US No country has been able to topple the United States at either the FIBA World Cup or the Olympics since 2006. Here's what Sandy Brondello is doing to try to get Australia's Opals over the hump.

Reese took to social media after the game, posting: "ARE WE SURPRISED?!" and tagging Brondello's account, followed by a clown face emoji.

"I also understand that my words carried an impact beyond what I intended, particularly for black women in our league, and I'm deeply sorry for that," Brondello posted.

"I've spent my career competing with, coaching and learning from incredible black women."

Brondello added: "I regret that my words caused hurt to a community I respect so deeply.

"I have a lot of respect for you as both a player and a person, and I sincerely apologise to you, your teammates, and the Dream organisation for my comment."

AP

World.title: 'Why do you care how I choose to dress?': Boxer on critics of her hijab
World.content:
Australian boxer Tina Rahimi used to have a lot of nerves when she walked out to a fight.

It wasn't because she was anxious about copping a glove to the face or her own ability in throwing a punch the other way. It was because of a piece of clothing: her hijab.

"People always have something to say about the way I dress," Rahimi tells ABC Sport.

"Just go onto my Facebook, scroll through the comments. There's always just random people commenting 'You don't belong here', 'Why is she dressed like that?', 'Why is there a towel on her head?'

"It's something that I've just gotten used to over the years and learnt to block out that noise, but it's like, 'Why do you care how I choose to dress?' I'm not forcing anything on anyone. 'Do you know me?'"

Tina Rahimi says her professional debut has been a long time coming. (ABC: Monish Nand)

Rahimi says it got to the point where she does not care anymore. When she stepped out for her opening bout at the Paris Olympics, it was the most confident she had ever been.

"It was more about performing for my fight; that's where the nerves [now] really come from," she says.

Rahimi made history at the Paris 2024 Games as Australia's first female Muslim boxer to participate in the Olympics. She did so while wearing a full-coverage uniform and hijab, an Islamic head covering that the host nation had banned its athletes from wearing, which created a lot of public attention.

She was also a strong voice against France's hijab ban, writing at the time on social media: "Women have the right to choose how they want to dress. With or without hijab.

"I choose to wear the hijab as a part of my religion, and I am proud to do so. You shouldn't have to choose between your beliefs/religion or your sport."

Ahead of the Games, Rahimi did numerous podcast guest spots and had profiles written in media publications. Then at the tournament, she had microphones pointed at her face while moving around the athletes' village.

Rahimi did a lot of media around the Paris Games. (Getty: Ryan Pierse)

Regarding things Down Under, she hoped her profile would help show that Australia is a very multicultural country.

Even so, two years on, she still admits: "Oh yeah, 100 per cent, I definitely feel different [in Australia]."

In the country's current political and cultural climate regarding the prevalence of Islamophobia, the noise is always there in the background for Rahimi - and sometimes the foreground.

This May, the Australian Human Rights Commission documented a massive and sustained surge in Islamophobia, particularly in online abuse directed at visibly Muslim individuals.

The Islamophobia Register of Australia — an organisation set up to monitor incidents — recorded 366 cases of online abuse between January 2023 and November 2024, according to its latest report.

Rahimi of Team Australia was eliminated after her opening-round fight. (Getty: Ryan Pierse)

It came as Muslim community leaders raised the alarm about the rise in Islamophobia in the country.

"I feel like there's more eyes on me, and it's not always in a good way. I mean, people are just waiting for you to stuff up or to say something for them to hold against you," she says.

"You've just got to block out that noise … It's just a part of being an athlete, so people are always just going to have something to say.

" If you're winning, they're behind you; if you're losing, they're not always going to be behind you. "

She says the representation that comes with her profile is obviously "really, really good".

But admits she finds it baffling having to be on the receiving end of comments about her not being "Australian enough" when she has represented the country at the Olympics, the Commonwealth Games and World Championships.

Rahimi was a strong voice against France’s hijab ban for the Paris 2024 Games. (Getty: Ryan Pierse)

"I feel more Australian than anyone could," she says.

"So sometimes when you hear those comments, you're just like, 'Oh, what does a typical Australian look like?'

" I just feel like we've got to accept that we're not all going to look the same. I find myself a proud Australian, so people need to suck it up. "

Rahimi's religion is an important aspect of her life and part of everything she does.

She chose to put the hijab on at 18 when she was feeling closer to God and going to the mosque more.

She prays five times a day, starting before dawn for Fajr and ending with Isha before going to sleep.

"My religion has taught me that discipline, so I feel like it goes hand in hand with boxing," she says.

"I've shared rooms with a lot of female athletes (and) when they hear me or see me getting up at that time, they're like, 'wow', they understand where I've got that discipline from."

Rahimi trains at a gym in her hometown in Sydney. (ABC: Monish Nand)

Rahimi will make her professional debut later this month on July 25 against fellow Aussie boxer Sacha Dryden.

The fight is billed on the same card as Tim Tszyu vs Errol Spence's blockbuster night. It will be her first without headgear.

It has been a long time coming. Rahimi has not fought since she secured a bronze medal for Australia at the World Boxing Cup in March last year in Brazil.

Loading Instagram content

A few months after that win, she broke her hand and required surgery, sidelining her for four months.

When she was ready to box again, she worked hard on her fitness and started to reach out to promoters. She got offers here and there, but wanted it to be large event.

Rahimi was the first Muslim woman to represent Australia in boxing. (ABC: Monish Nand)

"I just kept training and training, and they said 'We'll get you on a show', and it just wasn't working out. I just didn't want to fight on any show. I wanted it to be big," she says.

"I wanted it to be something that's televised. And then we got the call from No Limit Boxing (a boxing promotions company with a broadcast partnership with Foxtel and Kayo), and we're on."

It just so happens that her return to the ring will be in her hometown of Sydney. That adds pressure, but she welcomes it.

The fight also falls nearly two years to the week since her Olympics appearance, which ended in heartbreak.

Rahimi is proud of have represented Australia. (ABC: Monish Nand)

Rahimi lost her Olympic round-of-16 bout in the Women's Featherweight (57kg) to the eventual silver medallist, Poland's Julia Szeremeta.

Immediately following this, Rahimi felt she lost her identity.

"I feel like when you're an athlete, and you dedicate your time to something, and you have that goal, and then that goal is gone, and it's finished, you have an identity crisis," she says.

"Because your identity is that athlete, it's that boxer."

She says the only way to win in the sport was to go in believing you would. So for the Olympics, she genuinely thought she would finish at the top of the podium.

"I'm thinking 'My life is going to turn around completely because I'm going to be a gold medallist,'" she says

"That's how you think … And then when things don't go your way, or you lose, you just have an identity crisis. Like, [it's] four years until the next Olympics, so what now?"

Rahimi was a makeup artist before finding boxing. (ABC: Monish Nand)

In part, it was why she set her sights on a professional debut. She needed something to chase.

"I like the process, I like the hustle, the grind … I love the way it makes me feel," she says.

"[It] makes me feel like I have a purpose, having that goal to work towards.

" I felt so lost being out for quite some time ... It just made me hungrier and made me want to work harder towards that day, towards that fight. "

When she looks back on the last five years, Rahimi does so with pride.

She knows she can be a little bit hard on herself, but it comes from self-belief.

But that reflection can come later; right now, she's focused on beating Dryden and putting on a show.

So, from here on out, I’m just going to refer to ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ by his more well-known alias, Four Tet, and the album as Wingdings. My apologies to Kieran Hebden for disregarding his intent, but I’ve got readers to consider. Also, shoutout to subscriber morgannels for bringing this one to my attention in last week’s what are you listening to thread. ʅ͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡͡(̸̢̛̼̞̭͋ͅ)̸͚̰͛̔̾̀̿͒͂:̴͓̞̑̌̂̆̊͋̀:̸͎̟̯̂̓̌ ҉ ͡ ͞ ͞ ͞ ҉● ࿀ ● ࿀ ● ҉⃝ ⃝͢ ͞ ͘ ͞⃝̕ ͢ ̛ ⃝ ̸ ̡ ͢⃝̧ ͡ ͡ ̀ ̧ ̢⃝͜ ҉ ͞ ͞ ⃝͞ ͞ ͡⃝ ⃝҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉҈҉ :̶̢͙͙͕̠̩͆(̷̮͍͚̫͚͂̍)̵̳̗̊( ̟̞̝̜̙̘̗̖҉̵̴̨̧̢̡̼̻̺̹̳̲̱̰̯̮̭̬̫̪̩̦̥ by ⣎⡇ꉺლ༽இ•̛)ྀ◞ ༎ຶ ༽ৣৢ؞ৢ؞ؖ ꉺლ For years, Hebden has kept this alias somewhat of a secret. But now that this collection of wingdings has racked up millions of listens on services like Spotify, it’s get a more formal release with wingdings. Some of the tracks here have been released previously, including track five, which Fred Again dropped during his incredible Boiler Room set as “Feelings,” under one of Hebdens’ other aliases, KH. Wingdings leans heavily towards Four Tet’s dancier outputs. And, despite what the project’s origins as some sort of secret b-side dumping ground might lead you to believe, these are not throwaways. They’re undeniable, infectious, and highly polished. Four Tet’s sense for sound design shines from crushed 8-bit drums to the hypnotic handpan grooves and sharp synth melodies. While the songs are definitely groovy and danceable, they’re not high-octane rave-ups, for the most part. Instead, tracks like number seven build to a more ecstatic and spiritual climax as layers pile up and textures demand you turn your eyes towards the sky. Not unlike last week’s recommendation, Shall We Go On Sinning So That Grace May Increase?, Wingdings is a celebration. No, I might not drop the triphop-esque track one at the club, but it’s perfect for finding your groove while trying to write, or cleaning, or any other activity where you want good vibes and grooves. Track two would feel more at home on a dance floor with its deep four-on-the-floor thump and plucked arpeggios that seem to be constantly climbing off into infinity as house hi-hats tick along. Track three blends metallic gamelan-inspired melodies and ultradeep EDM wubs, while track eight is beautiful comedown ambiance. Four Tet’s Wingdings is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, Spotify, Deezer, and Qobuz.

Following the success of its $99 Kodak-branded Snapic A1, Reto Project is releasing the Kodak EC35, an even more affordable 35mm film camera for just $34.99. The EC35 certainly isn’t fancy. The lens covers are a slightly darker shade than the rest of the camera body, giving them some nice subtle contrast.
